steps.overview: This step sets up a safe AWS account. You will lock the root user with MFA, create a separate identity for daily work, add a budget alert so you never get a surprise bill, and learn how AWS global infrastructure is organised. Root user rules, IAM best practice, Budgets and Regions/AZs/edge locations are tested heavily in CLF-C02 and appear again in every Associate and Professional exam.
objectives: Create an AWS account and secure the root user with MFA
Set up IAM Identity Center (or an IAM admin user) and use it instead of root for all daily work
Configure an AWS Budgets cost alert with email notifications and explain the Free Tier model
Distinguish Regions, Availability Zones and edge locations and choose a Region for a workload
Identify which tasks truly need the root user

concepts.explanation: The identity created with the email address used to open the account. It has complete, unrestricted access, and IAM policies cannot limit it inside its own account. Use it only for the few tasks that need it, such as changing account settings, changing the support plan, closing the account or restoring IAM access. Never create access keys for root.

A second factor on top of the password. Options are passkeys or security keys (FIDO2), virtual authenticator apps, and hardware TOTP tokens. AWS now enforces MFA for root users, and you can register more than one MFA device per user for backup. Exam answers about 'securing the root account' almost always include enabling MFA.

The AWS-recommended way for people to sign in. It works with AWS Organizations, gives users a single access portal, and issues short-term credentials. You assign permission sets (for example AdministratorAccess) to users or groups for specific accounts. It replaces long-lived IAM user passwords and access keys for human users.

An IAM user is a long-term identity inside one account, with a password and optional access keys. It is acceptable for a simple lab account but not the preferred pattern for people at scale. Grant permissions through groups and policies, and give only the access needed (least privilege). Prefer IAM roles for applications and AWS services.

A service that tracks cost, usage, Reserved Instance or Savings Plans coverage against a limit you set. Alerts can fire on actual spend or forecasted spend crossing a threshold, and they notify by email or Amazon SNS. Budget actions can go further, for example by applying an IAM policy or a Service Control Policy (SCP) to stop new spend. Use Cost Explorer to analyse past spend and Budgets to alert on future spend.

For accounts created from 15 July 2025, new customers get a credit-based free plan: sign-up credits plus extra credits for exploring services, valid for a limited period. Some 'always free' offers continue on top, such as monthly AWS Lambda requests. Usage beyond the credits or the free plan period is billed only if you move to a paid plan, but lab resources can still burn credits. Older accounts stay on the legacy 12-month Free Tier. Always check the current Free Tier page.

A Region is a separate geographic area, such as ap-south-1 (Mumbai) or ap-south-2 (Hyderabad). A Region contains multiple Availability Zones (AZs). Each AZ is one or more discrete data centres with independent power, cooling and networking, joined to the other AZs by low-latency links. Deploy across multiple AZs for high availability and across Regions for disaster recovery.

Points of presence, many more than there are Regions, used by Amazon CloudFront, Route 53 and AWS Global Accelerator to serve users with low latency. Edge locations cache content and answer DNS queries. They do not run your EC2 instances. Local Zones and Wavelength Zones are different things: they extend compute close to users.

keyFacts: Root user best practice: enable MFA, delete or never create root access keys, use root only for root-only tasks, and keep the root email and phone details secure.
IAM policies cannot restrict the root user in a standalone account; only SCPs in AWS Organizations can limit root in member accounts.
IAM is a global service; IAM Identity Center is enabled in one home Region and requires AWS Organizations.
IAM users cannot see billing data until root turns on 'IAM user and role access to Billing information' in Account settings.
AWS Budgets can alert on actual or forecasted cost; each budget supports multiple thresholds, delivered to email or SNS subscribers.
Billing data is not real time; budget evaluation runs a few times a day, so an alert can arrive hours after the spend happens.
Choose a Region by four factors: data residency and compliance, latency to users, service availability, and price.
Each Region has multiple isolated AZs (new Regions launch with at least three); AZ names like ap-south-1a are mapped differently per account, and AZ IDs (aps1-az1) are consistent.
Shared responsibility: AWS secures the cloud (facilities, hardware, global infrastructure); you secure what is in the cloud (identities, MFA, data, configuration).

example.caption: Create a USD 5 monthly cost budget with 80% actual and 100% forecasted email alerts using the AWS CLI (run as your admin user, not root)
example.code:
ACCOUNT_ID=$(aws sts get-caller-identity --query Account --output text)

cat > budget.json <<'EOF'
{
  "BudgetName": "monthly-5-usd",
  "BudgetLimit": {"Amount": "5", "Unit": "USD"},
  "TimeUnit": "MONTHLY",
  "BudgetType": "COST"
}
EOF

cat > notifications.json <<'EOF'
[
  {"Notification": {"NotificationType": "ACTUAL", "ComparisonOperator": "GREATER_THAN",
    "Threshold": 80, "ThresholdType": "PERCENTAGE"},
   "Subscribers": [{"SubscriptionType": "EMAIL", "Address": "you@example.com"}]},
  {"Notification": {"NotificationType": "FORECASTED", "ComparisonOperator": "GREATER_THAN",
    "Threshold": 100, "ThresholdType": "PERCENTAGE"},
   "Subscribers": [{"SubscriptionType": "EMAIL", "Address": "you@example.com"}]}
]
EOF

aws budgets create-budget \
  --account-id "$ACCOUNT_ID" \
  --budget file://budget.json \
  --notifications-with-subscribers file://notifications.json

aws budgets describe-budgets --account-id "$ACCOUNT_ID" --query 'Budgets[].BudgetName'

pitfalls: Using the root user 'just this once' for daily tasks, or creating root access keys. On the exam, any answer that uses root for routine work is wrong.
Assuming a budget stops spending. A plain budget only alerts; you need budget actions, or you must delete the resources yourself.
Confusing AZs with edge locations. CloudFront caches at edge locations, but EC2, RDS and subnets live in AZs.
Forgetting to enable IAM access to billing, so the admin user sees 'access denied' on the Billing and Budgets pages.
Leaving lab resources running, such as NAT gateways, idle EC2 instances, Elastic IPs or RDS instances. These quietly consume Free Tier credits or create charges.
Mixing up Cost Explorer (analyse past and current spend) with AWS Budgets (alert on thresholds) and the Pricing Calculator (estimate before you build).

workflow.title: Secure a new AWS account in one sitting

steps.label: Create the account
steps.detail: Sign up with a dedicated email address and a payment method, then choose the free or paid plan and a Support plan (Basic is free).

steps.label: Lock down the root user
steps.detail: Sign in as root, register an MFA device (preferably a passkey or security key plus a backup), and confirm that no root access keys exist.

steps.label: Enable billing access for IAM
steps.detail: In Account settings, turn on IAM user and role access to Billing information so non-root identities can manage Budgets.

steps.label: Create a daily-use admin identity
steps.detail: Enable IAM Identity Center with an AdministratorAccess permission set, or create an IAM user in an Admins group, and turn on MFA for it.

steps.label: Sign out of root, sign in as admin
steps.detail: Use the Identity Center access portal URL or the account sign-in URL, and from now on never sign in as root for routine work.

steps.label: Set the USD 5 budget alert
steps.detail: In AWS Budgets, create a monthly cost budget of USD 5 with actual and forecasted email alerts, and confirm the alert email arrives.

steps.label: Pick your home Region
steps.detail: Select a nearby Region such as ap-south-1 (Mumbai) in the console, and note its AZ IDs for later labs.

objective.question: You have just created a new AWS account for learning. Which action should you take first to protect the account?
options: Launch a test EC2 instance to confirm the account works
Change the default Region to ap-south-1
Enable multi-factor authentication (MFA) on the root user
Create access keys for the root user so you can use the AWS CLI
objective.explanation: The root user has full, unrestricted access, so protecting it with MFA is the first security step. Root access keys should never be created, and launching resources or changing Regions does nothing for security.

objective.question: A startup uses AWS Organizations and expects to grow to several AWS accounts. Developers need daily console and CLI access with short-lived credentials and one sign-in for all accounts. What should the administrator set up?
options: IAM Identity Center with permission sets assigned to users and groups
The root user with MFA, shared among the developers
A shared IAM admin user whose password is stored in a team password manager
One IAM user per developer in every account
objective.explanation: IAM Identity Center gives central sign-in across Organizations accounts, uses permission sets, and issues temporary credentials. Separate IAM users per account do not scale, and shared users or a shared root break accountability and least privilege.

objective.question: An IAM user has the AdministratorAccess policy attached but sees an access denied message on the Billing and Cost Management pages. What is the most likely cause?
options: The user is signed in to the wrong Region
The account has not enabled AWS Budgets yet
The root user has not turned on 'IAM user and role access to Billing information' in Account settings
IAM users can never view billing data
objective.explanation: Billing access for IAM identities works only after the root user activates this setting, in addition to the IAM permissions. Billing is not tied to a Region, and Budgets is not a prerequisite.

objective.question: A security team wants to stop the root user of member accounts in AWS Organizations from deleting CloudTrail trails. Which control can do this?
options: An IAM permissions boundary on the root user
A resource-based policy on the CloudTrail trail
A service control policy (SCP) attached to the member accounts or their OU
An IAM identity-based policy attached to the root user
objective.explanation: SCPs set the maximum permissions for a member account, including its root user. IAM policies and permissions boundaries cannot be attached to or restrict the root user.

objective.question: You set a budget alert at USD 5. You launch an expensive resource in the morning, but the alert email arrives in the evening. Why?
options: The alert was sent to the wrong Region
Email notifications are slower than SNS by design
Billing data is not real time, and budgets are evaluated only a few times a day
AWS Budgets only sends emails once a week
objective.explanation: Cost data takes time to process, and budget evaluation runs periodically, so alerts can arrive hours after the spend. Budgets are not weekly-only and are not Region-specific.

objective.question: A learner wants a warning before the monthly bill actually reaches USD 5, based on the current spending trend. Which budget setting should they use?
options: A forecasted cost threshold
A Reserved Instance utilization budget
A Savings Plans coverage budget
An actual cost threshold at 100%
objective.explanation: A forecasted threshold alerts when AWS predicts that month-end cost will cross the limit. An actual threshold fires only after the cost is incurred, and the RI and Savings Plans budgets track commitment use, not total spend.

objective.question: Which of these tasks can be done only by the root user?
options: Creating an AWS Budgets alert
Launching an EC2 instance in a new Region
Closing the AWS account
Creating an IAM role for EC2
objective.explanation: Closing the account is a root-only task. Roles, budgets and EC2 instances can all be managed by IAM identities that have the right permissions.

objective.question: A security review shows that the root user of an account has an active access key that was used by a script last year. What is the best action?
options: Attach a deny policy to the root access key
Keep the key but enable MFA on the root user
Delete the root access key and move the script to an IAM role or a least-privilege identity
Rotate the root access key every 90 days
objective.explanation: AWS best practice is to have no root access keys at all, so delete the key and give the script its own limited credentials. Rotating the key still leaves full-power keys in place, IAM policies cannot restrict root, and MFA does not protect access keys used by the CLI.

objective.question: Two teams in different AWS accounts agree to deploy into ap-south-1a so they share the same physical Availability Zone. Later they find their resources are in different zones. What should they use instead?
options: Edge location names
Local Zone names
AZ IDs such as aps1-az1
The Region code ap-south-1
objective.explanation: AZ names are mapped differently in each account, but AZ IDs point to the same physical zone in every account. The Region code does not identify a zone, and edge locations and Local Zones are different infrastructure.

objective.question: Which AWS service mainly uses edge locations to deliver content with low latency to users?
options: AWS IAM
Amazon EBS
Amazon RDS
Amazon CloudFront
objective.explanation: CloudFront caches content at edge locations close to users, as do services like Route 53 and Global Accelerator. RDS and EBS run inside Regions and AZs, and IAM is a global identity service.

objective.question: An Indian bank must keep customer data within India because of regulation. It is choosing an AWS Region. Which factor must be decided first?
options: The Region with the most AWS services
The Region closest to the developers' office
Data residency and compliance requirements
The Region with the lowest price
objective.explanation: Compliance and data residency are hard constraints, so they limit the options before latency, service availability and price are compared. A cheaper or feature-rich Region outside India would fail the legal requirement.

objective.question: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, which task is the customer's responsibility?
options: Replacing failed hardware in an Availability Zone
Enabling MFA and managing IAM permissions
Maintaining the global network between Regions
Physical security of AWS data centres
objective.explanation: Customers are responsible for security in the cloud, including identities, MFA, data and configuration. Facilities, hardware and global infrastructure are AWS's responsibility.

objective.question: A team wants budget alerts sent to several email addresses and also to an automated workflow that posts to a chat tool. What should they configure in AWS Budgets?
options: An Amazon SNS topic as a subscriber, with the workflow subscribed to the topic
A CloudFront distribution for notifications
An IAM policy that forwards billing data
Only an email subscriber, because Budgets supports nothing else
objective.explanation: Budgets can notify email subscribers and Amazon SNS topics, and other systems can subscribe to the SNS topic. CloudFront and IAM policies do not deliver budget notifications.

objective.question: A learner on the AWS Free Tier receives a charge after launching an EC2 instance for a lab. What is the most likely reason?
options: The instance type or usage was outside Free Tier eligibility or limits
EC2 is never covered by the Free Tier
Free Tier is available only in the us-east-1 Region
The Free Tier applies only to IAM users, not root
objective.explanation: Free Tier covers only specific services, sizes and usage levels, so a non-eligible instance type or extra usage is billed. It is not limited to one Region and has nothing to do with root versus IAM users.

objective.question: You open the IAM console to create an admin user and notice the Region selector shows 'Global'. What does this mean?
options: IAM is a global service, so users and policies apply across all Regions in the account
IAM works only in us-east-1
You must enable IAM Identity Center before using IAM
IAM users must be created separately in each Region
objective.explanation: IAM is global, so identities and policies are not tied to a Region. IAM does not need Identity Center, and you do not create users per Region.

subjective.question: Why should you stop using the root user for daily work after setting up an AWS account?
subjective.answer: The root user has complete, unrestricted access to everything in the account, including billing, account closure and changing the root email. In a standalone account, no IAM policy can limit it. If its password or keys leak, an attacker owns the account with no guardrail. Daily work also creates more chances for the credentials to leak, for example on a shared laptop. So the practice is: secure root with a strong password and MFA, never create root access keys, and use root only for root-only tasks like closing the account or restoring IAM permissions. For daily work I use an IAM Identity Center user or an IAM admin user, and later move to least-privilege roles. This also gives clear CloudTrail records of who did what.
keyPoints: Root has unrestricted access and cannot be limited by IAM policies in a standalone account
Leaked root credentials mean full account takeover
Use root only for root-only tasks
Use Identity Center or IAM identities for daily work for accountability

subjective.question: List the steps you would take to secure the root user of a new AWS account.
subjective.answer: First, I set a long, unique password stored in a password manager. Second, I enable MFA on the root user, ideally a phishing-resistant FIDO security key, with a backup device registered. Third, I check that no root access keys exist; if any do, I delete them. Fourth, I make sure the root email address is a monitored mailbox, ideally a group alias rather than one person's inbox, and that the phone number and alternate contacts for billing, operations and security are correct. Fifth, I create an admin identity for daily work and sign out of root. Finally, I note the root-only tasks so root is used only for those. In an Organization, I would also add SCPs to limit root in member accounts.
keyPoints: Strong unique password and MFA, with a backup MFA device
No root access keys
Secure, monitored root email and correct contact details
Create a daily admin identity and stop using root
Use SCPs for member accounts in an Organization

subjective.question: Compare IAM Identity Center and IAM users for human access. When would you pick each?
subjective.answer: IAM users are identities inside one account with long-term credentials: a password and optional access keys. They are simple for a single learning account but do not scale, because each account needs its own users, and long-term keys are a leak risk. IAM Identity Center is the recommended way for people to access AWS. It is enabled in one home Region, works with AWS Organizations, and gives one sign-in portal across many accounts. Access is defined with permission sets, and users get temporary credentials for the console and CLI. It can use its own directory or connect to an external identity provider like Microsoft Entra ID or Okta. I would pick Identity Center for any team or multi-account setup, and an IAM user only for a quick solo lab or a case where Identity Center is not possible.
keyPoints: IAM users have long-term credentials in a single account
Identity Center gives central sign-in and temporary credentials
Identity Center uses permission sets and works with AWS Organizations
Identity Center can connect to external identity providers
Prefer Identity Center for teams and multi-account setups

subjective.question: Explain the principle of least privilege with a practical AWS example.
subjective.answer: Least privilege means giving an identity only the permissions it needs for its task, and nothing more. This limits damage if credentials leak or someone makes a mistake. For example, a developer who only uploads files to one S3 bucket should get a policy allowing s3:PutObject and s3:GetObject on that bucket's ARN, not AmazonS3FullAccess and certainly not AdministratorAccess. In practice, I start with AWS managed policies while learning, then tighten them. Tools like IAM Access Analyzer can generate policies from CloudTrail activity and show unused permissions, and last-accessed information helps remove permissions nobody uses. I also prefer roles with temporary credentials over long-term access keys. On day one an admin user is fine for a personal lab, but it should not be the long-term pattern in a team.
keyPoints: Grant only the permissions needed for the task
Scope actions and resources tightly, for example one bucket ARN
Refine broad managed policies over time
Use Access Analyzer and last-accessed data to remove unused permissions
Prefer roles and temporary credentials

subjective.question: Walk through how you would set up a USD 5 budget alert for a learning account, and which thresholds you would choose.
subjective.answer: I open Billing and Cost Management, go to Budgets and create a cost budget with a monthly period and a fixed amount of USD 5. I then add more than one alert threshold. For example, one actual cost alert at 50 percent so I hear early, one actual alert at 100 percent, and one forecasted alert at 100 percent so I get warned if the month is trending over USD 5. I add my email as a subscriber and, if I want automation, an SNS topic. I also turn on Free Tier usage alerts in billing preferences. Because budgets are evaluated only a few times a day, I keep the thresholds low. After saving, I check that the budget appears and the notification emails are confirmed.
keyPoints: Create a monthly cost budget of USD 5
Use several thresholds, both actual and forecasted
Notify by email and optionally SNS
Keep thresholds low because alerts are delayed
Also enable Free Tier usage alerts

subjective.question: A budget alert is not a hard spending limit. Explain why, and how you would protect yourself from a large surprise bill.
subjective.answer: AWS Budgets watches costs and notifies you; by default it does not stop resources. Billing data is also not real time, and budgets are evaluated only a few times a day, so an alert can arrive hours after the spend. An expensive resource can keep running in that gap. To protect myself, I set low thresholds and a forecasted alert so I am warned early. I can configure budget actions, for example applying a restrictive IAM policy or SCP or stopping specific EC2 or RDS instances when a threshold is crossed. I also delete lab resources right after use, check Cost Explorer and the Billing dashboard regularly, stick to Free Tier eligible sizes, and use least-privilege identities so nobody can launch large resources by accident.
keyPoints: Budgets notify; they do not stop spend by default
Billing data and budget evaluation are delayed
Use low and forecasted thresholds
Budget actions can apply policies or stop some resources
Clean up lab resources and check costs regularly

subjective.question: What four factors do you consider when choosing an AWS Region? Apply them to an app for users mainly in India.
subjective.answer: The four factors are compliance and data residency, latency to users, service availability, and price. Compliance comes first because it is a hard rule. If Indian regulation or a customer contract needs data to stay in India, I must pick an Indian Region: Asia Pacific (Mumbai), ap-south-1, or Asia Pacific (Hyderabad), ap-south-2. Next is latency. Users in India get the lowest latency from an Indian Region. Third, I check that every service I need is available in that Region, because new services and features do not launch everywhere at once. Mumbai is older and usually has wider service coverage. Last, I compare prices, since they vary by Region. If no residency rule exists, I could weigh a cheaper Region, but latency for Indian users would usually make Mumbai or Hyderabad the right choice.
keyPoints: Compliance and data residency first, as a hard constraint
Latency to end users
Service and feature availability differs by Region
Price differs by Region
Mumbai (ap-south-1) and Hyderabad (ap-south-2) for Indian users

subjective.question: Explain the difference between a Region, an Availability Zone and an edge location.
subjective.answer: A Region is a separate geographic area, such as ap-south-1 in Mumbai. Regions are isolated from each other, and you choose where your resources and data live. Each Region has multiple Availability Zones. An AZ is one or more discrete data centres with its own power, cooling and networking, physically separated from other AZs but linked by low-latency networks. New Regions launch with at least three AZs. You spread resources across AZs for high availability, so one AZ failure does not take down your app. Edge locations are a separate, much larger set of sites in many cities. They do not host your EC2 instances; they are used by services like CloudFront for caching, Route 53 for DNS, and Global Accelerator to bring traffic closer to users and cut latency.
keyPoints: Region is an isolated geographic area you choose for resources
AZs are isolated data centre groups inside a Region
Multi-AZ design gives high availability
Edge locations serve CloudFront, Route 53 and Global Accelerator
Edge locations are more numerous and closer to users

subjective.question: What is the difference between an AZ name and an AZ ID, and why does it matter?
subjective.answer: An AZ name looks like ap-south-1a. AWS maps these names to physical zones independently for each account, so ap-south-1a in my account may be a different physical zone from ap-south-1a in yours. This spreads load across zones. An AZ ID looks like aps1-az1 and always refers to the same physical zone in every account. It matters when work involves more than one account. For example, if a shared service runs in one account and consumers run in another, using the same AZ ID keeps traffic in one physical zone, which reduces latency and cross-AZ data transfer cost. It also matters for resilience planning, when you want to be sure two accounts are really in different zones. You can see AZ IDs in the EC2 console or with the describe-availability-zones API.
keyPoints: AZ names are mapped per account
AZ IDs are consistent across accounts
Use AZ IDs when coordinating between accounts
Affects latency, data transfer cost and resilience planning

subjective.question: Apply the shared responsibility model to the setup tasks in this week. What does AWS handle and what do you handle?
subjective.answer: AWS is responsible for security of the cloud: the physical data centres, hardware, the network between Regions and AZs, and the software that runs services like IAM itself. I am responsible for security in the cloud. For this week's setup, that means everything about my account's identities and configuration. I must enable MFA on the root user, keep the root email secure, and avoid root access keys. I must create a non-root identity for daily work and give it sensible permissions. I must set up budgets to watch my own spending. I must choose a Region that meets my data rules. If my root password leaks because I reused it, that is my failure, not AWS's. AWS gives the tools, like MFA, IAM and Budgets, but I must turn them on and use them correctly.
keyPoints: AWS secures facilities, hardware and global infrastructure
Customer secures identities, MFA, data and configuration
Root security and IAM setup are the customer's job
AWS provides tools; the customer must configure them

subjective.question: Your finance colleague has an IAM user but cannot see the bill. Explain what needs to change and why.
subjective.answer: By default, billing pages are restricted. Even an IAM user with full permissions cannot see them until the root user enables 'IAM user and role access to Billing information' in the Account settings. This is a root-only task. It exists so the account owner decides whether anyone besides root can see costs. After root enables it, the IAM identity still needs IAM permissions for billing, for example the AWS managed Billing job-function policy for full billing work, or a read-only policy if the colleague should only view. Following least privilege, a finance person who only reviews costs should get read-only billing and Cost Explorer access, not admin. In a multi-account setup, it is usually better to give finance access through IAM Identity Center with a billing permission set in the management account.
keyPoints: Root must enable IAM user and role access to Billing information
This is a root-only task
IAM permissions for billing are still required
Give read-only billing access where possible
Use an Identity Center permission set in multi-account setups

subjective.question: Can you restrict what the root user does? Explain for a standalone account and for an account in AWS Organizations.
subjective.answer: In a standalone account, no. IAM policies, permissions boundaries and roles cannot be attached to the root user, so it always has full access. The only protection is to secure it well with MFA, no access keys, a secure email, and rare use. In AWS Organizations it is different for member accounts. Service control policies set the maximum permissions for every principal in a member account, and that includes the member account's root user. For example, an SCP can deny deleting CloudTrail trails or leaving the Organization, and even root in that member account cannot do it. SCPs do not affect the management account, so the management account's root must be guarded very carefully. AWS also offers centralized root access management for member accounts, so organizations can remove root credentials from member accounts.
keyPoints: IAM policies cannot restrict root in a standalone account
SCPs limit all principals in member accounts, including root
SCPs do not apply to the management account
Secure the management account root with extra care
Central root access management can remove member root credentials

subjective.question: What are common ways learners get unexpected bills while on the AWS Free Tier, and how do you avoid them?
subjective.answer: The Free Tier covers only certain services, sizes and usage amounts, and some offers have time limits. Common mistakes are launching an instance type that is not Free Tier eligible, leaving resources running after a lab, and forgetting things that bill on their own, like NAT gateways, Elastic IP addresses not attached to a running instance, EBS volumes and snapshots left after deleting an instance, or load balancers. Another mistake is launching resources in a Region you do not normally check, then forgetting them. To avoid this, I read the Free Tier details for each service before using it, set a low budget with actual and forecasted alerts, turn on Free Tier usage alerts, tag lab resources, and delete everything after each lab. I also check the Billing dashboard and Cost Explorer weekly, filtering by service and Region.
keyPoints: Free Tier covers specific services, sizes and limits only
Non-eligible instance types and leftover resources cause charges
Watch NAT gateways, unused Elastic IPs, EBS and snapshots
Check all Regions for forgotten resources
Use budgets, Free Tier alerts and cleanup after labs

subjective.question: You get an email saying your root password was changed, but you did not do it. What do you do?
subjective.answer: I treat it as a security incident and act fast. First, I try to sign in as root and reset the password using the root email. If I cannot, I contact AWS Support through the account recovery process. Once I am back in, I change the root password, check and re-register MFA devices, and delete any root access keys. I verify the root email, phone number and alternate contacts have not been changed. Then I review IAM for new users, roles, access keys or policies I did not create, and remove them. I use CloudTrail and the Billing dashboard to look for unknown activity, especially new EC2 instances in unusual Regions. I rotate credentials for all IAM users. Finally, I fix the cause, for example password reuse, and confirm MFA is in place.
keyPoints: Regain root access and reset the password, using AWS Support if needed
Check MFA, delete root access keys, verify contact details
Remove unknown IAM users, keys and roles
Review CloudTrail and billing for unauthorized resources in all Regions
Rotate credentials and fix the root cause

subjective.question: Design a safe starting setup for a small team of five developers who are new to AWS and will soon need separate dev and prod accounts.
subjective.answer: I would create the first account as the management account and enable AWS Organizations. I secure its root user with MFA, no access keys and a group email, and never use it for workloads. I create separate member accounts for dev and prod so mistakes in dev cannot touch prod. I enable IAM Identity Center in a chosen home Region, for example ap-south-1, create a group for developers, and assign permission sets: wider access in dev, read-only or limited deploy access in prod. Everyone signs in through the access portal with MFA and temporary credentials, so there are no IAM users with long-term keys. I add SCPs to block risky actions like disabling CloudTrail or using unapproved Regions. I set budgets per account with actual and forecasted alerts to a team email and SNS. Finally, I turn on CloudTrail across the organization.
keyPoints: Organizations with a protected management account
Separate dev and prod member accounts
IAM Identity Center with groups and permission sets, MFA and temporary credentials
SCPs as guardrails, including Region restrictions
Budgets per account and organization-wide CloudTrail

steps.overview: This step prepares you for AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02), the foundation exam on the AWS path. It covers four domains: Cloud Concepts (24%), Security and Compliance (30%), Cloud Technology and Services (34%) and Billing, Pricing, and Support (12%). The exam tests whether you can pick the right service or model for a business need, not whether you can configure it. That same vocabulary is the base for every Associate and Professional exam that follows.
objectives: Explain the benefits of cloud computing, the six Well-Architected pillars and the AWS shared responsibility model.
Choose the correct core service (EC2, S3, RDS, DynamoDB, Lambda, VPC, CloudFront, Route 53) for a given scenario.
Differentiate IAM, KMS, Shield, WAF and GuardDuty, and say which threat or task each one handles.
Compare On-Demand, Reserved Instances, Savings Plans and Spot pricing, and match support plans to customer needs.
Deploy a private S3 static website served through CloudFront using Origin Access Control.

concepts.explanation: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud: hardware, global infrastructure, facilities and the virtualisation layer. The customer is responsible for security IN the cloud: data, IAM, guest OS patching on EC2, security groups and encryption choices. The split shifts with the service type. On EC2 (IaaS) you patch the OS. On Lambda, S3 or DynamoDB (managed or serverless), AWS handles the OS and platform.

A Region is a separate geographic area, for example ap-south-1 Mumbai or ap-south-2 Hyderabad. Each Region contains multiple Availability Zones (AZs), and each AZ is one or more discrete data centres with independent power and networking. Edge locations are used by CloudFront and Route 53 to sit closer to users. You choose a Region based on compliance or data residency, latency, service availability and price.

EC2 gives you virtual servers where you control the OS, which suits long-running or custom workloads. Lambda is serverless and event-driven. You pay per request and per duration, and each invocation can run for at most 15 minutes. If a question says 'no servers to manage' or 'run code in response to events', the answer is Lambda. If it says 'full control of the OS', the answer is EC2.

concepts.term: Storage and databases: S3, RDS, DynamoDB
concepts.explanation: S3 is object storage with 11 nines (99.999999999%) durability. It offers storage classes such as Standard, Intelligent-Tiering, Standard-IA and the Glacier tiers for archives. RDS is managed relational SQL; Aurora is the AWS-built engine within RDS, and Multi-AZ provides high availability. DynamoDB is a serverless NoSQL key-value database with single-digit millisecond latency at any scale.

A VPC is your logically isolated network, with subnets, route tables and internet gateways. Security groups are stateful and work at the instance level. Network ACLs are stateless and work at the subnet level. CloudFront is the CDN that caches content at edge locations. Route 53 is the DNS service, with routing policies such as latency-based, weighted, failover and geolocation.

concepts.term: Identity and encryption: IAM and KMS
concepts.explanation: IAM manages users, groups, roles and policies, and it is a global, free service. Best practices: lock away the root user, enable MFA, grant least privilege, and use roles instead of long-term access keys. KMS creates and manages the encryption keys used by S3, EBS, RDS and other services. CloudHSM is the option when you need dedicated single-tenant hardware security modules.

Shield protects against DDoS attacks. Shield Standard is automatic and free; Shield Advanced is paid and adds the Shield Response Team and cost protection. WAF filters web requests at layer 7, for example SQL injection, cross-site scripting and rate limits, and attaches to CloudFront, ALB or API Gateway. GuardDuty uses CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs to find threats, but it detects only and does not block.

On-Demand has no commitment. Reserved Instances and Savings Plans need a 1- or 3-year commitment for up to about 72% savings. Spot uses spare capacity at up to 90% off, but AWS can interrupt it. Cost Explorer visualises and forecasts past spend, AWS Budgets alerts you against thresholds, and the Pricing Calculator estimates future workloads. Cost allocation tags split the bill by team or project.

keyFacts: Exam format: 65 questions (50 scored, 15 unscored), 90 minutes, USD 100, pass mark 700/1000. Questions are multiple choice or multiple response, and there is no penalty for guessing.
Domain weights: Cloud Concepts 24%, Security and Compliance 30%, Cloud Technology and Services 34%, Billing, Pricing, and Support 12%.
The six Well-Architected pillars are Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization and Sustainability.

Savings Plans: Compute Savings Plans apply across EC2, Fargate and Lambda in any Region or instance family. EC2 Instance Savings Plans give deeper discounts but are locked to one instance family in one Region.
Spot Instances give up to 90% off but can be interrupted with a 2-minute warning, so use them only for fault-tolerant or flexible jobs.

Support plans, from lowest to highest: Basic (free), Developer, Business, Enterprise On-Ramp and Enterprise. Business is the lowest plan with 24/7 phone support and the full Trusted Advisor check set. Enterprise On-Ramp gives access to a pool of TAMs, and Enterprise gives a designated TAM.
Fastest support response targets: Business is under 1 hour for a production system down. Enterprise On-Ramp is under 30 minutes and Enterprise is under 15 minutes for a business-critical system down.
Lambda's maximum timeout is 15 minutes. A single S3 object can be up to 5 TB. IAM is global; most other services are Regional.

AWS Artifact provides compliance reports such as SOC and ISO. CloudTrail records who made which API call, CloudWatch handles metrics, logs and alarms, and AWS Config records resource configuration history.
Quick decision rules: DDoS → Shield; SQL injection or XSS → WAF; threat detection → GuardDuty; finding sensitive data in S3 → Macie; vulnerability scanning → Inspector.

example.caption: Hands-on: a private S3 bucket served through CloudFront with Origin Access Control (OAC). The bucket stays private and only your distribution can read it. Replace ACCOUNT_ID and DIST_ID with your own values.
example.code:
BUCKET=masterclass-site-$RANDOM
aws s3 mb s3://$BUCKET --region ap-south-1
aws s3 sync ./site s3://$BUCKET   # index.html, css, images

# Create an OAC so CloudFront signs requests to S3 (keep Block Public Access ON)
aws cloudfront create-origin-access-control \
  --origin-access-control-config Name=site-oac,SigningProtocol=sigv4,SigningBehavior=always,OriginAccessControlOriginType=s3

# dist-config.json: origin = $BUCKET.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com, OriginAccessControlId,
# DefaultRootObject=index.html, ViewerProtocolPolicy=redirect-to-https
aws cloudfront create-distribution --distribution-config file://dist-config.json

# Allow ONLY this distribution to read objects
cat > policy.json <<EOF
{"Version":"2012-10-17","Statement":[{"Effect":"Allow",
 "Principal":{"Service":"cloudfront.amazonaws.com"},
 "Action":"s3:GetObject","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::$BUCKET/*",
 "Condition":{"StringEquals":{"AWS:SourceArn":"arn:aws:cloudfront::ACCOUNT_ID:distribution/DIST_ID"}}}]}
EOF
aws s3api put-bucket-policy --bucket $BUCKET --policy file://policy.json

# After updating files, clear the edge cache
aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id DIST_ID --paths "/*"
# Test: open https://dXXXX.cloudfront.net; the direct S3 URL should return AccessDenied

pitfalls: Confusing who patches what: the customer patches the guest OS on EC2, while AWS patches the infrastructure and the managed services such as RDS engines and Lambda runtimes. Physical security is always AWS's job.
Mixing up GuardDuty (detects threats), WAF (blocks web exploits), Shield (stops DDoS), Inspector (scans for vulnerabilities) and Macie (finds PII in S3). Read the verb in the question carefully.

Choosing Spot for workloads that cannot be interrupted, or Reserved Instances or Savings Plans for short, unpredictable jobs. Steady 24/7 usage points to Savings Plans or RIs; short-term or spiky usage points to On-Demand.
Using Cost Explorer to estimate a new workload's cost. Cost Explorer only analyses existing spend; the Pricing Calculator is the tool for estimates, and Budgets is the tool for alerts.
Making the S3 bucket public for the website. The secure pattern is a private bucket plus CloudFront OAC, and the exam favours least-privilege answers.
Booking the exam after a single practice test. Wait until you score consistently above 80% on several different full-length sets, and review every wrong answer against the official documentation.

objective.question: A company runs its application on Amazon EC2 instances. Under the AWS shared responsibility model, which task is the customer's responsibility?
options: Maintaining the physical servers in the data centre
Patching the hypervisor that runs the instances
Securing the physical network cables between Availability Zones
Patching the guest operating system on the instances
objective.explanation: EC2 is infrastructure as a service, so the customer manages the guest OS, its patches, the applications and security group rules. AWS handles the physical hardware, the hypervisor and the global network, which is security 'of' the cloud.

objective.question: A data team has a nightly processing job that takes about 40 minutes to finish. They want to avoid managing servers. A colleague suggests AWS Lambda. What is the main problem with this suggestion?
options: Lambda can only be triggered by API Gateway
Lambda is billed per hour, so it would be expensive
Lambda functions have a maximum timeout of 15 minutes
Lambda cannot read data from Amazon S3
objective.explanation: A Lambda invocation can run for at most 15 minutes, so a 40-minute job will be stopped. Lambda can read from S3, has many triggers, and is billed per request and duration in milliseconds, not per hour.

objective.question: A company uses EC2 today but plans to move part of its workload to AWS Fargate and Lambda, and may change Regions next year. It wants a commitment-based discount that stays useful through these changes. Which option fits best?
options: Compute Savings Plans
Spot Instances
Standard Reserved Instances
EC2 Instance Savings Plans
objective.explanation: Compute Savings Plans apply across EC2, Fargate and Lambda, in any Region and instance family. EC2 Instance Savings Plans and Standard Reserved Instances are tied to specific instance families or Regions, and Spot is not a commitment discount and can be interrupted.

objective.question: A research group runs image-rendering jobs that can be paused and restarted at any time without losing work. They want the lowest possible EC2 cost. Which purchasing option should they use?
options: Dedicated Hosts
EC2 Instance Savings Plans
Spot Instances
On-Demand Instances
objective.explanation: Spot Instances give up to 90% off On-Demand prices and suit fault-tolerant, flexible jobs; they can be reclaimed with a 2-minute warning. On-Demand and Savings Plans cost more, and Dedicated Hosts are the most expensive and used for licensing or compliance needs.

objective.question: A startup needs 24/7 phone support from AWS and access to the full set of AWS Trusted Advisor checks. It wants the lowest-cost plan that meets both needs. Which support plan should it choose?
options: Developer
Business
Enterprise On-Ramp
Basic
objective.explanation: Business is the lowest plan with 24/7 phone, chat and email access to Cloud Support Engineers and the full Trusted Advisor check set. Basic and Developer do not include 24/7 phone support, and Enterprise On-Ramp meets the need but costs more.

objective.question: A large bank wants a designated Technical Account Manager (TAM) and a response target of under 15 minutes when a business-critical system is down. Which AWS Support plan meets this requirement?
options: Enterprise On-Ramp
Enterprise
Developer
Business
objective.explanation: Only Enterprise gives a designated TAM and a response target of under 15 minutes for a business-critical system down. Enterprise On-Ramp gives access to a pool of TAMs with a 30-minute target, and Business has a 1-hour target for a production system down.

objective.question: A web application behind Amazon CloudFront is receiving requests that try SQL injection and cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks. Which AWS service should be used to block these requests?
options: AWS WAF
Amazon GuardDuty
Amazon Inspector
AWS Shield Standard
objective.explanation: AWS WAF is a web application firewall that filters HTTP requests using rules, including managed rules for SQL injection and XSS. Shield protects against DDoS attacks, GuardDuty detects threats from logs, and Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities.

objective.question: An S3 bucket was deleted yesterday, and the security team needs to find out which IAM user did it and when. Which service provides this information?
options: AWS Config
AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS CloudTrail
Amazon CloudWatch
objective.explanation: CloudTrail records API calls, including who made the call, when and from where, so it shows who ran DeleteBucket. CloudWatch handles metrics, logs and alarms, Config records resource configuration history, and Trusted Advisor gives best-practice checks.

objective.question: A healthcare company stores millions of documents in Amazon S3. It must find out which objects contain personally identifiable information (PII) such as names and phone numbers. Which service should it use?
options: Amazon GuardDuty
AWS Artifact
AWS KMS
Amazon Macie
objective.explanation: Amazon Macie uses machine learning and pattern matching to discover sensitive data such as PII in S3. GuardDuty detects threats, Artifact provides compliance reports, and KMS manages encryption keys but does not classify data.

objective.question: An auditor asks a company to provide AWS's SOC 2 and ISO 27001 reports for the infrastructure the company uses. Where can the company download these reports?
options: AWS Artifact
AWS Trusted Advisor
AWS Audit Manager
AWS Security Hub
objective.explanation: AWS Artifact is the self-service portal for AWS compliance reports such as SOC and ISO, and for agreements. Security Hub collects security findings, Audit Manager helps you collect evidence about your own resources, and Trusted Advisor gives best-practice checks.

objective.question: A company wants its application to keep running if one data centre in a Region fails, without moving to another Region. What is the recommended design?
options: Put the application in an edge location using CloudFront
Use a single instance with an Elastic IP address
Run all instances in one Availability Zone using larger instance types
Run instances in multiple Availability Zones in the same Region
objective.explanation: Each Availability Zone is one or more separate data centres with independent power and networking, so spreading across AZs survives the loss of one. A single AZ or single instance is a single point of failure, and edge locations cache content but do not run the whole application.

objective.question: A gaming company needs a fully managed, serverless database for player sessions. It stores key-value data and must give single-digit millisecond response at any scale. Which service fits best?
options: Amazon DynamoDB
Amazon S3
Amazon Redshift
Amazon RDS for MySQL
objective.explanation: DynamoDB is a serverless NoSQL key-value and document database built for single-digit millisecond performance at any scale. RDS is relational and runs on instances you size, Redshift is a data warehouse for analytics, and S3 is object storage.

objective.question: A team hosts a static website in an S3 bucket and serves it through Amazon CloudFront. They want users to reach the files only through CloudFront, and the bucket must stay private. What should they configure?
options: Attach an IAM user access key to the CloudFront distribution
Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration for the bucket
Configure CloudFront Origin Access Control (OAC) and a bucket policy that allows only that distribution
Enable S3 static website hosting and make the bucket public
objective.explanation: Origin Access Control lets CloudFront sign requests to S3, and the bucket policy allows only that distribution, so Block Public Access can stay on. A public website endpoint breaks the private requirement, CloudFront does not use IAM user keys, and Transfer Acceleration speeds up uploads only.

objective.question: A company must create its own encryption keys, control who can use them, rotate them automatically and log every use of the keys. Which service should it use?
options: AWS Certificate Manager
Amazon Cognito
AWS Key Management Service (KMS)
AWS Secrets Manager
objective.explanation: AWS KMS creates and manages encryption keys, uses key policies to control access, supports automatic rotation, and logs key use through CloudTrail. Secrets Manager stores secrets such as passwords, ACM manages TLS certificates, and Cognito handles application user sign-in.

objective.question: Which statement correctly compares security groups and network ACLs in an Amazon VPC?
options: Both are stateful and support only allow rules
Both work at the subnet level, but only network ACLs can be changed by the customer
Security groups are stateful and work at the instance level; network ACLs are stateless and work at the subnet level
Security groups are stateless and work at the subnet level; network ACLs are stateful and work at the instance level
objective.explanation: Security groups act on instances (network interfaces), are stateful so return traffic is allowed automatically, and support only allow rules. Network ACLs act on subnets, are stateless so return traffic needs its own rule, and support both allow and deny rules.

subjective.question: Explain the AWS shared responsibility model. How does the customer's share change between Amazon EC2, Amazon RDS and AWS Lambda?
subjective.answer: The shared responsibility model splits security work between AWS and the customer. AWS is responsible for security 'of' the cloud: physical data centres, hardware, the hypervisor, and the global network. The customer is responsible for security 'in' the cloud: their data, IAM permissions, network rules and encryption choices. The split moves with the service type. With EC2, I manage the guest operating system, its patches, installed software and security groups. With RDS, AWS patches the database engine and the OS, and handles backups if I enable them, but I still control who can connect, encryption settings and the data. With Lambda, AWS runs and patches the whole runtime environment, so I mainly look after my code, its IAM role and the data it handles. In every case, data, identity and access remain the customer's job. The more managed the service, the less I patch.
keyPoints: AWS: security of the cloud (hardware, facilities, hypervisor, network)
Customer: security in the cloud (data, IAM, configuration, encryption)
EC2: customer patches guest OS and applications
RDS and Lambda: AWS takes over OS and runtime patching
Data and access control always stay with the customer

subjective.question: Describe AWS global infrastructure: Regions, Availability Zones and edge locations. What factors would you consider when choosing a Region?
subjective.answer: A Region is a separate geographic area, such as Mumbai (ap-south-1). Each Region has multiple Availability Zones. An AZ is one or more discrete data centres with independent power, cooling and networking, connected to other AZs in the Region by low-latency links. Spreading resources across AZs gives high availability inside a Region. Edge locations are smaller sites used by CloudFront and Route 53 to cache content and answer DNS close to users. To choose a Region, I look at four factors. First, compliance and data residency, for example rules that data must stay in India. Second, latency, so I pick a Region close to most users. Third, service availability, because not every service or feature is launched in every Region. Fourth, pricing, since costs differ between Regions. Note that some services, such as IAM, are global, while most services, such as EC2 and RDS, are Regional.
keyPoints: Region = geographic area with multiple isolated AZs
AZ = one or more data centres with independent power and networking
Edge locations serve CloudFront caching and Route 53 DNS
Region choice: compliance, latency, service availability, pricing
IAM is global; most services are Regional

subjective.question: A client asks you whether to run a new workload on Amazon EC2 or AWS Lambda. How would you decide?
subjective.answer: I would start with how the workload runs. Lambda is serverless and event-driven. It suits short tasks triggered by events, such as an S3 upload, an API Gateway request or a message in a queue. It scales automatically, I pay only per request and execution time, and I do not manage servers. But each invocation can run for at most 15 minutes, and I have limited control over the underlying environment. EC2 gives virtual servers where I choose the OS, instance type, storage and networking. It suits long-running processes, steady traffic, legacy applications, special software or licences, and jobs longer than 15 minutes. The trade-off is that I must patch, scale and monitor the instances, and I pay while they run even if idle. So: spiky, short, event-driven work points to Lambda; long-running, steady or highly customised work points to EC2. Containers on Fargate are a middle option.
keyPoints: Lambda: event-driven, auto-scaling, pay per request and duration
Lambda maximum timeout is 15 minutes
EC2: full control of OS and software, suits long-running and steady workloads
EC2 needs customer patching and scaling; Lambda does not
Fargate as a middle option for containers without servers

subjective.question: Explain the main Amazon S3 storage classes and give a use case for each.
subjective.answer: S3 Standard is for frequently accessed data, such as website images, with low latency and data stored across multiple AZs. S3 Intelligent-Tiering automatically moves objects between access tiers based on usage, which is good when access patterns are unknown. S3 Standard-Infrequent Access is cheaper to store but charges a retrieval fee, so it suits backups that are rarely read but needed quickly. S3 One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, so it is cheaper but less resilient; use it for data you can recreate. The Glacier classes are for archives. Glacier Instant Retrieval gives millisecond access for rarely used data, Glacier Flexible Retrieval takes minutes to hours, and Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost class, with retrieval in hours, for long-term compliance records. Lifecycle rules can move objects between classes automatically. A single object can be up to 5 TB.
keyPoints: Standard for frequent access; Intelligent-Tiering for unknown patterns
Standard-IA and One Zone-IA for infrequent access, with a retrieval fee
One Zone-IA stores data in only one AZ
Glacier Instant, Flexible and Deep Archive for archives with different retrieval times
Lifecycle policies automate moves; maximum object size 5 TB

subjective.question: Compare Amazon RDS and Amazon DynamoDB. When would you choose each?
subjective.answer: Amazon RDS is a managed relational database service. It supports engines such as MySQL, PostgreSQL, MariaDB, Oracle and SQL Server, plus Amazon Aurora. It suits structured data with fixed schemas, SQL queries, joins and transactions, for example an order or billing system. AWS handles patching, backups and Multi-AZ failover, but I still pick the instance size and storage. DynamoDB is a serverless NoSQL key-value and document database. There are no servers to size, it scales automatically, and it gives single-digit millisecond performance at any scale. It suits high-traffic workloads with simple access patterns by key, such as shopping carts, session stores, gaming leaderboards and IoT data. I would choose RDS when the application needs complex queries and relational integrity, or when migrating an existing SQL database. I would choose DynamoDB when I need massive scale, predictable low latency and flexible schemas, and my queries are known in advance.
keyPoints: RDS: managed relational, SQL, joins, transactions, multiple engines
RDS supports Multi-AZ for high availability; you size instances
DynamoDB: serverless NoSQL key-value and document
DynamoDB: single-digit millisecond latency at any scale
Choose by data model and query pattern

subjective.question: Walk through how you hosted a static website on Amazon S3 behind Amazon CloudFront. What security choices did you make?
subjective.answer: First, I created an S3 bucket and uploaded the site files, such as index.html, CSS and images. I kept S3 Block Public Access turned on, so the bucket stayed private. Next, I created a CloudFront distribution with the bucket's REST endpoint as the origin and set index.html as the default root object. I set up Origin Access Control, so CloudFront signs its requests to S3. Then I added a bucket policy that allows only the CloudFront service principal, for that specific distribution, to read objects. I set the viewer protocol policy to redirect HTTP to HTTPS. For a custom domain, I requested a certificate in AWS Certificate Manager in us-east-1, which CloudFront requires, and pointed a Route 53 alias record at the distribution. Optionally, I could attach AWS WAF. The result is a private bucket, HTTPS for users, edge caching for speed, and lower S3 request costs.
keyPoints: Private S3 bucket with Block Public Access on
CloudFront Origin Access Control plus bucket policy limited to the distribution
HTTPS via viewer protocol policy; ACM certificate in us-east-1
Route 53 alias record for the custom domain
Edge caching improves speed and reduces origin load

subjective.question: What are the key IAM best practices you would apply to a new AWS account?
subjective.answer: First, protect the root user. Enable MFA on it, do not create access keys for it, and use it only for the few tasks that need root. Second, follow least privilege. Give each identity only the permissions it needs, starting small and adding more when required. Third, prefer roles and temporary credentials over long-term access keys. EC2 instances and Lambda functions should use IAM roles. Human users should ideally sign in through IAM Identity Center with federation, rather than as individual IAM users with permanent keys. Fourth, manage permissions through groups or permission sets, not by attaching policies to each person. Fifth, require MFA for human users and rotate any keys that must exist. Finally, audit regularly with CloudTrail and IAM Access Analyzer, and remove unused users and permissions. Remember that IAM is a global service, so its users, roles and policies are not tied to one Region.
keyPoints: Lock down root: MFA, no access keys, rare use
Least privilege for all identities
Use roles and temporary credentials; IAM Identity Center for people
Groups or permission sets instead of per-user policies
Audit with CloudTrail and IAM Access Analyzer; IAM is global

subjective.question: Explain encryption at rest and in transit on AWS, and the role of AWS KMS.
subjective.answer: Encryption at rest protects stored data, such as S3 objects, EBS volumes and RDS databases. Encryption in transit protects data moving over the network, usually with TLS, for example HTTPS to CloudFront or an Application Load Balancer. AWS KMS is the managed service that creates and controls the keys used for encryption at rest. Many services integrate with it, so enabling encryption is often one setting. There are AWS managed keys, which AWS creates for a service, and customer managed keys, which I create and control. With customer managed keys, I set key policies that decide who can use or manage the key, I can enable automatic rotation, and every use of the key is logged in CloudTrail. This supports audits. Under the shared responsibility model, AWS gives the encryption tools, but the customer decides to use them and controls who can access the keys. Note that S3 now encrypts new objects by default.
keyPoints: At rest: stored data; in transit: TLS/HTTPS
KMS creates and manages encryption keys and integrates with many services
AWS managed keys vs customer managed keys
Key policies, automatic rotation and CloudTrail logging of key use
Customer chooses and controls encryption settings

subjective.question: Compare AWS Shield, AWS WAF, Amazon GuardDuty, Amazon Inspector and Amazon Macie. Give one scenario for each.
subjective.answer: These services solve different security problems. AWS Shield protects against DDoS attacks. Shield Standard is automatic and free for all customers, while Shield Advanced adds stronger protection and access to the Shield Response Team; use it when a public site faces large flood attacks. AWS WAF is a web application firewall that filters HTTP requests at CloudFront, an Application Load Balancer or API Gateway; use it to block SQL injection, XSS or bad IP ranges. GuardDuty is threat detection. It analyses sources such as CloudTrail events, VPC Flow Logs and DNS logs to find suspicious activity, such as an instance talking to a known malicious IP. Inspector does automated vulnerability scanning of EC2 instances, container images and Lambda functions for known software vulnerabilities. Macie discovers sensitive data such as PII in S3 buckets. My quick rule: DDoS → Shield, web exploits → WAF, threats → GuardDuty, vulnerabilities → Inspector, sensitive data → Macie.
keyPoints: Shield: DDoS; Standard is free, Advanced is paid
WAF: filters web requests, blocks SQL injection and XSS
GuardDuty: threat detection from logs
Inspector: vulnerability scanning
Macie: sensitive data discovery in S3

subjective.question: What is the difference between AWS CloudTrail, Amazon CloudWatch and AWS Config? Give an example question each one answers.
subjective.answer: All three help with visibility, but they answer different questions. CloudTrail records API calls made in the account. It answers 'who did what, when and from where?' For example, which user stopped this EC2 instance at 2 a.m.? It is the main audit trail for security and compliance. CloudWatch is for monitoring. It collects metrics, logs and events, and lets you set alarms and dashboards. It answers 'how is my system performing right now?' For example, is CPU on my web servers above 80%, and should I trigger an alarm or Auto Scaling? AWS Config records the configuration of resources over time and checks them against rules. It answers 'what did this resource look like before, and is it compliant?' For example, when did this security group start allowing SSH from anywhere, and are all my S3 buckets encrypted? In practice, they work together: CloudTrail shows who changed it, Config shows what changed, and CloudWatch shows the effect.
keyPoints: CloudTrail: API call history, who did what and when
CloudWatch: metrics, logs, alarms and dashboards
Config: resource configuration history and compliance rules
Each answers a different question
Used together for audit, monitoring and governance

subjective.question: Design a basic VPC for a web application with a public web tier and a private database tier. Explain each component.
subjective.answer: I would create a VPC in one Region with a CIDR range, such as 10.0.0.0/16. Inside it, I would create subnets in at least two Availability Zones for high availability. Public subnets hold the load balancer. Their route table sends internet traffic to an internet gateway attached to the VPC. Private subnets hold the application servers and the RDS database, with no direct route from the internet. If private instances need outbound internet access, for example for updates, I would add a NAT gateway in a public subnet and route outbound traffic to it. For security, I would use security groups as stateful, instance-level firewalls. The load balancer allows HTTPS from anywhere, the app tier allows traffic only from the load balancer's security group, and the database allows its port only from the app tier. Network ACLs can add stateless, subnet-level allow and deny rules. Users reach the site via Route 53 and CloudFront.
keyPoints: VPC with CIDR range; subnets across at least two AZs
Public subnets route to an internet gateway
Private subnets for app and database; NAT gateway for outbound only
Security groups: stateful, instance-level, chained by tier
Network ACLs: stateless, subnet-level, allow and deny rules

subjective.question: Explain the EC2 pricing options: On-Demand, Savings Plans, Reserved Instances, Spot Instances and Dedicated Hosts. Which would you use for a mixed workload?
subjective.answer: On-Demand has no commitment. You pay by the second or hour, so it suits short-term, unpredictable or new workloads. Savings Plans give a lower price in exchange for committing to a set amount of spend per hour for one or three years. Compute Savings Plans apply across EC2, Fargate and Lambda in any Region and instance family. EC2 Instance Savings Plans give deeper discounts but are locked to one instance family in one Region. Reserved Instances are an older commitment model for a specific instance configuration. Spot Instances use spare capacity at up to 90% off, but AWS can reclaim them with a 2-minute warning, so they suit fault-tolerant batch jobs only. Dedicated Hosts are physical servers for your use, needed for some licensing or compliance rules, and are the most expensive. For a mixed workload, I would cover the steady baseline with Savings Plans, handle peaks with On-Demand, and run flexible batch work on Spot.
keyPoints: On-Demand: no commitment, flexible
Compute Savings Plans flexible; EC2 Instance Savings Plans deeper but locked
Spot: up to 90% off, 2-minute interruption warning
Dedicated Hosts for licensing or compliance
Mix: Savings Plans baseline, On-Demand peaks, Spot for batch

subjective.question: Your manager says the AWS bill is growing and nobody knows why. Which AWS cost tools would you use and how?
subjective.answer: First, I would open AWS Cost Explorer to see spending by service, account, Region and time. It shows which service is growing and gives forecasts, plus Savings Plans and rightsizing recommendations. Second, I would check whether resources are tagged, for example by project and environment, and activate cost allocation tags. Then I can break costs down by team. Third, I would set up AWS Budgets with alerts, so the team gets an email or notification when actual or forecast spend passes a threshold. Fourth, for detailed analysis, I would enable the Cost and Usage Report, which gives the most detailed billing data for tools like Athena. Trusted Advisor and Compute Optimizer can point to idle or oversized resources. If the company uses AWS Organizations, consolidated billing gives one bill and combined volume discounts. Before launching new projects, the AWS Pricing Calculator helps estimate costs in advance.
keyPoints: Cost Explorer: analyse trends, forecast, get recommendations
Cost allocation tags to split costs by team or project
AWS Budgets for alerts on actual or forecast spend
Cost and Usage Report for detailed data; Pricing Calculator for estimates
Trusted Advisor and consolidated billing in Organizations

subjective.question: Compare the AWS Support plans. Which plan would you recommend for a student testing AWS, a startup running production, and a large bank?
subjective.answer: From lowest to highest, the plans are Basic, Developer, Business, Enterprise On-Ramp and Enterprise. Basic is free, with account and billing help, documentation, forums and core Trusted Advisor checks. Developer adds business-hours email access to Cloud Support, good for testing and development. Business is the lowest plan with 24/7 phone, chat and email support and the full Trusted Advisor check set, with a response target of under 1 hour for a production system down. Enterprise On-Ramp gives access to a pool of TAMs and a target of under 30 minutes for a business-critical system down. Enterprise gives a designated TAM, a target of under 15 minutes for business-critical outages, and more proactive guidance. So for a student, Basic is enough. For a startup running production, Business is the right minimum because of 24/7 access. For a large bank with critical systems, Enterprise fits best because of the designated TAM and fastest response.
keyPoints: Order: Basic, Developer, Business, Enterprise On-Ramp, Enterprise
Business: lowest with 24/7 phone and full Trusted Advisor; under 1 hour for production down
Enterprise On-Ramp: pool of TAMs; under 30 minutes for business-critical down
Enterprise: designated TAM; under 15 minutes for business-critical down
Match plan to criticality and budget

subjective.question: Name the six pillars of the AWS Well-Architected Framework and give one practical example for each.
subjective.answer: The six pillars are Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization and Sustainability. Operational Excellence is about running and improving systems, for example using infrastructure as code with CloudFormation and making small, reversible changes. Security protects data and systems, for example least-privilege IAM, MFA and encryption with KMS. Reliability means the workload recovers from failure, for example deploying across multiple Availability Zones and testing backups. Performance Efficiency is using resources well as demand changes, for example choosing the right instance type, using serverless, or caching with CloudFront. Cost Optimization avoids waste, for example rightsizing instances, using Savings Plans for steady load and Spot for flexible jobs. Sustainability reduces environmental impact, for example removing idle resources, using managed services and choosing efficient instance types. The AWS Well-Architected Tool lets teams review a workload against these pillars and track improvements.
keyPoints: Six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, Sustainability
Reliability example: Multi-AZ and tested backups
Cost example: rightsizing, Savings Plans, Spot
Sustainability: reduce idle resources and environmental impact
Well-Architected Tool for workload reviews

steps.overview: This step prepares you for AWS Certified AI Practitioner (AIF-C01): 65 questions, 90 minutes, USD 100, pass mark 700/1000. The exam tests whether you can explain AI, ML and generative AI concepts and choose the right AWS service and technique, such as prompting, RAG or fine-tuning. It also tests responsible AI, security and governance. It is not a coding exam, but building a Bedrock knowledge base yourself makes the scenario questions much easier.
objectives: Explain the differences between AI, ML, deep learning and generative AI, and match each type of ML (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement) to a use case.
Choose between Amazon Bedrock, Amazon SageMaker AI and Amazon Q for a given business scenario.
Decide between prompt engineering, RAG, fine-tuning and continued pre-training using cost, freshness and accuracy needs.
Build a Bedrock chat that answers questions from your own PDFs using Knowledge Bases, and tune inference parameters.
Apply responsible AI and security controls using Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock, SageMaker Clarify, IAM, KMS and audit logging.

concepts.explanation: A foundation model is a large model pre-trained on huge, broad data that can be adapted to many tasks. An LLM is a foundation model for text that works on tokens, which are pieces of words. Models have a context window, the maximum number of tokens they can take in at once. Models are non-deterministic, so the same prompt can give different outputs.

Temperature controls randomness: low values give focused, repeatable answers and high values give creative ones. Top P (nucleus sampling) and Top K limit which candidate tokens the model can choose from. Maximum tokens caps the length of the response. Stop sequences tell the model where to end its output.

Prompt engineering improves output without changing the model. Zero-shot gives only the instruction. Few-shot adds examples inside the prompt, which is called in-context learning. Chain-of-thought asks the model to reason step by step. Know the prompt attacks for the exam: prompt injection, jailbreaking and prompt leaking.

RAG works in stages. Documents are split into chunks, converted into embeddings and stored in a vector database. At query time, the most relevant chunks are retrieved and added to the prompt. This grounds the answer in current, private data without retraining, and it can return citations. Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock is the fully managed AWS way to do RAG.

Fine-tuning trains a model further on labelled prompt-and-response pairs. It teaches a style, format or task-specific behaviour. Continued pre-training uses large amounts of unlabelled domain text, such as medical or legal documents, to teach domain vocabulary. Both change the model weights and cost more than RAG or prompting. Neither keeps the model up to date with fast-changing facts.

Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed, serverless service. It gives API access to foundation models from Amazon (Nova, Titan) and third parties such as Anthropic, Meta, Mistral and Cohere. Its features include Knowledge Bases, Agents (multi-step tasks that call APIs through action groups), Guardrails, Model Evaluation and model customisation. Your prompts and data are not used to train the base models.

SageMaker AI is the full ML platform for building, training, tuning, deploying and monitoring your own models. Know these features: JumpStart (pre-trained models), Canvas (no-code ML), Data Wrangler (data preparation), Ground Truth (data labelling, including human labelling), Clarify (bias detection and explainability), Model Monitor (drift detection) and Model Cards (documentation).

Amazon Q Business is a generative AI assistant for employees. It answers questions from company data through connectors and respects existing access permissions. Amazon Q Developer helps with code, AWS console questions and code transformation. Choose Amazon Q when the scenario wants a ready-made assistant with little building effort.

Guardrails apply policies to both prompts and responses. The policy types are content filters (hate, insults, sexual, violence, misconduct, prompt attack), denied topics, word filters, sensitive information filters (mask or block PII) and contextual grounding checks to reduce hallucination. One guardrail can be reused across models and applications.

AWS lists these dimensions: fairness, explainability, privacy and security, safety, controllability, veracity and robustness, governance, and transparency. Map each to a tool. Bias detection maps to SageMaker Clarify. Human review maps to Amazon Augmented AI (A2I). Documentation maps to SageMaker Model Cards and AWS AI Service Cards.

keyFacts: AIF-C01 domains and weights: Fundamentals of AI and ML 20%, Fundamentals of Generative AI 24%, Applications of Foundation Models 28%, Guidelines for Responsible AI 14%, Security, Compliance and Governance for AI Solutions 14%.
The exam has 65 questions (50 scored and 15 unscored) in 90 minutes, with a scaled pass mark of 700/1000. Question types include multiple choice, multiple response, ordering, matching and case study.

Decision rule: need current or private facts with citations, use RAG. Need a consistent style, format or task behaviour, use fine-tuning. Need domain language from lots of unlabelled text, use continued pre-training. Try prompt engineering first because it is the cheapest.
Approximate cost and effort order, lowest to highest: prompt engineering, then RAG, then fine-tuning, then continued pre-training, then training a model from scratch.

Bedrock pricing modes: On-Demand is pay per input and output token. Batch is cheaper for large offline jobs. Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity and is usually required to serve custom (fine-tuned) models.

Generative AI evaluation metrics: ROUGE for summarisation, BLEU for translation, BERTScore for semantic similarity. Classic ML metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and AUC for classification; MAE and RMSE for regression.
Overfitting means good on training data but poor on new data (high variance). Underfitting means poor on both (high bias). Fixes for overfitting include more data, regularisation and early stopping.

Security services: IAM for access, KMS for encryption, PrivateLink (VPC endpoints) for private access, CloudTrail for API audit, Bedrock model invocation logging to CloudWatch or S3, Amazon Macie to find PII in S3.

Governance services: AWS Config, AWS Audit Manager, AWS Artifact for compliance reports, and Amazon Inspector. Remember the shared responsibility model: you secure your data, prompts and access policies.
