A Bedrock knowledge base needs four parts: a data source (for example S3), an embeddings model (for example Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2), a vector store (OpenSearch Serverless, Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector and others) and a generation model.

example.caption: Query a Bedrock knowledge base built over your PDFs (Python, boto3). Replace the knowledge base ID and model ARN with your own.

pitfalls: Choosing fine-tuning to add new or frequently changing facts. Fine-tuning is costly and goes stale. For up-to-date company knowledge, the exam answer is almost always RAG with a Bedrock knowledge base.

Confusing Bedrock with SageMaker AI. Use Bedrock to call or customise existing foundation models with no infrastructure. Use SageMaker AI to build, train and host your own ML models with full control.

Mixing up the knobs. Temperature, Top P and Top K control randomness. Maximum tokens controls length. Lowering temperature does not stop hallucinations about missing facts; grounding through RAG and contextual grounding checks does.

Forgetting to enable model access. Each foundation model must be enabled in your account and Region before use. Also, the PDFs only become searchable after a sync (ingestion job) of the knowledge base.
Assuming AWS trains base models on your prompts. Bedrock does not, and this is a common exam distractor. Data is encrypted, and you can use your own KMS keys and PrivateLink.
Picking SageMaker Model Monitor for bias questions. Clarify detects bias and explains predictions. Model Monitor watches deployed models for data and quality drift.

workflow.title: Hands-on: Bedrock chat with a knowledge base over your PDFs

steps.label: Enable model access
steps.detail: In the Bedrock console, request access to an embeddings model (Titan Text Embeddings V2) and a text model (for example Amazon Nova or Claude) in one Region.

steps.label: Upload PDFs to S3
steps.detail: Create a private S3 bucket in the same Region, keep default encryption on, and upload a few of your own PDFs.

steps.label: Create the knowledge base
steps.detail: Choose S3 as the data source, select the embeddings model, keep default chunking, and let Bedrock quick-create an OpenSearch Serverless vector store.

steps.label: Sync the data source
steps.detail: Run the sync so Bedrock chunks, embeds and indexes your PDFs, then confirm the documents show as indexed.

steps.label: Test in the console
steps.detail: Ask questions in the test window and check that each answer cites the correct PDF chunks.

steps.label: Add a guardrail
steps.detail: Create a guardrail with a denied topic, PII masking and a contextual grounding check, then attach it to your chat.

steps.label: Call from code, then clean up
steps.detail: Use RetrieveAndGenerate from boto3 as in the example, then delete the OpenSearch Serverless collection to stop its charges, because it bills even when idle.

objective.question: A company wants an internal chatbot that answers employee questions from HR policy documents. The policies change every week, and each answer must cite its source document. Which approach is the MOST suitable?
options: Use Retrieval Augmented Generation with Knowledge Bases for Amazon Bedrock
Raise the temperature so the model gives more complete answers
Run continued pre-training on the HR documents
Fine-tune a foundation model on the HR documents every week
objective.explanation: RAG fetches current, private content at query time and can return citations, so weekly changes only need a data sync. Fine-tuning and continued pre-training bake knowledge into the weights, which costs more and goes stale. Temperature does not add knowledge.

objective.question: A retailer needs a model that always writes product descriptions in its brand tone and returns them in a fixed JSON structure. Careful prompting has not been consistent enough. The team has several thousand labelled input-output examples. What should they do next?
options: Run continued pre-training on unlabelled web text
Fine-tune the foundation model on the labelled examples
Switch from On-Demand to Batch inference
Add a vector store and use RAG
objective.explanation: Fine-tuning with labelled prompt-completion pairs teaches consistent style, format and task behaviour. RAG adds facts, not style. Continued pre-training uses unlabelled data to learn domain language. Batch inference only changes how requests are priced and processed.

objective.question: A developer wants the same prompt to give more predictable, less creative answers from a model on Amazon Bedrock. Which change helps MOST?
options: Remove all stop sequences
Raise top-p to its maximum value
Increase the maximum output tokens
Lower the temperature
objective.explanation: A lower temperature makes the model favour high-probability tokens, so output is more deterministic. Max tokens only controls length, and stop sequences control where output ends. A higher top-p widens the token pool and increases variety.

objective.question: A team is setting up a Knowledge Base for Amazon Bedrock over PDF files. Which component is NOT required?
options: An embeddings model such as Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2
A vector store such as Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
An Amazon SageMaker AI training job
A data source such as an Amazon S3 bucket
objective.explanation: A knowledge base needs a data source, an embeddings model, a vector store and a generation model to answer questions. No model training is involved, so a SageMaker training job is not needed.

objective.question: A company has fine-tuned a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock and now wants to use it in production. Which pricing option is usually required to run inference on this custom model?
options: Provisioned Throughput
Batch inference
Amazon EC2 Spot Instances
On-Demand pay-per-token pricing
objective.explanation: Custom (fine-tuned) models in Bedrock are usually served through Provisioned Throughput, which reserves model capacity. On-Demand and Batch are mainly for base models. Spot Instances are an EC2 option and do not apply to Bedrock models.

objective.question: A media company must summarise several million archived articles. Results are needed within a day, not in real time, and cost is the main concern. Which Amazon Bedrock option fits BEST?
options: On-Demand inference with many parallel calls
Provisioned Throughput with a long commitment
A real-time Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint
Batch inference
objective.explanation: Batch inference is designed for large offline jobs and costs less than On-Demand. Provisioned Throughput suits steady, predictable traffic or custom models. A real-time endpoint adds cost and running effort that this job does not need.

objective.question: A team is comparing two models that summarise customer support tickets against reference summaries written by humans. Which metric is MOST commonly used for this task?
options: ROUGE
AUC
RMSE
BLEU
objective.explanation: ROUGE measures overlap with reference text and is the standard metric for summarisation. BLEU is mainly used for translation. RMSE is for regression, and AUC is for classification.

objective.question: A classification model scores 98% accuracy on training data but only 70% on new test data. What is the problem, and which fix is appropriate?
options: High bias; remove regularisation
Overfitting; add more training data, apply regularisation or use early stopping
Underfitting; train for fewer epochs
Underfitting; make the model simpler
objective.explanation: Strong training results with weak results on new data mean overfitting (high variance). More data, regularisation and early stopping all reduce it. Underfitting means the model performs poorly on both training and test data.

objective.question: A bank builds a customer assistant on Amazon Bedrock. It must never give investment advice and must mask account numbers in responses. Which feature meets both needs with the LEAST custom code?
options: Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock with a denied topic and a sensitive information filter
AWS WAF rules on the API endpoint
A system prompt that asks the model to behave
Amazon Macie
objective.explanation: Guardrails can block denied topics and detect, then mask or block, PII in prompts and responses. Macie scans data stored in S3, not live model output. WAF inspects web requests, not meaning. A system prompt alone can be bypassed.

objective.question: Before loading thousands of documents from Amazon S3 into a RAG knowledge base, a security team wants to find any files that contain personal data. Which service should they use?
options: Amazon Inspector
AWS Audit Manager
AWS Artifact
Amazon Macie
objective.explanation: Macie uses machine learning to find sensitive data such as PII in S3. Inspector scans workloads for software vulnerabilities. Artifact provides AWS compliance reports. Audit Manager collects evidence for audits.

objective.question: An auditor asks which IAM users and roles called Amazon Bedrock APIs last month, and when. Which service provides this record?
options: Amazon Macie
AWS Config
AWS CloudTrail
Amazon CloudWatch metrics
objective.explanation: CloudTrail records API calls, including who made them, when and from where. Bedrock model invocation logging captures prompt and response content, which is a different need. Config tracks resource configuration changes, and CloudWatch metrics show numbers, not callers.

objective.question: A healthcare company's application runs in private subnets with no internet access. It must call Amazon Bedrock without any traffic going over the public internet. What should the architect use?
options: An internet gateway with security groups
An interface VPC endpoint (AWS PrivateLink) for Amazon Bedrock
AWS Direct Connect only
A NAT gateway
objective.explanation: A PrivateLink interface endpoint gives private access to Bedrock from inside the VPC. A NAT gateway and an internet gateway both route traffic to public endpoints. Direct Connect links on-premises sites to AWS but does not, on its own, give private subnets access to Bedrock.

objective.question: A lender wants to check its loan-approval training data for bias across age groups and explain which features drive each prediction. Which AWS service fits BEST?
options: Amazon SageMaker Clarify
AWS Audit Manager
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor
objective.explanation: SageMaker Clarify detects bias in data and models and explains feature importance. Model Monitor watches deployed models for drift. Comprehend is an NLP service, and Audit Manager handles audit evidence.

objective.question: A software team wants an AI assistant inside their IDE that suggests code, explains code and scans code for security issues. Which service should they choose?
options: Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
Amazon Q Business
Amazon Q Developer
objective.explanation: Amazon Q Developer is built for software development: code suggestions, explanations, transformations and security scans in the IDE. Q Business answers questions from company data. Knowledge Bases and JumpStart are building blocks for your own applications, not ready-made coding assistants.

objective.question: A pharmaceutical firm has millions of unlabelled research papers. A general model handles its specialised drug vocabulary poorly. The firm wants the model to learn this domain language. Which approach is MOST appropriate?
options: Fine-tuning on labelled prompt-completion pairs
Training a new foundation model from scratch
Continued pre-training on the unlabelled corpus
Prompt engineering with few-shot examples
objective.explanation: Continued pre-training uses large amounts of unlabelled domain text to teach domain language. Fine-tuning needs labelled pairs and mainly shapes task behaviour. Few-shot prompting cannot teach a large vocabulary. Training from scratch is the most expensive option and is not needed.

subjective.question: When would you use RAG, and when would you fine-tune a foundation model? Give the decision rule you follow.
subjective.answer: I always try prompt engineering first because it is the cheapest. If the model lacks knowledge, especially current or private facts that need citations, I use RAG. For example, an HR bot over policies that change every week: I update the documents, sync the knowledge base and get cited answers without retraining. If the problem is behaviour, such as a consistent tone, a fixed output format or a specific task the model does badly, I fine-tune using labelled examples. If the model does not understand the domain language at all and I have a lot of unlabelled text, I consider continued pre-training. The cost order, from lowest to highest, is prompt engineering, RAG, fine-tuning, continued pre-training, then training from scratch. The approaches can be combined. A fine-tuned model for format can still use RAG for facts.
keyPoints: Start with prompt engineering because it is the cheapest
RAG for current or private knowledge with citations
Fine-tuning for style, format and task behaviour
Continued pre-training for domain language from unlabelled text
Know the cost order; approaches can be combined

subjective.question: What is a foundation model, and how is an LLM related to it?
subjective.answer: A foundation model is a large model pre-trained on huge, broad datasets, usually with self-supervised learning. It can then be adapted to many tasks without building a new model each time. A large language model, or LLM, is a type of foundation model that works with text. It predicts the next token, which lets it write, summarise, translate, classify, answer questions and generate code. Not every foundation model is an LLM. Some generate images, such as Stable Diffusion or Amazon Nova Canvas. Others create embeddings, such as Amazon Titan Text Embeddings, and some are multimodal. On AWS, Amazon Bedrock gives API access to foundation models from Amazon and other providers such as Anthropic, Meta, Mistral and Cohere. Their key strength is general ability. Their main risks are hallucination, bias and knowledge limited to the training cutoff.
keyPoints: Pre-trained on broad data and adaptable to many tasks
An LLM is a text-focused FM that predicts tokens
Other FMs handle images, embeddings or several modalities
Bedrock offers many FMs through one API
Limits: hallucination, bias, training cutoff

subjective.question: Explain the main inference parameters you can set when calling a model on Amazon Bedrock.
subjective.answer: Inference parameters change the output without retraining the model. Temperature controls randomness. Low values give focused, repeatable answers, and high values give more creative ones. Top-p, or nucleus sampling, limits choices to the smallest group of tokens whose combined probability reaches p. Top-k limits choices to the k most likely tokens. Lower top-p or top-k makes output more conservative. Maximum tokens caps response length, which controls both cost and latency. Stop sequences tell the model where to stop, which is useful for structured output. In practice, I use low temperature for factual Q&A, extraction and RAG answers, and higher temperature for brainstorming or marketing copy. I usually tune temperature or top-p, not both at once, so I can see clearly what each change does. Supported parameters vary by model, and the Converse API gives a common way to set the main ones.
keyPoints: Temperature controls randomness
Top-p and top-k restrict which tokens can be chosen
Max tokens controls length, cost and latency
Stop sequences end the output
Low temperature for facts, higher for creativity

subjective.question: Describe the prompt engineering techniques you would use, and the prompt-related risks you would guard against.
subjective.answer: Zero-shot prompting gives only the instruction. Few-shot prompting adds a few examples, which works well for format and classification. Chain-of-thought prompting asks the model to reason step by step, which helps with multi-step problems. A good prompt has clear instructions, context, the input data and an output indicator, such as 'Answer in JSON with fields X and Y'. I also use a system prompt to set the role, and negative prompts to say what to avoid. Prompt templates keep this consistent across an application. The risks include prompt injection, where a user or a document tries to override the instructions, and jailbreaking, which tries to bypass safety rules. Prompt leaking exposes the system prompt, and poisoning places harmful content in data the model reads. To reduce these risks, I validate input, keep instructions separate from untrusted data, apply Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock, and never put secrets in prompts.
keyPoints: Zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought
Prompt structure: instruction, context, input, output format
Use templates and system prompts
Risks: injection, jailbreak, leaking, poisoning
Mitigate with Guardrails and input validation

subjective.question: Walk me through how you built a Bedrock chat with a knowledge base over your own PDFs.
subjective.answer: I uploaded the PDFs to an S3 bucket, which was the data source. In the Bedrock console, I created a knowledge base and chose Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 as the embeddings model. I let Bedrock create an OpenSearch Serverless vector store. Aurora PostgreSQL with pgvector was another option. I left the chunking strategy at the default, then synced the data source. Syncing splits the PDFs into chunks, embeds each chunk and stores the vectors. To answer questions, I used the RetrieveAndGenerate API with a generation model. It embeds the question, retrieves the most similar chunks, adds them to the prompt and returns an answer with citations. For access, I gave an IAM role least-privilege rights to S3 and the model. I tested questions whose answers I knew, adjusted chunk size and the number of results, and added a guardrail. When the PDFs change, I re-sync the data source. No retraining is needed.
keyPoints: S3 data source, embeddings model, vector store, generation model
Sync: chunk, embed, store vectors
RetrieveAndGenerate returns cited answers
Least-privilege IAM role
Tune chunking and retrieval; re-sync on updates

subjective.question: How is fine-tuning different from continued pre-training in Amazon Bedrock?
subjective.answer: Both create a custom model by changing the model's weights, but they use different data and solve different problems. Fine-tuning is supervised. It uses labelled prompt-completion pairs to teach a specific task or behaviour, such as answering in our support style or extracting fields into a fixed format. It needs a smaller, high-quality labelled dataset. Continued pre-training is self-supervised. It uses large amounts of unlabelled domain text, such as legal contracts or medical papers, so the model learns the vocabulary and patterns of that domain. It needs much more data and compute, so it costs more. In both cases, the training data stays in my S3 bucket. The custom model is private to my account, and I usually need Provisioned Throughput to serve it. Neither method is a good way to keep facts current. For changing facts, RAG is better.
keyPoints: Fine-tuning uses labelled pairs for tasks and behaviour
Continued pre-training uses unlabelled text for domain language
Continued pre-training needs more data and costs more
Custom models are private and usually need Provisioned Throughput
Use RAG, not training, for changing facts

subjective.question: Compare the Amazon Bedrock pricing modes and say when you would choose each.
subjective.answer: On-Demand charges per input and output token, with no commitment. I use it for prototypes, variable traffic and most base-model applications. Since cost depends on tokens, shorter prompts, fewer retrieved chunks and a cap on max tokens all save money. Batch inference processes a large set of prompts stored in S3 and writes the results back to S3. It costs less than On-Demand, so I use it for offline jobs such as summarising an archive overnight, where real-time answers are not needed. Provisioned Throughput reserves model capacity for a fixed period. I choose it for high, steady production traffic that needs guaranteed throughput. It is also usually required to run a custom fine-tuned or continued pre-trained model. Choosing a smaller, cheaper model that still meets the quality bar is often the biggest saving of all.
keyPoints: On-Demand: pay per token, flexible
Batch: cheaper for large offline jobs via S3
Provisioned Throughput: reserved capacity
Usually required for custom models
Control cost with tokens and model choice

subjective.question: When would you choose Amazon Bedrock and when Amazon SageMaker AI?
subjective.answer: Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed, serverless service. It gives one API to foundation models from Amazon and other providers. It also offers Knowledge Bases for RAG, Agents for multi-step tasks, Guardrails, model evaluation and simple customisation. I choose Bedrock when I want to build generative AI applications quickly without managing infrastructure. Amazon SageMaker AI is a full machine learning platform. I use it to build, train, tune, deploy and monitor my own models, including classic ML such as fraud scoring or demand forecasting. It also gives detailed control over training jobs, instance types and endpoints. SageMaker JumpStart offers pre-trained models, including open foundation models, that I can deploy and fine-tune with more control. Clarify covers bias and explainability, Model Monitor covers drift, and Model Cards cover documentation. In short, Bedrock is for consuming and lightly adapting foundation models. SageMaker AI is for full control of the ML lifecycle.
keyPoints: Bedrock: serverless API access to many FMs
Bedrock features: Knowledge Bases, Agents, Guardrails, evaluation
SageMaker AI: build, train, deploy and monitor your own models
JumpStart for deployable pre-trained models
Clarify, Model Monitor and Model Cards for governance

subjective.question: What is Amazon Q, and how do Amazon Q Business and Amazon Q Developer differ?
subjective.answer: Amazon Q is AWS's generative AI assistant family. It is built on foundation models available through Bedrock, but you use it as a finished product rather than building one. Amazon Q Business is for employees. It connects to company data sources such as S3, SharePoint, Confluence and Salesforce. It answers questions, summarises content and creates content, and it respects users' existing access permissions. Admins can control which topics it covers, and it can also be used to build simple apps. Amazon Q Developer is for builders. It works in IDEs, the command line and the AWS console. It generates and explains code, writes tests, scans for security issues, helps upgrade code, and answers questions about your AWS resources and best practices. In the exam, the key is matching the user. Employees asking questions about company knowledge need Q Business. Developers writing or fixing code need Q Developer. A custom application with its own logic is a job for Bedrock.
keyPoints: Q is a ready-made assistant, not a building block
Q Business: enterprise data connectors, respects permissions
Q Developer: IDE, CLI and console help, code and security scans
Match the service to the user type
Use Bedrock for custom applications

subjective.question: What can Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock do, and why not rely on the system prompt alone?
subjective.answer: Guardrails is a set of safety policies that apply to both user prompts and model responses. Content filters block harmful categories such as hate, insults, sexual content, violence and misconduct. They also include protection against prompt attacks. Denied topics block subjects you define, such as investment advice. Word filters block specific words or phrases. Sensitive information filters detect PII and can block or mask it, with custom regex patterns for your own data types. Contextual grounding checks flag responses that are not supported by the source material or are not relevant to the question, which helps reduce hallucinations in RAG. A guardrail can be attached to models, knowledge bases and agents, and the ApplyGuardrail API can also apply it to other models. A system prompt alone is not enough. It is only an instruction, and users can override it through prompt injection. Guardrails apply the same policy every time, outside the model.
keyPoints: Content filters and prompt attack protection
Denied topics and word filters
PII detection with block or mask
Contextual grounding checks reduce hallucination
Applied outside the model, so harder to bypass than a system prompt

subjective.question: What are the dimensions of responsible AI, and which AWS tools support them?
subjective.answer: AWS lists these dimensions: fairness, explainability, privacy and security, safety, controllability, veracity and robustness, governance, and transparency. Fairness means outcomes do not unfairly harm groups. Explainability means people can understand why a model gave an output. Veracity and robustness mean accurate results even with unexpected inputs. Transparency means users know they are dealing with AI and know its limits. The tools map to these. SageMaker Clarify detects bias and explains features. Guardrails for Amazon Bedrock supports safety and controllability. Bedrock model evaluation and human review through Amazon Augmented AI (A2I) check quality. SageMaker Model Cards and AWS AI Service Cards document intended use and limits. SageMaker Model Monitor catches drift after deployment. Practices also matter: diverse, representative and balanced data, human oversight for high-impact decisions, and choosing an interpretable model when explainability matters more than a small gain in accuracy.
keyPoints: Fairness, explainability, privacy and security, safety
Controllability, veracity and robustness, governance, transparency
Clarify, Guardrails, A2I, Model Cards, Model Monitor
Representative data and human oversight
Trade-off between interpretability and performance

subjective.question: How would you secure a generative AI application on AWS? Mention the shared responsibility model.
subjective.answer: Under the shared responsibility model, AWS secures the infrastructure and the managed Bedrock service. I am responsible for my data, prompts, access policies and how my application uses the outputs. For access, I use IAM with least privilege, for example allowing only specific model IDs to be invoked. Data is encrypted at rest with AWS KMS, using customer managed keys where needed, and encrypted in transit with TLS. For network privacy, I use AWS PrivateLink interface endpoints so traffic stays off the public internet. For auditing, CloudTrail records API calls. Bedrock model invocation logging sends prompts and responses to CloudWatch Logs or S3. Before ingesting data, I run Amazon Macie to find PII in S3. Guardrails then filters inputs and outputs at runtime. Bedrock does not use customer prompts or data to train the base models, which is an important exam point. I also protect against prompt injection and data poisoning.
keyPoints: Shared responsibility: customer owns data, prompts and access
IAM least privilege, KMS encryption, PrivateLink
CloudTrail for API audit; invocation logging for content
Macie for PII; Guardrails at runtime
Customer data not used to train base models

subjective.question: Which AWS services support governance and compliance for AI workloads, and what does each do?
subjective.answer: AWS Config records resource configurations and checks them against rules. For example, it can flag an S3 bucket holding training data that is not encrypted. AWS Audit Manager continuously collects evidence and maps it to frameworks, which makes audits easier. AWS Artifact is a self-service portal for AWS compliance reports, such as SOC and ISO reports, and for agreements. Auditors often ask for these reports. Amazon Inspector scans EC2 instances, container images and Lambda functions for software vulnerabilities. CloudTrail provides the API audit trail, and AWS Trusted Advisor gives best-practice checks. For the AI side, I add data governance: data lineage, data catalogues, retention policies and data residency. I also document models with SageMaker Model Cards. Governance also needs people and process: a review board, defined policies, human oversight and regular monitoring.
keyPoints: Config: configuration compliance rules
Audit Manager: audit evidence collection
Artifact: AWS compliance reports
Inspector: vulnerability scanning
Data lineage, Model Cards, policies and human review

subjective.question: How do you evaluate a generative AI model, and which metrics apply to which tasks?
subjective.answer: I combine automatic metrics, human review and business measures. ROUGE measures overlap with reference text and is used for summarisation. BLEU measures n-gram precision against references and is used for machine translation. BERTScore compares embeddings, so it captures meaning even when the wording differs. Amazon Bedrock model evaluation can run automatic evaluation on built-in or custom datasets. It covers measures such as accuracy, robustness and toxicity. It also supports human evaluation with my own team or AWS-managed reviewers, and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation. For RAG, I also check whether retrieval found the right chunks and whether answers are grounded in them. Automatic metrics miss tone and helpfulness, so human review matters. Finally, I track business results such as task completion, resolution rate, latency and cost per request, because a high ROUGE score alone does not prove business value.
keyPoints: ROUGE for summarisation
BLEU for translation; BERTScore for meaning
Bedrock model evaluation: automatic, human, LLM-as-a-judge
Check RAG retrieval quality and grounding
Business metrics such as resolution rate and cost

subjective.question: Explain overfitting and underfitting, and how to choose between precision and recall for a classification model.
subjective.answer: Overfitting means the model learns the training data, including its noise, too closely. It does well on training data but poorly on new data, which is high variance. Fixes are more data, data augmentation, regularisation, early stopping, or a simpler model. Underfitting means the model is too simple and does poorly on both training and test data, which is high bias. Fixes are more features, a more complex model, or longer training. For classification, accuracy can mislead when classes are imbalanced. Precision is the share of predicted positives that are correct. I prioritise it when false positives are costly, such as flagging genuine emails as spam. Recall is the share of actual positives found. I prioritise it when missing a case is costly, such as fraud or disease detection. F1 balances the two. AUC measures how well the model separates the classes across all thresholds. For regression, I use MAE or RMSE.
keyPoints: Overfitting: high variance; fix with data, regularisation, early stopping
Underfitting: high bias; fix with more complexity or features
Precision when false positives are costly
Recall when false negatives are costly
F1, AUC; MAE and RMSE for regression

steps.overview: This step covers the core of SAA-C03: VPC networking, compute, storage, databases, decoupling and resilient design. The exam has 65 scenario questions in 130 minutes, and you need 720/1000 to pass. The four domains are Secure (30%), Resilient (26%), High-Performing (24%) and Cost-Optimized (20%). Most questions ask you to pick the best service combination for stated constraints such as lowest cost, least operational overhead, or a given RTO/RPO.
objectives: Design a VPC with public and private subnets, route tables, NAT gateways, VPC endpoints, security groups and NACLs across multiple AZs.
Choose the right compute option (EC2 family, Auto Scaling, ALB/NLB, ECS/EKS on EC2 or Fargate, Lambda) for a given workload.
Select storage and database services (S3 classes and lifecycle, EBS, EFS, FSx, RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, ElastiCache) based on access pattern, durability and cost.
Decouple architectures with SQS, SNS, EventBridge and Step Functions, and match DR strategies to RTO/RPO targets.
Build and tear down a three-tier ALB → Auto Scaling EC2 → RDS Multi-AZ application without leaving billable resources behind.

concepts.explanation: A subnet is public only if its route table has a 0.0.0.0/0 route to an Internet Gateway. Private subnets reach the internet outbound through a NAT gateway placed in a public subnet. For high availability, deploy one NAT gateway per AZ and point each private route table at the NAT gateway in its own AZ. AWS reserves 5 IP addresses in every subnet.

Security groups work at the instance/ENI level. They are stateful, have allow rules only, and all rules are evaluated together. A security group can reference another security group, for example 'allow 3306 from the app-tier SG'. NACLs work at the subnet level. They are stateless, so you must allow ephemeral return ports. They support allow and deny rules, evaluated in rule-number order. Use a NACL when you must explicitly block an IP range.

Gateway endpoints support only S3 and DynamoDB. They are added as route-table targets and have no charge. Interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) create ENIs with private IPs for most other AWS services, and they are billed per hour and per GB. When a question says 'private access to S3 without traversing the internet, at lowest cost', the answer is a gateway endpoint, not a NAT gateway.

An ALB works at Layer 7 (HTTP/HTTPS). It supports path- and host-based routing, and its targets can be instances, IPs, Lambda functions or containers. An NLB works at Layer 4 (TCP/UDP/TLS). It offers static IPs per AZ, ultra-low latency and very high throughput. A Gateway Load Balancer inserts third-party virtual appliances such as firewalls. Set the ASG health check type to ELB so instances that fail the load balancer's health checks get replaced.

An Auto Scaling group launches instances from a launch template across multiple AZs and keeps capacity between min and max. Target tracking is the default choice, for example average CPU at 50%. Scheduled scaling suits known peaks, and predictive scaling suits recurring patterns. Purchase options to combine: On-Demand, Savings Plans/Reserved for steady baseline, and Spot for fault-tolerant, interruptible work.

The classes are Standard, Intelligent-Tiering (for unknown access patterns), Standard-IA, One Zone-IA (data you can re-create), Glacier Instant Retrieval, Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Glacier Deep Archive (cheapest, retrieval in hours). Lifecycle rules transition objects between classes or expire them, and IA and Glacier classes have minimum storage-duration charges. S3 is designed for 11 nines of durability.

EBS is block storage attached to an instance in a single AZ: gp3 for general use, io2 for high IOPS, st1/sc1 HDD for throughput or cold data. Instance store is ephemeral. EFS is managed NFS for Linux, mountable across AZs by many instances. FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB with Active Directory. FSx for Lustre is for HPC and ML and integrates with S3. FSx for NetApp ONTAP and FSx for OpenZFS also exist for those specific file systems.

concepts.term: RDS Multi-AZ vs read replicas vs Aurora
concepts.explanation: RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ for automatic failover. It is for availability, not read scaling. Read replicas use asynchronous replication to scale reads and can be cross-Region for DR. Aurora stores 6 copies of data across 3 AZs, supports up to 15 low-latency replicas and offers Aurora Global Database for cross-Region DR. Aurora Serverless v2 suits variable load.

DynamoDB is a serverless key-value store with single-digit-millisecond latency. It offers on-demand or provisioned capacity, global tables for multi-Region active-active, DAX for microsecond read caching, and Streams for change events. ElastiCache (Redis OSS/Valkey or Memcached) caches database query results or session state to cut read load and latency. Redis/Valkey supports replication, persistence and Multi-AZ, and Memcached does not.

SQS is a pull-based queue. Standard queues give at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering, and FIFO queues give ordering and exactly-once processing. SNS is push pub/sub; SNS-to-multiple-SQS is the fan-out pattern. EventBridge routes events by rules, including SaaS and scheduled events. Step Functions orchestrates multi-step workflows with retries. DR strategies in order of rising cost and falling RTO/RPO: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active/active.

keyFacts: SAA-C03: 65 questions (50 scored, 15 unscored), 130 minutes, USD 150, pass mark 720/1000.
Gateway VPC endpoints exist only for S3 and DynamoDB and have no hourly charge. All other services use interface endpoints (PrivateLink).
Security groups are stateful and allow-only. NACLs are stateless, support allow and deny, and are evaluated lowest rule number first.
A NAT gateway is zonal and lives in a public subnet. Use one per AZ for HA. A NAT gateway cannot be used by resources outside its VPC through peering.
Lambda maximum timeout is 15 minutes. For longer or multi-step jobs, use Step Functions, ECS/Fargate or Batch.
SQS default visibility timeout is 30 seconds (max 12 hours). Message retention defaults to 4 days (max 14 days). Use a dead-letter queue for poison messages.
S3 minimum storage durations: Standard-IA and One Zone-IA 30 days, Glacier Instant and Flexible Retrieval 90 days, Deep Archive 180 days.
RDS Multi-AZ uses synchronous replication (HA). Read replicas use asynchronous replication (read scaling and cross-Region DR). Aurora keeps 6 copies across 3 AZs and supports up to 15 replicas.
DynamoDB maximum item size is 400 KB. Store large objects in S3 and keep a pointer in DynamoDB.
Decision rule: 'least operational overhead' usually points to a managed or serverless option (Fargate, Lambda, Aurora Serverless, DynamoDB) over self-managed EC2.

example.caption: Hands-on: three-tier app (ALB → Auto Scaling EC2 → RDS Multi-AZ) with AWS CLI, then teardown. Assumes a VPC with 2 public and 2 private subnets, NAT gateways and security groups already exist.
example.code:
# Data tier: Multi-AZ RDS in private subnets
aws rds create-db-subnet-group --db-subnet-group-name app-db --db-subnet-group-description private --subnet-ids $PRIV_A $PRIV_B
aws rds create-db-instance --db-instance-identifier app-db --engine mysql --db-instance-class db.t3.micro --allocated-storage 20 --master-username admin --manage-master-user-password --multi-az --db-subnet-group-name app-db --vpc-security-group-ids $DB_SG --no-publicly-accessible

# Web tier: ALB in public subnets
ALB_ARN=$(aws elbv2 create-load-balancer --name app-alb --subnets $PUB_A $PUB_B --security-groups $ALB_SG --query 'LoadBalancers[0].LoadBalancerArn' --output text)
TG_ARN=$(aws elbv2 create-target-group --name app-tg --protocol HTTP --port 80 --vpc-id $VPC --health-check-path /health --query 'TargetGroups[0].TargetGroupArn' --output text)
aws elbv2 create-listener --load-balancer-arn $ALB_ARN --protocol HTTP --port 80 --default-actions Type=forward,TargetGroupArn=$TG_ARN

# App tier: Auto Scaling group in private subnets
aws ec2 create-launch-template --launch-template-name app-lt --launch-template-data "{\"ImageId\":\"$AMI\",\"InstanceType\":\"t3.micro\",\"SecurityGroupIds\":[\"$APP_SG\"],\"UserData\":\"$USERDATA_B64\"}"
aws autoscaling create-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name app-asg --launch-template LaunchTemplateName=app-lt --min-size 2 --max-size 4 --desired-capacity 2 --vpc-zone-identifier "$PRIV_A,$PRIV_B" --target-group-arns $TG_ARN --health-check-type ELB --health-check-grace-period 300
aws autoscaling put-scaling-policy --auto-scaling-group-name app-asg --policy-name cpu50 --policy-type TargetTrackingScaling --target-tracking-configuration '{"PredefinedMetricSpecification":{"PredefinedMetricType":"ASGAverageCPUUtilization"},"TargetValue":50}'

# Teardown (reverse order) - stop all billing
aws autoscaling delete-auto-scaling-group --auto-scaling-group-name app-asg --force-delete
aws elbv2 delete-load-balancer --load-balancer-arn $ALB_ARN
sleep 60; aws elbv2 delete-target-group --target-group-arn $TG_ARN
aws ec2 delete-launch-template --launch-template-name app-lt
aws rds delete-db-instance --db-instance-identifier app-db --skip-final-snapshot
aws ec2 delete-nat-gateway --nat-gateway-id $NAT_A   # then release its Elastic IP

pitfalls: Confusing RDS Multi-AZ with read replicas. The Multi-AZ standby does not serve reads, so 'scale reads' means read replicas or Aurora replicas.
Choosing a NAT gateway for private S3 or DynamoDB access. A gateway endpoint is cheaper and keeps traffic on the AWS network.
Forgetting that NACLs are stateless. Blocked ephemeral return ports (1024-65535) break connections that the security groups allow.
Picking SNS when messages must be buffered and processed later, or SQS when many subscribers each need a copy. Use SNS fan-out to multiple SQS queues when you need both.
Leaving NAT gateways, Elastic IPs, RDS instances or final snapshots running after the lab. These keep billing even when idle. Check AWS Cost Explorer the next day.
Over-engineering. When a question asks for lowest cost and the RTO is hours, backup and restore beats warm standby or multi-site.

workflow.title: How a request flows through the three-tier lab, and how to build it

steps.label: Design VPC across two AZs
steps.detail: Create public subnets for the ALB and NAT gateways, and private subnets for EC2 and RDS, each with the correct route table.

steps.label: Chain security groups by tier
steps.detail: Allow 80/443 from the internet to the ALB SG, the app port from the ALB SG to the app SG, and 3306 from the app SG to the DB SG.

steps.label: Launch RDS Multi-AZ privately
steps.detail: Place the database in a private DB subnet group with Multi-AZ enabled, and store credentials in Secrets Manager.

steps.label: Create ALB and target group
steps.detail: The internet-facing ALB receives the request and forwards it to healthy targets based on the /health check.

steps.label: Attach Auto Scaling group
steps.detail: The launch template and ASG spread instances across private subnets, use ELB health checks, and scale on target-tracking CPU.

steps.label: Test failover and scaling
steps.detail: Reboot RDS with failover, terminate an instance, and load-test to confirm the app stays available.

steps.label: Tear down in reverse
steps.detail: Delete the ASG, ALB, target group, RDS, NAT gateways and Elastic IPs, then confirm zero spend in billing.

objective.question: EC2 instances in a private subnet must read objects from an S3 bucket in the same Region. The subnet has no NAT gateway. The company wants the lowest-cost solution that keeps traffic off the internet. What should a solutions architect do?
options: Deploy a NAT gateway in a public subnet and route 0.0.0.0/0 to it
Attach an internet gateway and give the instances Elastic IP addresses
Create a gateway VPC endpoint for S3 and add it to the private subnet's route table
Create an interface VPC endpoint for S3 and update the security group
objective.explanation: Gateway endpoints exist for S3 and DynamoDB, use route table entries and have no hourly charge, so they are the cheapest private path. An interface endpoint works but costs per hour and per GB, and NAT or an internet gateway sends traffic toward the internet path at extra cost.

objective.question: A web server in a public subnet allows inbound TCP 443 in both its security group and the subnet's network ACL. The NACL outbound rules allow only TCP 443. Clients cannot complete HTTPS connections. What is the most likely cause?
options: The internet gateway must be attached to the subnet, not the VPC
NACL rules are evaluated highest number first, so the allow rule is ignored
The NACL is stateless and must allow outbound traffic to the client's ephemeral ports
Security groups block return traffic unless an outbound rule is added
objective.explanation: NACLs are stateless, so response traffic to client ephemeral ports (for example 1024-65535) needs an explicit outbound allow. Security groups are stateful, internet gateways attach to the VPC, and NACLs evaluate the lowest rule number first.

objective.question: A company runs private EC2 instances in three Availability Zones. All of them use a single NAT gateway in AZ-a for outbound internet access. The architect must remove this single point of failure. What should be done?
options: Replace the NAT gateway with a gateway VPC endpoint
Place the NAT gateway in a private subnet in each AZ
Create a NAT gateway in a public subnet in each AZ and point each AZ's private route table to its local NAT gateway
Enable Multi-AZ on the existing NAT gateway
objective.explanation: A NAT gateway is zonal and must sit in a public subnet, so HA means one per AZ with per-AZ route tables; this also avoids cross-AZ data charges. There is no Multi-AZ setting for NAT gateways, and a gateway endpoint only reaches S3 or DynamoDB.

objective.question: A nightly job processes files and runs for about 40 minutes. It has several dependent steps and needs retries on failure. The team wants the least operational overhead. Which solution fits best?
options: Orchestrate the steps with AWS Step Functions, running long steps as Amazon ECS tasks on AWS Fargate
Chain Lambda functions by having each one invoke the next synchronously
Run a cron job on a self-managed EC2 instance
Run the whole job in one AWS Lambda function with the timeout set to 60 minutes
objective.explanation: Lambda's maximum timeout is 15 minutes, so a 40-minute single function is not possible. Step Functions gives managed orchestration with retries, and Fargate runs long tasks without servers; self-managed EC2 adds overhead and chained Lambdas are fragile.

objective.question: Consumers of an Amazon SQS standard queue take about 2 minutes to process each message. The team sees the same message processed multiple times. The queue uses default settings. What is the best fix?
options: Increase the queue's visibility timeout to longer than the processing time
Reduce the delivery delay to 0 seconds
Switch to long polling
Increase the message retention period to 14 days
objective.explanation: The default visibility timeout is 30 seconds, so the message becomes visible again before processing finishes and another consumer picks it up. Retention, long polling and delivery delay do not control re-delivery during processing.

objective.question: A lifecycle rule moves objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-IA after 30 days. Many objects are deleted 10 days after the transition. What will the company see on its bill?
options: A charge for the remaining days up to the 30-day minimum storage duration for Standard-IA
A charge for 90 days of storage
A retrieval fee for every deleted object
No storage charge after deletion
objective.explanation: Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum storage duration, so early deletion is billed for the remaining days. The 90-day minimum applies to Glacier Instant and Flexible Retrieval, and deletion itself is not a retrieval.

objective.question: An RDS for MySQL database is overloaded by reporting queries. The primary must also survive an AZ failure with automatic failover. Which combination meets both needs?
options: Enable Multi-AZ for high availability and add one or more read replicas for the reporting queries
Add read replicas only, since they replicate synchronously
Take hourly snapshots and restore them for reporting
Enable Multi-AZ and send reporting queries to the Multi-AZ standby
objective.explanation: Multi-AZ (standard deployment with one standby) uses synchronous replication for failover, and that standby does not serve reads. Read replicas use asynchronous replication and offload reads; snapshots do not give live reporting or HA.

objective.question: Which statement about Amazon Aurora's storage and replicas is correct?
options: Aurora keeps 3 copies across 3 Regions and supports unlimited replicas
Aurora replicas must be in the same AZ as the writer
Aurora keeps 6 copies of data across 3 AZs and supports up to 15 Aurora Replicas
Aurora keeps 2 copies of data in one AZ and supports up to 5 replicas
objective.explanation: Aurora's shared cluster volume stores 6 copies across 3 AZs, and a cluster can have up to 15 Aurora Replicas that also act as failover targets. The other options give wrong numbers or wrong placement.

objective.question: An application stores user profiles in DynamoDB. A new feature attaches documents up to 5 MB to each profile. What is the recommended design?
options: Store documents in Amazon S3 and save the S3 object key in the DynamoDB item
Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to raise the item size limit
Split each document across many DynamoDB items
Store the documents as binary attributes in the DynamoDB item
objective.explanation: DynamoDB's maximum item size is 400 KB, so large objects go to S3 with a pointer in DynamoDB. Splitting items adds complexity, and DAX is a cache that does not change item limits.

objective.question: An e-commerce site behind an ALB stores session state on each EC2 instance. Users are logged out when Auto Scaling removes instances. The company wants stateless web servers with fast session access. What should the architect use?
options: Store sessions in Amazon ElastiCache
Store sessions on an EBS volume attached to each instance
Store sessions in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
Enable sticky sessions on the ALB
objective.explanation: ElastiCache gives an external, in-memory session store so any instance can serve any user. Sticky sessions still lose state when an instance terminates, EBS is per instance, and Glacier is not designed for session data.

objective.question: Linux EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across three AZs need a shared POSIX file system that grows automatically. Which service fits?
options: Amazon EFS
Amazon S3 mounted as a block device
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Amazon EBS gp3 with Multi-Attach
objective.explanation: EFS is a managed NFS file system that many Linux instances across AZs can mount, and it scales automatically. EBS Multi-Attach works only within one AZ for specific volume types, FSx for Windows is SMB for Windows workloads, and S3 is object storage.

objective.question: A company needs a load balancer that routes /api/* to one target group and /images/* to another, based on the HTTP path. Which option should be used?
options: Application Load Balancer with path-based listener rules
Classic Load Balancer with sticky sessions
Gateway Load Balancer
Network Load Balancer with TCP listeners
objective.explanation: ALB works at Layer 7 and supports path- and host-based routing rules. NLB is Layer 4 and cannot inspect paths, and Gateway Load Balancer is for inserting third-party virtual appliances.

objective.question: An Auto Scaling group should keep average CPU near 50% with the least manual tuning. Which scaling policy is best?
options: Target tracking scaling with a CPU target of 50%
Manually changing desired capacity
Scheduled scaling every hour
Simple scaling with a CloudWatch alarm at 80%
objective.explanation: Target tracking automatically creates and manages the alarms to hold a metric at the target value. Simple and scheduled scaling need more tuning and do not track the metric continuously.

objective.question: A company needs DR in a second Region with an RTO of minutes and accepts some running cost. A scaled-down but fully working copy of the stack should always run there. Which strategy is this?
options: Warm standby
Multi-site active/active
Pilot light
Backup and restore
objective.explanation: Warm standby keeps a smaller, always-running full copy that can scale up quickly. Pilot light keeps only core pieces such as replicated data with app servers off, backup and restore has the longest RTO, and active/active serves full production traffic in both Regions.

objective.question: When an order is placed, three independent services (billing, shipping, analytics) must each receive and process the event at their own pace, and no message should be lost if a service is down. What design should be used?
options: An SNS topic with three SQS queues subscribed (fan-out)
Three Lambda functions invoked synchronously by the order service
An Amazon ElastiCache pub/sub channel
One SQS queue polled by all three services
objective.explanation: SNS-to-SQS fan-out gives each service its own durable queue, so each consumes at its own rate and messages wait if a service is down. A single queue delivers each message to only one consumer, synchronous calls couple the services, and cache pub/sub does not keep messages durably.

subjective.question: What makes a subnet public or private in a VPC, and where would you place each tier of a three-tier app?
subjective.answer: A subnet is public when its route table has a route, usually 0.0.0.0/0, to an internet gateway attached to the VPC. Instances there also need a public IP or Elastic IP to be reached. A private subnet has no route to the internet gateway. If it needs outbound internet, it routes 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway in a public subnet. In a three-tier app I put the Application Load Balancer in public subnets across at least two AZs. The web or app EC2 instances in the Auto Scaling group go in private subnets, and the RDS database goes in separate private database subnets with no internet route at all. Security groups then chain the tiers: the ALB accepts 443 from the internet, the app tier accepts traffic only from the ALB's security group, and the database accepts its port only from the app tier's security group.
keyPoints: Public means a route table entry to an internet gateway
Private subnets use a NAT gateway for outbound-only access
ALB in public subnets, app and DB in private subnets across AZs
Security groups reference each other to chain tiers

subjective.question: Compare security groups and network ACLs. When would you use a NACL instead of only security groups?
subjective.answer: Security groups attach to network interfaces such as EC2 instances. They are stateful, so if inbound traffic is allowed, the response is allowed automatically. They support allow rules only, and all rules are evaluated together. They can reference other security groups, which makes tier-to-tier rules clean. NACLs attach to subnets. They are stateless, so return traffic needs its own rule, usually for the ephemeral port range. They support both allow and deny, and rules are evaluated in order from the lowest rule number, stopping at the first match. I use security groups as the main control. I add a NACL when I need an explicit deny, for example blocking a known bad IP range for a whole subnet, or as a coarse second layer of defence. On the exam, 'block a specific IP address' almost always points to a NACL, because security groups cannot deny.
keyPoints: SG: instance level, stateful, allow only, can reference SGs
NACL: subnet level, stateless, allow and deny
NACL rules evaluated lowest number first, first match wins
Use NACL for explicit deny of IP ranges

subjective.question: Explain gateway VPC endpoints and interface VPC endpoints. How do you choose between them?
subjective.answer: Both let resources in a VPC reach AWS services privately without an internet gateway or NAT. A gateway endpoint exists only for S3 and DynamoDB. It works by adding a prefix-list route to chosen route tables, and it has no hourly charge. It is reachable only from within that VPC, not from on-premises over VPN or Direct Connect, or from peered VPCs. An interface endpoint uses AWS PrivateLink. It creates elastic network interfaces with private IPs in your subnets, protected by security groups, and private DNS can make the normal service name resolve to them. It costs per hour per AZ plus per GB processed, but it works for most AWS services and can be reached from on-premises. My rule: for S3 or DynamoDB access from inside the VPC, use the gateway endpoint for cost. Use an interface endpoint for other services, or when on-premises clients need private access.
keyPoints: Gateway endpoints: S3 and DynamoDB only, route-table based, no hourly charge
Interface endpoints: PrivateLink ENIs, security groups, private DNS
Interface endpoints are billed hourly and per GB
On-premises access needs interface endpoints

subjective.question: How would you design NAT for high availability and cost, and what are its limits?
subjective.answer: A NAT gateway is a managed, zonal service placed in a public subnet with an Elastic IP. It gives private instances outbound-only internet access. Because it lives in one AZ, a single NAT gateway is a single point of failure for the other AZs and also adds cross-AZ data charges. For HA I create one NAT gateway per AZ and give each AZ's private subnets their own route table pointing to the local NAT gateway. For cost, I send S3 and DynamoDB traffic through gateway endpoints so it does not pass through NAT, because NAT charges per GB processed. Limits to remember: a NAT gateway does not allow inbound connections from the internet, and resources in a peered VPC or on-premises cannot use it through peering. For a non-production environment, a single NAT gateway may be an acceptable cost trade-off if downtime is tolerable.
keyPoints: NAT gateway is zonal and sits in a public subnet
One per AZ with per-AZ route tables for HA
Use gateway endpoints to cut NAT data charges
No inbound connections and no use via VPC peering

subjective.question: Compare Application Load Balancer, Network Load Balancer and Gateway Load Balancer with a use case for each.
subjective.answer: The Application Load Balancer works at Layer 7. It understands HTTP and HTTPS, so it can route by path, host header, query string or headers, and it can target EC2, IP addresses, containers and Lambda. It is the default for web apps and microservices. The Network Load Balancer works at Layer 4 for TCP, UDP and TLS. It handles very high throughput with low latency and gives a static IP per AZ, and you can attach Elastic IPs. I use it for gaming, IoT, non-HTTP protocols, or when clients need to allow-list fixed IPs. It can also front a PrivateLink endpoint service. The Gateway Load Balancer is for inserting third-party virtual appliances such as firewalls or intrusion detection systems transparently into the traffic path, using GENEVE encapsulation. On the exam, 'path-based routing' means ALB, 'static IP or extreme performance' means NLB, and 'third-party firewall appliances' means GWLB.
keyPoints: ALB: Layer 7, path/host routing, Lambda targets
NLB: Layer 4, static IPs, very high performance, PrivateLink
GWLB: third-party appliances, GENEVE
Map exam keywords to each type

subjective.question: Describe how EC2 Auto Scaling works with an ELB, including scaling policies and health checks.
subjective.answer: An Auto Scaling group uses a launch template and keeps capacity between a minimum and maximum, aiming at a desired count. I spread it across subnets in multiple AZs and register it with an ALB target group. For health, I enable ELB health checks on the group, so an instance that fails the load balancer's check is replaced, not just one that fails EC2 status checks. For scaling, target tracking is my default, for example average CPU at 50% or ALB requests per target. Step scaling gives finer control based on alarm size. Scheduled scaling suits known patterns like business hours, and predictive scaling forecasts cyclical load. A health check grace period stops new instances from being killed before the app starts. Lifecycle hooks let me run setup or drain tasks during launch or termination. The group also rebalances across AZs, which supports high availability.
keyPoints: Launch template, min/max/desired across multiple AZs
Enable ELB health checks for app-level replacement
Target tracking, step, scheduled and predictive policies
Grace period and lifecycle hooks

subjective.question: A company keeps logs that are read often for 30 days, rarely for a year, and must be kept for 7 years for audit. Design an S3 storage and lifecycle plan.
subjective.answer: I would land logs in S3 Standard because they are read often in the first month. A lifecycle rule then transitions them to S3 Standard-IA at day 30, since access drops but quick retrieval is still needed. Standard-IA has a 30-day minimum storage duration and a per-GB retrieval fee, which is fine for rare reads. After one year I would move them to S3 Glacier Deep Archive, which is the lowest-cost class, with retrieval in hours and a 180-day minimum. If auditors might need data in milliseconds, Glacier Instant Retrieval is the alternative, with a 90-day minimum. An expiration action deletes objects after 7 years. For compliance, I would turn on S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a retention period, plus versioning. I would also avoid moving very small objects to IA classes, because they are billed at a minimum object size. If access patterns were unknown, S3 Intelligent-Tiering would be the simpler choice.
keyPoints: Standard → Standard-IA at 30 days → Deep Archive after 1 year
Respect minimum durations: IA 30, Glacier IR/Flexible 90, Deep Archive 180 days
Expiration at 7 years; Object Lock for compliance
Intelligent-Tiering for unknown patterns

subjective.question: Compare Amazon EBS, EFS and FSx. Give a scenario for each.
subjective.answer: EBS is block storage attached to an EC2 instance in a single AZ. It suits boot volumes and databases on EC2. gp3 is general purpose with performance set independently of size, and io2 gives high, consistent IOPS. Multi-Attach is limited to certain io1/io2 volumes within one AZ. Snapshots go to S3 and can be copied across Regions for DR. EFS is a managed NFS file system for Linux. Many instances across AZs can mount it at once and it grows automatically, so it fits shared web content or home directories for an Auto Scaling group. Lifecycle management can move cold files to cheaper storage classes. FSx gives managed third-party file systems: FSx for Windows File Server for SMB and Active Directory workloads, FSx for Lustre for high-performance computing and ML that can link to S3, and FSx for NetApp ONTAP and OpenZFS for multi-protocol or migration needs. I choose by protocol, sharing needs and operating system.
keyPoints: EBS: single-AZ block storage, gp3/io2, snapshots
EFS: shared NFS for Linux across AZs, elastic
FSx for Windows (SMB/AD), Lustre (HPC/ML), ONTAP, OpenZFS
Choose by protocol, OS and sharing

subjective.question: Explain RDS Multi-AZ, read replicas and Aurora. How would you pick one for a given requirement?
subjective.answer: RDS Multi-AZ, in its standard form, keeps a standby in another AZ using synchronous replication. If the primary fails, RDS fails over automatically by updating the DNS endpoint. The standby does not serve reads, so its purpose is high availability. Read replicas use asynchronous replication. They serve read traffic, can be in another Region for DR, and can be promoted to a standalone database, but they may lag. Aurora is AWS's MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible engine. It stores 6 copies across 3 AZs on a shared cluster volume and supports up to 15 Aurora Replicas that serve reads and act as failover targets, usually with faster failover than standard RDS. Aurora Global Database adds low-lag cross-Region replication, and Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity automatically. My mapping: survive AZ failure means Multi-AZ; scale reads means read replicas; cross-Region DR means a cross-Region replica or Aurora Global Database; highest availability with less overhead usually means Aurora.
keyPoints: Multi-AZ: synchronous, automatic failover, standby not readable
Read replicas: asynchronous, read scaling, cross-Region, promotable
Aurora: 6 copies in 3 AZs, up to 15 replicas
Global Database and Serverless v2 options

subjective.question: When would you choose DynamoDB over RDS, and what design rules matter most?
subjective.answer: I choose DynamoDB when access patterns are known, the workload needs single-digit millisecond latency at any scale, and I want no servers to manage. Examples are user sessions, shopping carts, game state and IoT data. RDS is better when I need complex joins, ad hoc SQL queries or strong relational constraints. Key design rules: pick a partition key with high cardinality so traffic spreads evenly and avoids hot partitions. Use a sort key and global or local secondary indexes to support query patterns, and avoid table scans. Keep items under the 400 KB limit; large files go to S3 with a pointer in the item. Choose on-demand capacity for unpredictable traffic and provisioned with auto scaling for steady traffic. Other features I mention: TTL to expire old items, Streams to trigger Lambda on changes, global tables for multi-Region active-active, point-in-time recovery for backups, and DAX for microsecond read caching.
keyPoints: DynamoDB for known access patterns, scale, serverless
High-cardinality partition key, indexes, avoid scans
400 KB item limit; large objects in S3
On-demand vs provisioned; TTL, Streams, global tables, DAX

subjective.question: How does ElastiCache help an architecture, and what caching strategies and engine choices would you discuss?
subjective.answer: ElastiCache is a managed in-memory cache. It reduces read load on databases and cuts latency, and it also stores session state so web servers can stay stateless behind a load balancer. Two common strategies: lazy loading (cache-aside), where the app reads the cache, and on a miss reads the database and writes the result to the cache. It caches only what is used, but data can be stale and the first read is slower. Write-through updates the cache whenever the database is written, so data stays fresh, but it can fill the cache with unused items. I add a TTL in both cases to limit staleness. For engines, Redis OSS or Valkey gives replication, Multi-AZ automatic failover, persistence options, and rich data types like sorted sets for leaderboards. Memcached is simple, multi-threaded and has no replication, suited to a basic cache. Note the app code must change to use the cache, unlike DAX, which is API-compatible with DynamoDB.
keyPoints: Reduces DB load and latency; external session store
Lazy loading vs write-through, with TTL
Redis OSS/Valkey: replication, failover, data types
Memcached: simple, no replication; app changes needed

subjective.question: Compare SQS, SNS and EventBridge for decoupling. When would you use each?
subjective.answer: SQS is a pull-based queue. A producer sends messages and consumers poll and delete them, so it buffers load and protects downstream systems. Standard queues give very high throughput with at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering. FIFO queues give ordering and exactly-once processing. Key settings: visibility timeout defaults to 30 seconds and can go to 12 hours; retention defaults to 4 days, maximum 14 days; a dead-letter queue catches poison messages after a set number of receives. SNS is push-based pub/sub. One message goes to many subscribers such as SQS, Lambda, HTTP endpoints, email or SMS, and SNS plus SQS gives durable fan-out. EventBridge is an event bus with content-based rules that route events from AWS services, your own apps and SaaS partners to many targets. It adds schema registry, archive and replay, and scheduling. I use SQS for buffering work, SNS for simple fan-out, and EventBridge for event-driven routing across many sources and filtering rules.
keyPoints: SQS: pull queue, buffering, Standard vs FIFO
Visibility timeout 30 s default (12 h max); retention 4 days default (14 max); DLQ
SNS: push pub/sub, fan-out with SQS
EventBridge: rule-based routing, SaaS sources, replay

subjective.question: A team has a Lambda function that sometimes times out because it now does several steps taking up to 30 minutes in total. How would you redesign it?
subjective.answer: Lambda has a hard maximum timeout of 15 minutes, so raising the timeout cannot fix this. I would split the work into smaller steps and orchestrate them with AWS Step Functions. Each short step can stay a Lambda function. Any step that runs long, like a big file transform, can run as an ECS task on Fargate, which Step Functions can start and wait for, or as an AWS Batch job for heavy batch compute. Step Functions gives built-in retries with backoff, catch blocks for errors, parallel and map states for fan-out, and a visual history of each run, which makes debugging easier. Standard workflows suit long-running, auditable jobs; Express workflows suit high-volume, short runs. If the trigger is bursty, I would put an SQS queue in front to buffer requests. This keeps the solution serverless with low operational overhead, which is what the exam usually rewards.
keyPoints: Lambda maximum timeout is 15 minutes
Step Functions for multi-step orchestration with retries and error handling
ECS on Fargate or Batch for long steps
Standard vs Express workflows; SQS for buffering

subjective.question: Explain the four disaster recovery strategies on AWS and how RTO, RPO and cost change across them.
subjective.answer: RTO is how long recovery may take; RPO is how much data loss, measured in time, is acceptable. Backup and restore is the cheapest: data is backed up to another Region using AWS Backup, snapshots or S3 replication, and infrastructure is rebuilt from code when needed. RTO and RPO are hours. Pilot light keeps core data live in the DR Region, for example a cross-Region read replica or Aurora Global Database, while app servers are off or not created; you start them in a disaster, giving RTO in tens of minutes. Warm standby runs a scaled-down but fully working copy that can take traffic and scale up quickly, giving RTO in minutes at higher cost. Multi-site active/active serves production traffic from two or more Regions, using Route 53 routing and services like DynamoDB global tables, giving near-zero RTO and RPO at the highest cost. I pick the cheapest option that meets the stated RTO and RPO.
keyPoints: Define RTO and RPO
Backup and restore: cheapest, hours
Pilot light: data live, compute off; warm standby: scaled-down running
Active/active: near-zero RTO/RPO, highest cost

subjective.question: Walk through how you built and tore down the three-tier lab (ALB → Auto Scaling EC2 → RDS Multi-AZ), and what you learned.
subjective.answer: I created a VPC with public subnets in two AZs for the ALB and NAT gateways, private app subnets, and private database subnets. I made three security groups: the ALB allowing HTTP/HTTPS from the internet, the app tier allowing traffic only from the ALB's group, and the database allowing its port only from the app group. I wrote a launch template with user data to install the app, created an Auto Scaling group across both AZs with ELB health checks and a target tracking policy, and attached it to an ALB target group. I launched RDS in a DB subnet group with Multi-AZ enabled and stored credentials in Secrets Manager. I tested by terminating an instance and rebooting RDS with failover. For teardown I deleted in reverse: Auto Scaling group, ALB and target group, RDS with a final snapshot decision, NAT gateways, Elastic IPs, then the VPC. Lesson: NAT gateways, idle load balancers and RDS are the usual surprise costs, so check billing afterwards.
keyPoints: Subnet layout across two AZs with SG chaining
Launch template, ASG with ELB health checks, target tracking
RDS Multi-AZ in DB subnet group; test failover
Reverse-order teardown; watch NAT, EIP and RDS costs

subjective.question: How do you approach SAA-C03 scenario questions and manage the exam, including 'least operational overhead' wording?
subjective.answer: The exam has 65 questions, of which 50 are scored and 15 unscored, in 130 minutes, with a pass mark of 720 out of 1000. That is about two minutes per question, so I do a first pass, answer what I know, flag the doubtful ones and return later. There is no penalty for guessing, so I never leave a blank. For each scenario I read the last line first to find the real requirement: cost, performance, availability, security or operational overhead. Then I underline constraints such as 'without internet', 'in minutes' or 'existing SQL'. I remove options that break a hard limit, such as a Lambda running over 15 minutes or a DynamoDB item over 400 KB. When the question says 'least operational overhead', I prefer managed or serverless choices like Fargate, Lambda, Aurora Serverless or DynamoDB over self-managed EC2. When it says 'most cost-effective', I look for things like gateway endpoints, Spot, or lifecycle rules. Before booking, I aim for two full practice exams above 80% with time left over.
keyPoints: 65 questions (50 scored), 130 minutes, pass 720/1000
Read the requirement line first; note constraints
Eliminate options that break service limits
'Least operational overhead' favours managed/serverless; target 80%+ in practice

steps.overview: This step covers choosing one Associate specialisation after Solutions Architect – Associate. You can pick Developer (DVA-C02), Machine Learning Engineer (MLA-C01) or Data Engineer (DEA-C01). Each exam has 65 questions in 130 minutes, costs USD 150 and needs 720/1000 to pass. Over Weeks 16–22 you study one path deeply and ship a matching project. That project becomes your exam revision tool and your interview portfolio piece.
objectives: Choose the Associate exam that fits your role, then map its official domains to a 7-week study plan.
Build and deploy one project with infrastructure as code: a serverless API, a SageMaker endpoint or a data pipeline.
Apply the service limits and decision rules each exam tests, for example Lambda timeouts, DynamoDB capacity, SageMaker endpoint types and Kinesis shard throughput.
Instrument your project with CloudWatch, plus X-Ray or SageMaker Model Monitor, so you can troubleshoot it the way exam scenarios expect.
Publish the project in a public repository with a README, an architecture diagram and teardown steps.

concepts.explanation: Lambda can be invoked synchronously (API Gateway), asynchronously (S3, SNS, EventBridge) or through an event source mapping (SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams). Async invocations retry and can send failures to a destination or dead-letter queue. With event source mappings, Lambda polls the source and processes records in batches. Cold starts can be reduced with provisioned concurrency or SnapStart for supported runtimes.

concepts.term: API Gateway REST vs HTTP APIs (DVA)
concepts.explanation: REST APIs support API keys and usage plans, request validation, caching and edge-optimized endpoints. HTTP APIs are cheaper and faster, with native JWT authorizers, but have fewer features. Use Lambda authorizers or Cognito user pools for authentication. Use stages and stage variables to separate dev and prod.

Design the partition key for high cardinality so traffic spreads evenly; use a sort key for range queries. Choose GSIs for alternate access patterns and LSIs (created only at table creation) for an alternate sort key. On-demand mode suits spiky or unknown traffic; provisioned mode with auto scaling suits steady traffic. Query is efficient; Scan reads the whole table and is usually the wrong answer.

CodePipeline orchestrates the source, build (CodeBuild with buildspec.yml) and deploy stages. CodeDeploy runs canary or linear traffic shifting for Lambda using aliases, and can roll back automatically on CloudWatch alarms. SAM and CloudFormation define the infrastructure. X-Ray traces requests across services; use annotations (indexed, searchable) for filtering and metadata (not indexed) for extra detail.

Data Wrangler and Processing jobs clean and transform data; Feature Store holds features in online and offline stores. Training jobs read data from S3 and write model artefacts back to S3. You can use built-in algorithms like XGBoost, bring your own script, or bring your own container. Automatic Model Tuning searches hyperparameters, and Clarify detects bias and explains predictions.

Real-time endpoints serve low-latency, steady traffic. Serverless Inference suits intermittent traffic and tolerates cold starts. Asynchronous Inference handles large payloads and long processing times, and can scale to zero. Batch Transform scores whole datasets offline with no persistent endpoint. Model Registry versions approved models, and SageMaker Pipelines automates the ML workflow.

Model Monitor compares live traffic against a baseline to detect data quality drift, model quality drift, bias drift and feature attribution drift. It needs data capture enabled on the endpoint. Results go to S3, and metrics go to CloudWatch for alarms and retraining triggers.

Glue crawlers infer schemas into the Glue Data Catalog, and Glue ETL jobs (Spark or Python shell) transform the data. Job bookmarks prevent reprocessing old data. Athena queries S3 with SQL and is billed per data scanned, so use columnar formats (Parquet/ORC), compression and partitioning. Lake Formation adds fine-grained permissions on top of the Catalog, at database, table, column, row and cell level, including tag-based access control.

Kinesis Data Streams gives ordered, replayable streaming with on-demand or provisioned shards. Amazon Data Firehose loads streams into S3, Redshift or OpenSearch with buffering and no code. Redshift is the data warehouse: choose distribution style (AUTO, KEY, EVEN, ALL) and sort keys for performance, and load data with COPY from S3. Redshift Spectrum queries S3 data directly without loading it.

keyFacts:
Exam domain weights:
- DVA-C02: Development 32%, Security 26%, Deployment 24%, Troubleshooting and Optimization 18%.
- MLA-C01: Data Preparation 28%, Model Development 26%, Deployment and Orchestration 22%, Monitoring, Maintenance and Security 24%.
- DEA-C01: Ingestion and Transformation 34%, Store Management 26%, Operations and Support 22%, Security and Governance 18%.
Lambda limits: maximum timeout 15 minutes; memory 128 MB to 10,240 MB (CPU scales with memory); ephemeral /tmp storage up to 10 GB; synchronous request and response payload 6 MB each.
API Gateway has a default integration timeout of 29 seconds. Long-running work should go asynchronous, for example through SQS, Step Functions or SageMaker Async Inference.

DynamoDB: maximum item size 400 KB. 1 RCU = 1 strongly consistent read per second of up to 4 KB, or 2 eventually consistent reads. 1 WCU = 1 write per second of up to 1 KB. Transactional operations cost double.
Kinesis Data Streams provisioned shard: 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s for writes, and 2 MB/s for reads. Enhanced fan-out gives each consumer its own 2 MB/s per shard.

SageMaker endpoint choice:
- Real-time for steady, low-latency traffic.
- Serverless for spiky traffic with idle gaps.
- Asynchronous for payloads up to 1 GB and processing up to 1 hour.
- Batch Transform for offline scoring of whole datasets.
To reduce Athena cost and scan time: convert to Parquet or ORC, compress, partition (for example by date), and use partition projection when there are many partitions.
Secrets go in Secrets Manager (supports rotation) or SSM Parameter Store SecureString, never in code or plain environment variables. KMS envelope encryption is used for data over 4 KB.

example.caption: Developer path: a minimal AWS SAM template for a serverless notes API (API Gateway + Lambda + DynamoDB) with X-Ray tracing. Deploy with `sam build && sam deploy --guided`.
example.code:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31
Description: Notes API for DVA-C02 portfolio
