Globals:
  Function:
    Runtime: python3.12
    Timeout: 10
    MemorySize: 256
    Tracing: Active
Resources:
  NotesTable:
    Type: AWS::DynamoDB::Table
    Properties:
      BillingMode: PAY_PER_REQUEST
      AttributeDefinitions:
        - {AttributeName: noteId, AttributeType: S}
      KeySchema:
        - {AttributeName: noteId, KeyType: HASH}
  NotesFunction:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
    Properties:
      CodeUri: src/
      Handler: app.handler
      Environment:
        Variables: {TABLE_NAME: !Ref NotesTable}
      Policies:
        - DynamoDBCrudPolicy: {TableName: !Ref NotesTable}
      Events:
        GetNote: {Type: Api, Properties: {Path: /notes/{id}, Method: get}}
        PutNote: {Type: Api, Properties: {Path: /notes, Method: post}}
Outputs:
  ApiUrl:
    Value: !Sub https://${ServerlessRestApi}.execute-api.${AWS::Region}.amazonaws.com/Prod/notes

pitfalls: Picking an exam by hype, not by your job. Choose Developer if you write application code, ML Engineer if you train or deploy models, and Data Engineer if you build pipelines or warehouses. Interviewers will probe your project deeply.
Answering 'Scan' or 'increase Lambda timeout' by reflex. The exam usually prefers Query with a GSI, or an asynchronous pattern, because the API Gateway integration timeout is 29 seconds by default.

Confusing similar services:
- Kinesis Data Streams (custom consumers, replay) vs Amazon Data Firehose (managed delivery, near real-time).
- SageMaker Serverless Inference vs Asynchronous Inference.
- X-Ray annotations (indexed) vs metadata (not indexed).
Ignoring security questions, which carry 18–26% weight on every exam. Expect least-privilege IAM roles, KMS encryption, VPC endpoints, Lake Formation permissions and Secrets Manager rotation.
Leaving resources running after the project. SageMaker real-time endpoints, Redshift clusters, NAT gateways and provisioned Kinesis shards bill by the hour. Add budgets, alerts and a teardown script.
Publishing a repo with hard-coded access keys or account IDs. Use IAM roles and OIDC for CI, add a .gitignore, and run a secrets scanner before making the repo public.

objective.question: A developer has a Lambda function that processes uploaded video files. Some files take about 25 minutes to process, and the function fails on those files. What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Increase the function memory to 10,240 MB so it always finishes within the timeout
Move the long-running processing to AWS Fargate or split it into steps orchestrated by AWS Step Functions
Enable provisioned concurrency so the function does not time out
Increase the Lambda timeout to 30 minutes in the function configuration
objective.explanation: The maximum Lambda timeout is 15 minutes, so 25-minute jobs need a different compute option or must be broken into smaller steps. More memory may speed up the code but does not guarantee the job finishes in time. Provisioned concurrency only reduces cold starts; it does not change the timeout.

objective.question: A REST API in Amazon API Gateway invokes a Lambda function synchronously to generate a report. Report generation takes about 2 minutes, and clients receive HTTP 504 errors. Which design solves this with the least client-side waiting?
options: Switch from a REST API to an HTTP API, which has no integration timeout
Enable API Gateway caching so repeated requests return faster
Have the API send the request to an SQS queue, return HTTP 202 with a job ID, and let a worker process the queue and store the result for the client to fetch later
Increase the Lambda timeout to 15 minutes
objective.explanation: API Gateway has a default integration timeout of 29 seconds, so long work should be made asynchronous, for example with SQS and a job-status endpoint. Raising the Lambda timeout does not change the API Gateway limit, and HTTP APIs also have an integration timeout. Caching does not help the first request.

objective.question: An application performs 80 strongly consistent reads per second on a DynamoDB table. Each item is 6 KB. How many read capacity units (RCUs) are needed in provisioned mode?
objective.explanation: One RCU covers one strongly consistent read per second of up to 4 KB, so a 6 KB item rounds up to 8 KB and needs 2 RCUs. 80 reads × 2 RCUs = 160 RCUs. With eventually consistent reads the answer would be 80.

objective.question: A payment service uses DynamoDB TransactWriteItems to write 50 items per second. Each item is 1.5 KB. How many write capacity units (WCUs) are needed?
objective.explanation: One WCU covers one 1 KB write per second, so a 1.5 KB item rounds up to 2 WCUs. Transactional writes cost double, so each write needs 4 WCUs, and 50 × 4 = 200 WCUs.

objective.question: A team deploys a Lambda-based API with AWS SAM. They want new versions to receive 10% of traffic for 5 minutes and to roll back automatically if errors rise. What should they use?
options: AWS CodeBuild with a buildspec that deletes the old function version
An API Gateway stage variable switched manually after testing
Lambda reserved concurrency set to 10% of the account limit
AWS CodeDeploy with a canary deployment preference on a Lambda alias, linked to CloudWatch alarms
objective.explanation: SAM's DeploymentPreference uses CodeDeploy to shift traffic on a Lambda alias, for example with a canary 10% for 5 minutes setting, and rolls back when the linked CloudWatch alarms fire. CodeBuild only builds and tests. Stage variables and reserved concurrency do not give automatic traffic shifting or rollback.

objective.question: A company needs a public API that gives partners API keys with per-partner throttling and quotas. It must also validate request bodies before invoking Lambda. Which API Gateway option should they choose?
options: REST API with usage plans, API keys and request validation
HTTP API with a Lambda authorizer and stage variables
WebSocket API with a Lambda authorizer
HTTP API with a JWT authorizer
objective.explanation: API keys, usage plans and built-in request validation are REST API features. HTTP APIs are cheaper and simpler and support JWT authorizers, but they do not offer usage plans or request validation. WebSocket APIs are for two-way persistent connections.

objective.question: A developer uses AWS X-Ray to trace a Lambda function. The support team needs to search traces by customer ID in the X-Ray console using filter expressions. How should the developer record the customer ID?
options: Add it as an annotation on the segment or subsegment
Put it in the Lambda function's environment variables
Write it to CloudWatch Logs with console.log
Add it as metadata on the segment
objective.explanation: Annotations are indexed key-value pairs, so you can use them in X-Ray filter expressions. Metadata is stored with the trace but is not indexed for search. Logs and environment variables are not part of trace filtering.

objective.question: A Lambda function connects to an Amazon RDS database. Security requires that the password is not stored in code and is rotated automatically every 30 days. What is the best solution?
options: Store the password in an S3 object encrypted with SSE-S3
Hard-code the password and encrypt the deployment package with KMS
Store the password as a plain Lambda environment variable and update it monthly
Store the password in AWS Secrets Manager with rotation enabled and retrieve it at runtime
objective.explanation: Secrets Manager stores secrets securely and supports built-in automatic rotation, including for RDS. Plain environment variables and code are not acceptable for secrets. S3 is not a secrets store and gives no rotation.

objective.question: A retail company has a SageMaker model that gets traffic in bursts during sales hours and almost no requests overnight. They want to pay nothing for idle compute and can accept occasional cold-start latency. The model does not need a GPU. Which inference option fits best?
options: Serverless Inference
Batch Transform
Real-time inference on a GPU instance with auto scaling
Real-time inference endpoint with a fixed instance count
objective.explanation: Serverless Inference suits spiky traffic with idle gaps, scales automatically and charges only for compute used, at the cost of possible cold starts. Real-time endpoints keep instances running and billing all the time. Batch Transform is for offline scoring of whole datasets, not live requests.

objective.question: A medical imaging team sends 600 MB image files to a SageMaker model. Each inference takes about 20 minutes. Clients can wait for a notification when results are ready. Which option should they use?
options: Asynchronous Inference
A Lambda function that loads the model from S3
Serverless Inference
Real-time inference
objective.explanation: Asynchronous Inference supports payloads up to 1 GB and processing up to 1 hour, queues requests, writes results to S3 and can send SNS notifications. Real-time and Serverless Inference are for small payloads and short responses. Lambda has a 15-minute timeout and a 6 MB synchronous payload limit.

objective.question: An ML team computes customer features for training. They also need the same features with millisecond latency at inference time, and want to avoid training-serving skew. Which SageMaker capability should they use?
options: SageMaker Model Monitor
SageMaker Clarify
SageMaker Batch Transform
SageMaker Feature Store with both online and offline stores
objective.explanation: Feature Store keeps an online store for low-latency lookups at inference and an offline store in S3 for training. Both come from the same feature definitions, which reduces training-serving skew. Model Monitor and Clarify watch models and explain them; Batch Transform scores offline.

objective.question: A loan-approval model is deployed on a SageMaker real-time endpoint. Regulators require the company to detect if the model starts treating an age group unfairly over time. What should the ML engineer set up?
options: Endpoint auto scaling based on InvocationsPerInstance
A data quality monitor that checks only for missing values
A SageMaker Model Monitor bias drift monitoring schedule using SageMaker Clarify, with a baseline from training data
A CloudWatch alarm on the endpoint's Invocation5XXErrors metric
objective.explanation: Model Monitor's bias drift monitoring uses Clarify to compare live predictions against a bias baseline and flags changes in fairness metrics. Error and scaling metrics show health, not fairness. A data quality check finds schema and statistics drift, not bias.

objective.question: Analysts run daily Amazon Athena queries on 5 TB of CSV logs in S3. Most queries filter on a single day. Costs are high because each query scans the whole dataset. Which change reduces cost the most?
options: Convert the data to compressed Parquet and partition it by date in S3
Create more Glue crawlers to scan the data more often
Move the CSV files to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval
Run the queries in a larger Athena workgroup
objective.explanation: Athena charges by data scanned. Columnar, compressed Parquet reads only the needed columns, and date partitions let Athena skip days that are not queried. Workgroups and extra crawlers do not reduce scanned data, and Athena cannot query objects in Glacier Flexible Retrieval directly.

objective.question: A data lake on S3 is catalogued in the AWS Glue Data Catalog. The finance team must see all columns of the sales table. The marketing team must not see the customer_email column, and should see only rows for their region. What is the simplest way to enforce this for Athena users?
options: Use AWS Lake Formation permissions with data filters for column-level and row-level access
Encrypt the customer_email column with a separate KMS key
Use S3 bucket policies with conditions on column names
Create separate S3 buckets with copies of the data for each team
objective.explanation: Lake Formation provides fine-grained access, including column, row and cell-level security through data filters, and Athena enforces it. S3 bucket policies work at object level, not column level. Copying data adds cost and drift, and KMS keys do not filter rows.

objective.question: An IoT application writes 5 MB/s of data to Amazon Kinesis Data Streams in provisioned mode, at 3,000 records per second. What is the minimum number of shards required to handle the writes?
objective.explanation: Each provisioned shard accepts up to 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s for writes. 5 MB/s needs 5 shards and 3,000 records/s needs 3 shards, so the larger value, 5 shards, is the minimum.

subjective.question: Explain the AWS Lambda execution model. What is a cold start, and how would you reduce its impact?
subjective.answer: When Lambda receives a request and no warm execution environment is free, it creates one. It downloads the code, starts the runtime and runs the initialisation code outside the handler. This is a cold start. Later requests can reuse the same environment, so anything created during init, such as SDK clients or database connections, is reused. Each environment handles one request at a time, so concurrency equals the number of environments. To reduce cold starts, I keep the deployment package small, initialise clients outside the handler, and avoid heavy frameworks. For latency-sensitive APIs I use provisioned concurrency, which keeps environments initialised. For supported runtimes such as Java, SnapStart restores a snapshot of an initialised environment. Memory also matters: CPU scales with memory from 128 MB to 10,240 MB, so more memory can shorten init and run time, sometimes at the same or lower cost.
keyPoints: Cold start = new environment plus init code; warm environments are reused
Initialise SDK clients and connections outside the handler
One request per environment; concurrency equals environments
Provisioned concurrency and SnapStart reduce cold starts
CPU scales with memory, so tune memory for speed and cost

subjective.question: Describe synchronous, asynchronous and event source mapping invocations in Lambda. How are errors and retries handled in each?
subjective.answer: In synchronous invocation, for example from API Gateway, the caller waits for the response. Lambda does not retry; the client must handle errors. The request and response payloads are limited to 6 MB each, so large files should go through S3 with presigned URLs. In asynchronous invocation, for example from S3 or SNS, Lambda queues the event and returns immediately. On failure it retries twice by default, and you can send failed events to a dead-letter queue or, better, to an on-failure destination that includes more context. With event source mappings, Lambda polls sources such as SQS, Kinesis or DynamoDB Streams and invokes the function with batches. For SQS, failed messages return to the queue after the visibility timeout and can move to a DLQ via a redrive policy. For streams, a failed batch blocks the shard until it succeeds or expires, so I use bisect-on-error, maximum retry attempts and partial batch responses to avoid poison records.
keyPoints: Synchronous: caller handles errors; 6 MB payload limit each way
Asynchronous: two retries by default, DLQ or on-failure destinations
Event source mappings poll SQS, Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams in batches
Streams can block on bad records; use bisect, retry limits, partial batch response

subjective.question: Compare API Gateway REST APIs and HTTP APIs. When would you choose each?
subjective.answer: HTTP APIs are the newer, simpler option. They cost less and have lower latency. They support Lambda and HTTP proxy integrations, private integrations through VPC links, native JWT authorizers for Cognito or any OIDC provider, Lambda authorizers, IAM authorisation and simple CORS setup. REST APIs have more features. These include API keys and usage plans for per-client throttling and quotas, request validation, request and response mapping templates, response caching, AWS WAF integration, edge-optimised and private endpoint types, and a wider set of direct AWS service integrations. I choose an HTTP API for a straightforward serverless backend with JWT authentication where cost matters. I choose a REST API when I must monetise or meter partners with API keys, need WAF, caching or validation, or must expose a private API only inside a VPC. Both have a default integration timeout of 29 seconds, so long work should be made asynchronous.
keyPoints: HTTP API: cheaper, lower latency, native JWT authorizers
REST API: API keys, usage plans, validation, caching, WAF, private endpoints
Choose by required features first, then cost
Both have a default 29-second integration timeout

subjective.question: How do you design a DynamoDB data model? Explain partition keys, sort keys, GSIs and how to avoid hot partitions.
subjective.answer: I start from access patterns, not entities. I list every query the application needs, then design keys to serve them with Query operations rather than Scans. The partition key decides which partition stores an item, so it needs high cardinality and even traffic, such as userId rather than status. The sort key groups related items and supports range queries, for example ORDER#2026-01-15, which lets me fetch a user's orders by date. In single-table design, I store several entity types under shared keys so one query returns related data. Global secondary indexes give alternative keys for other patterns, with their own capacity, and are eventually consistent. Local secondary indexes share the partition key and must be created with the table. To avoid hot partitions, I avoid low-cardinality keys and can add write sharding with a random or calculated suffix. Items are limited to 400 KB, so large blobs go to S3 with a pointer in the item.
keyPoints: Design from access patterns; prefer Query over Scan
High-cardinality partition key for even distribution
Sort key for grouping and range queries; single-table design
GSIs for other patterns, eventually consistent; LSIs at table creation
Write sharding for hot keys; 400 KB item limit, large data in S3

subjective.question: Explain DynamoDB provisioned and on-demand capacity. Walk through a capacity calculation.
subjective.answer: On-demand mode charges per request and scales automatically. It suits new or unpredictable workloads. Provisioned mode lets you set RCUs and WCUs, usually with auto scaling. It is cheaper for steady, predictable traffic. One RCU gives one strongly consistent read per second for an item up to 4 KB, or two eventually consistent reads. One WCU gives one write per second for up to 1 KB. Sizes always round up. For example, 100 eventually consistent reads per second of 10 KB items: 10 KB rounds to 12 KB, which is 3 RCUs for a strongly consistent read, halved for eventually consistent, so 1.5 RCUs each, giving 150 RCUs. For 40 writes per second of 2.5 KB, each write is 3 WCUs, so 120 WCUs. If those writes use transactions, the cost doubles to 240 WCUs. If throughput exceeds capacity, you get ProvisionedThroughputExceededException, and the SDK retries with exponential backoff.
keyPoints: On-demand for unpredictable load; provisioned plus auto scaling for steady load
RCU = 4 KB strongly consistent read/s, or two eventually consistent
WCU = 1 KB write/s; always round up item size
Transactions cost double
Throttling errors handled by SDK retries with exponential backoff

subjective.question: Design a CI/CD pipeline for a serverless API using AWS developer tools. How do you make deployments safe?
subjective.answer: I keep the application and infrastructure as code with AWS SAM or CDK in a Git repository. CodePipeline triggers on a push to the main branch. In the build stage, CodeBuild runs unit tests, linting and a security scan, then runs sam build and sam package to upload artefacts to S3. The pipeline deploys to a test stage through CloudFormation, runs integration tests, and then waits for a manual approval before production. For safe releases, I publish a new Lambda version and use a SAM DeploymentPreference. This uses CodeDeploy to shift traffic on an alias using a canary or linear pattern. I add pre-traffic and post-traffic hook functions for smoke tests and link CloudWatch alarms on errors and latency, so CodeDeploy rolls back automatically. Secrets stay in Secrets Manager, and each stage uses a least-privilege IAM role.
keyPoints: Infrastructure as code with SAM or CDK in Git
CodePipeline with CodeBuild tests and packaging
Test stage, integration tests, manual approval for production
CodeDeploy canary or linear traffic shifting on Lambda aliases
Hooks and CloudWatch alarms for automatic rollback

subjective.question: How do you use AWS X-Ray and CloudWatch to troubleshoot a slow serverless API?
subjective.answer: First I enable active tracing on the Lambda functions and tracing on the API Gateway stage. I instrument the code with the X-Ray SDK or AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry so calls to DynamoDB, S3 and HTTP services appear as subsegments. The X-Ray trace map then shows each service, its latency and its error rate, so I can see whether time goes into a cold start, the function code or a downstream call. I add annotations such as customerId or orderType, because annotations are indexed and can be used in filter expressions. Metadata is for extra detail that I do not need to search. In CloudWatch I check Lambda Duration, Throttles, Errors and ConcurrentExecutions, plus API Gateway Latency and IntegrationLatency. I use structured JSON logs and CloudWatch Logs Insights to find slow requests. Once I find the cause, I fix it, for example by raising memory, adding a GSI or reusing connections.
keyPoints: Enable active tracing on Lambda and API Gateway
Instrument SDK calls to get subsegments for downstream services
Annotations are indexed for filtering; metadata is not
Use CloudWatch metrics and Logs Insights alongside traces
Compare Latency with IntegrationLatency to locate delay

subjective.question: How should a developer handle secrets and encryption in an AWS application? Explain envelope encryption.
subjective.answer: Secrets never go in code, Git or plain environment variables. I store database passwords and API tokens in AWS Secrets Manager, which supports automatic rotation. For simpler configuration values or secrets that do not need rotation, I use SSM Parameter Store SecureString, which is encrypted with KMS. The function's IAM role gets permission to read only the specific secrets it needs, and I cache values in memory to reduce calls and latency. For data encryption I use AWS KMS. KMS Encrypt directly handles only small data, up to 4 KB. For larger data I use envelope encryption. I call GenerateDataKey to get a plaintext data key and an encrypted copy. I encrypt the data locally with the plaintext key, then discard it, and store the encrypted data key with the ciphertext. To decrypt, I call KMS Decrypt on the data key, then decrypt the data locally. The AWS Encryption SDK does this for me.
keyPoints: Secrets Manager for secrets with rotation; Parameter Store SecureString as alternative
Least-privilege IAM access and in-memory caching
KMS direct encryption only for data up to 4 KB
Envelope encryption with GenerateDataKey for larger data
Store encrypted data key with the ciphertext

subjective.question: Describe how you would prepare data and train a model in Amazon SageMaker for the MLA-C01 exam scope.
subjective.answer: Data usually starts in S3. I explore and clean it with SageMaker Data Wrangler or a notebook, then run repeatable transformations as SageMaker Processing jobs, or with Glue for large ETL. I handle missing values, encode categories, scale numbers, check class imbalance and split into train, validation and test sets. Clarify can check pre-training bias. Shared features go into Feature Store. For training, I pick a built-in algorithm such as XGBoost, a framework container like PyTorch, or my own container. The training job reads data from S3 using File, Pipe or FastFile mode and writes model artefacts back to S3. To cut cost, I use managed Spot training with checkpoints so interrupted jobs can resume. I use automatic model tuning to search hyperparameters against a target metric, and Experiments to track runs. Finally, I register the best model in Model Registry with its metrics for approval.
keyPoints: Data Wrangler and Processing jobs for repeatable data prep
Handle missing values, encoding, imbalance, splits; Clarify for bias
Built-in algorithms, framework containers or custom containers
Managed Spot training with checkpoints; automatic model tuning
Register approved models in Model Registry

subjective.question: Compare SageMaker real-time, serverless, asynchronous and batch inference. How do you choose?
subjective.answer: Real-time endpoints run on dedicated instances, give low and steady latency and support GPUs and auto scaling. They fit steady traffic such as a fraud check on every payment, but you pay while instances run. Serverless Inference scales automatically and charges for compute used, so it fits spiky traffic with idle gaps. It has cold starts and no GPU support. Asynchronous Inference queues requests, supports payloads up to 1 GB and processing up to 1 hour, writes results to S3, can notify through SNS and can scale to zero. It fits large documents, images or video. Batch Transform has no endpoint at all. It scores a whole dataset in S3 and shuts down, which suits nightly scoring. I choose by traffic pattern, latency need, payload size and processing time. For cost, I also consider multi-model endpoints when many small models share traffic.
keyPoints: Real-time: steady, low-latency traffic, always-on cost
Serverless: spiky traffic with idle gaps, cold starts, no GPU
Async: up to 1 GB payload and 1 hour processing, results in S3
Batch Transform: offline scoring of full datasets
Decide on latency, traffic pattern, payload size and duration

subjective.question: How do you monitor a deployed ML model and keep it accurate over time?
subjective.answer: I enable data capture on the endpoint so SageMaker stores a sample of requests and responses in S3. Then I set up SageMaker Model Monitor with baselines created from the training data. Model Monitor has four types: data quality monitoring for schema and statistical drift, model quality monitoring that compares predictions with ground-truth labels, bias drift monitoring and feature attribution drift monitoring, the last two using SageMaker Clarify. Each runs on a schedule and publishes violations and metrics to CloudWatch. I create CloudWatch alarms on these metrics plus operational ones such as latency, errors and CPU or GPU use. When drift crosses a threshold, an EventBridge rule can trigger a SageMaker Pipeline that retrains, evaluates and registers a new model. Deployment then goes through Model Registry approval and a safe rollout, such as blue/green with traffic shifting. Security includes VPC endpoints, KMS encryption and least-privilege roles.
keyPoints: Enable data capture on the endpoint
Baselines from training data
Four monitor types: data quality, model quality, bias drift, feature attribution drift
CloudWatch alarms and EventBridge-triggered retraining pipeline
Model Registry approval and safe deployment

subjective.question: Explain how AWS Glue and AWS Lake Formation work together to build a governed data lake.
subjective.answer: S3 stores the raw, cleaned and curated layers of the data lake. Glue crawlers scan the data, infer schemas and create tables and partitions in the Glue Data Catalog, which Athena, Redshift Spectrum and EMR all use. Glue ETL jobs, written in PySpark or with Glue Studio, transform data, for example from CSV to partitioned Parquet. DynamicFrames handle messy schemas. Job bookmarks track processed data so incremental runs do not reprocess old files. Glue Data Quality can check rules, and workflows or Step Functions orchestrate the jobs. Lake Formation adds governance on top of the catalog. Instead of managing many S3 bucket policies, I grant database, table, column, row and cell-level permissions in Lake Formation, often using LF-Tags to scale. Data filters hide sensitive columns such as email and restrict rows by region. Integrated services such as Athena enforce these permissions, and access can be audited through CloudTrail.
keyPoints: Glue crawlers populate the Data Catalog
Glue ETL jobs transform to optimised formats; job bookmarks for incremental loads
Data Catalog shared by Athena, Redshift Spectrum and EMR
Lake Formation for fine-grained column, row and cell permissions
LF-Tags and data filters simplify governance at scale

subjective.question: A team says Athena is slow and expensive. What steps would you take to optimise it?
subjective.answer: Athena charges by data scanned, so the goal is to scan less. First, I convert raw CSV or JSON to a columnar format such as Parquet or ORC, usually with a Glue job or an Athena CTAS query. Columnar formats let Athena read only the needed columns and skip blocks using statistics. Second, I compress with Snappy or ZSTD. Third, I partition by columns used in filters, often date, and make sure queries filter on partition columns. When there are very many partitions, I use partition projection, so Athena calculates partitions from table properties instead of looking them up in the catalog. It also removes the need for MSCK REPAIR or crawlers to add partitions. I also fix the small-files problem by compacting into larger files, and select only needed columns instead of SELECT *. Workgroups can set data-scanned limits per query for cost control.
keyPoints: Athena pricing is per data scanned
Convert to Parquet or ORC and compress
Partition by commonly filtered columns such as date
Partition projection for many partitions
Compact small files, avoid SELECT *, use workgroup limits

subjective.question: Compare Kinesis Data Streams and Amazon Data Firehose. Explain shard limits and enhanced fan-out.
subjective.answer: Kinesis Data Streams is a real-time stream that you read with your own consumers, such as Lambda, Managed Service for Apache Flink or KCL applications. Data is retained for replay, and ordering is kept per shard using the partition key. In provisioned mode each shard accepts 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s for writes and gives 2 MB/s for reads. On-demand mode scales capacity automatically. With standard consumers, all consumers share the 2 MB/s read limit per shard. Enhanced fan-out gives each registered consumer its own 2 MB/s per shard using push delivery, with lower latency. It is good when several applications read the same stream. Amazon Data Firehose is fully managed delivery. It buffers data and loads it into S3, Redshift, OpenSearch and other destinations, with optional Lambda transformation and format conversion to Parquet. It needs no shard management, but it is near real time, not for custom replay. I use Data Streams for custom real-time processing and Firehose for simple loading.
keyPoints: Data Streams: custom consumers, replay, per-shard ordering
Shard: 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s write, 2 MB/s read
Enhanced fan-out: 2 MB/s per shard per consumer
Firehose: managed buffered delivery to S3, Redshift, OpenSearch
Firehose can transform and convert formats with no shards to manage

subjective.question: How do you design Amazon Redshift tables and loads for good performance? Walk through the project you shipped for this step.
subjective.answer: For Redshift, I load data with the COPY command from S3, which loads in parallel. Splitting input into multiple compressed files helps. I avoid single-row inserts. I choose a distribution style: KEY on the join column for large fact tables, ALL for small dimension tables, EVEN when there is no clear join, or AUTO to let Redshift decide. Sort keys on commonly filtered columns, such as date, let Redshift skip blocks. I use materialised views for repeated aggregations, Redshift Spectrum to query cold data in S3, and Redshift Serverless when workloads are irregular. For my project, I built a pipeline: Firehose ingests clickstream data to S3, a Glue job converts it to date-partitioned Parquet, Lake Formation controls access, Athena serves ad-hoc queries and Redshift serves dashboards. The public repository contains infrastructure as code, a README and an architecture diagram showing data flow, IAM boundaries and monitoring.
keyPoints: COPY from S3 in parallel with multiple compressed files
Distribution styles: KEY, ALL, EVEN, AUTO
Sort keys for block skipping; materialised views
Spectrum for S3 data; Serverless for irregular workloads
Project in public repo with IaC, README and architecture diagram

steps.overview: This step prepares you for the two Professional exams: SAP-C02 (Solutions Architect) and DOP-C02 (DevOps Engineer). Both have 75 questions in 180 minutes and a 750/1000 pass mark. They test design trade-offs across many accounts, hybrid networks, migrations, cost, infrastructure as code, safe deployments and incident response. Long, dense scenarios are the real challenge, so speed-reading and elimination matter as much as service knowledge.
objectives: Design a multi-account landing zone using AWS Organizations, Control Tower, OUs and SCPs
Choose the right hybrid connectivity (Site-to-Site VPN, Direct Connect, Transit Gateway) for a given scenario
Select a migration strategy from the 7 Rs and the right migration tools
Build and explain a blue/green or canary pipeline using CloudFormation or CDK, CodePipeline and CodeDeploy
Answer 75 long scenario questions in 180 minutes and score above 75% on practice exams

concepts.explanation: Organizations groups accounts into OUs under one management account, with consolidated billing. Service control policies (SCPs) set the maximum permissions for member accounts. They never grant access, so IAM policies are still needed. SCPs do not apply to the management account, so keep workloads out of it.

Control Tower automates a landing zone on top of Organizations. It creates a Security OU with Log Archive and Audit accounts, sets up IAM Identity Center, and applies controls (guardrails). Controls are preventive (SCPs), detective (AWS Config rules) or proactive (CloudFormation hooks). Account Factory vends new, pre-configured accounts.

Site-to-Site VPN is quick, encrypted, runs over the internet, and gives about 1.25 Gbps per tunnel. Direct Connect is a private, consistent-latency link but takes weeks to provision and is not encrypted by default (use MACsec or a VPN over it). Transit Gateway is a hub that connects many VPCs and on-premises networks. A Direct Connect gateway links one DX connection to VPCs in many Regions.

The 7 Rs are Retire, Retain, Rehost, Relocate, Repurchase, Replatform and Refactor. Rehost (lift and shift) usually uses AWS Application Migration Service. Databases use AWS DMS, plus the Schema Conversion Tool for engine changes. Use Migration Hub to track progress and Application Discovery Service to inventory servers. Use Snowball for large offline data transfers.

Right-size first with Compute Optimizer. Then commit with Savings Plans (Compute is most flexible; EC2 Instance is cheaper but tied to one family and Region) or Reserved Instances. Use Spot for fault-tolerant work. Reduce data transfer costs with VPC endpoints and CloudFront, and use S3 lifecycle rules or Intelligent-Tiering. Cost Explorer, Budgets and cost allocation tags give visibility.

StackSets deploy one template to many accounts and Regions, and can auto-deploy to new accounts in an OU. Change sets preview changes before you apply them. DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy (Retain or Snapshot) protect data. Drift detection finds manual changes. CreationPolicy with cfn-signal waits for instances to report that they are healthy.

CDK lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python and other languages. It synthesises (cdk synth) to CloudFormation templates. Each account and Region must be bootstrapped (cdk bootstrap) before deployment. CDK Pipelines provides a self-mutating CodePipeline for multi-account delivery.

Choose between in-place, rolling, immutable, blue/green and canary or linear. CodeDeploy supports blue/green for EC2, ECS and Lambda. ECS and Lambda can shift traffic in canary, linear or all-at-once steps. CloudWatch alarms can trigger automatic rollback.

CloudWatch provides metrics, Logs, alarms, composite alarms and Synthetics canaries. X-Ray provides tracing. EventBridge rules route events such as GuardDuty findings or Config non-compliance to Lambda, SSM Automation or Step Functions for auto-remediation. Systems Manager OpsCenter and Incident Manager help run the incident process.

keyFacts: SAP-C02 and DOP-C02: 75 questions (65 scored + 10 unscored), 180 minutes, USD 300, pass 750/1000. That is about 2.4 minutes per question.
SCPs restrict permissions but never grant them. They do not affect the management account.
Control Tower's core accounts are Management, Log Archive and Audit. The last two sit in the Security OU.
A Site-to-Site VPN tunnel gives about 1.25 Gbps. Use ECMP over Transit Gateway to aggregate bandwidth.
Direct Connect has no encryption by default. Add MACsec or an IPsec VPN over it if encryption is required.
For DX resilience, use two connections at two different DX locations for maximum resiliency, or a VPN as a low-cost backup.
A Compute Savings Plan covers EC2, Fargate and Lambda across Regions and families. An EC2 Instance Savings Plan gives the deepest discount but is locked to one family and Region.
CodeDeploy predefined configs include Canary10Percent5Minutes, Linear10PercentEvery1Minute and AllAtOnce, for Lambda and ECS.
Use StackSets with service-managed permissions and automatic deployment to cover accounts that join an OU later.
Decision rule: if the question says 'least operational overhead', prefer a managed service such as Control Tower, MGN or managed rotation over custom scripts.

example.caption: Landing zone SCP: deny actions outside approved Regions (ap-south-1, ap-south-2), but allow global services and a break-glass admin role

pitfalls: Picking an answer that puts workloads or SCP-based controls in the management account. SCPs do not apply there.
Assuming Direct Connect is encrypted, or choosing Direct Connect when the scenario needs connectivity within days. VPN is the fast option.
Choosing a custom Lambda or script solution when a managed feature (Control Tower controls, StackSets, Config remediation) meets the need with less effort.
Confusing blue/green (two full environments, instant switch, fast rollback) with rolling or in-place updates, which reduce capacity and roll back slowly.
Reading every option in full before reading the last sentence of the question. Read the actual ask first ('most cost-effective', 'least downtime').
Spending more than 4 minutes on one question. Flag it, move on and come back. Unanswered questions score zero, and there is no penalty for guessing.

workflow.title: Hands-on: design a multi-account landing zone end to end

steps.label: Set up Control Tower
steps.detail: Enable Control Tower in your home Region (for example ap-south-1) to create the Log Archive and Audit accounts and IAM Identity Center.

steps.label: Design the OU structure
steps.detail: Create Security, Infrastructure, Workloads/Prod, Workloads/NonProd and Sandbox OUs, each with different controls.

steps.label: Apply SCPs and controls
steps.detail: Attach Region-deny, root-user-deny and 'do not disable CloudTrail or GuardDuty' SCPs, then enable detective Config controls.

steps.label: Build shared networking
steps.detail: In a Network account, deploy Transit Gateway, shared via RAM, plus Direct Connect or VPN to on-premises and centralised egress.

steps.label: Centralise security and logs
steps.detail: Delegate GuardDuty, Security Hub and Config aggregation to the Audit account, and send organisation CloudTrail logs to Log Archive.

steps.label: Automate account baselines
steps.detail: Use Account Factory and CloudFormation StackSets with auto-deployment to push VPCs, roles and budgets into every new account.

steps.label: Add cost governance
steps.detail: Enable cost allocation tags, AWS Budgets alerts and Cost Explorer, and buy Savings Plans centrally in the management account.

objective.question: A company uses AWS Organizations. A security engineer attaches an SCP that denies all EC2 actions to the root of the organization. Which accounts can still launch EC2 instances, provided their IAM policies allow it?
options: Only the management account
Only accounts that have a delegated administrator
Only accounts in the Security OU
No account in the organization
objective.explanation: SCPs never affect users or roles in the management account, so it can still launch EC2 if IAM allows it. Every member account is restricted, including Security OU and delegated administrator accounts.

objective.question: An OU has an SCP that allows only Amazon S3 and Amazon EC2 actions. The default FullAWSAccess SCP has been removed from that OU. An IAM user in a member account in this OU has the AdministratorAccess policy. What happens when the user tries to create a DynamoDB table?
options: The action is denied because the SCP does not allow DynamoDB
The action succeeds only if a permissions boundary also allows it
The action succeeds because SCPs only apply to roles, not users
The action succeeds because AdministratorAccess grants all actions
objective.explanation: Effective permissions are the intersection of what SCPs allow and what IAM policies grant. SCPs never grant permissions, so AdministratorAccess cannot go beyond the SCP allow list, and DynamoDB is blocked. SCPs apply to both users and roles in member accounts.

objective.question: A company sets up a new landing zone with AWS Control Tower. Where are the Log Archive and Audit accounts placed by default?
options: In the Sandbox OU
In the Infrastructure OU
In the Security OU
In the Root, next to the management account
objective.explanation: Control Tower creates the Log Archive and Audit accounts inside the Security OU. The management account stays at the root. The Sandbox OU is for workload accounts.

objective.question: A platform team uses AWS Control Tower. They want to stop non-compliant resources, such as unencrypted S3 buckets, before CloudFormation provisions them, instead of finding them after creation. Which type of control should they enable?
options: Detective controls implemented as AWS Config rules
Detective controls implemented as Amazon GuardDuty findings
Proactive controls implemented as CloudFormation hooks
Preventive controls implemented as SCPs
objective.explanation: Proactive controls use CloudFormation hooks to check resources before provisioning. Detective controls only report after a resource exists. Preventive SCPs block API actions but cannot inspect resource properties in a template.

objective.question: A company needs about 4 Gbps of encrypted bandwidth between its data centre and many VPCs. Direct Connect will take months to arrive. What should a solutions architect do now?
options: Create multiple Site-to-Site VPN connections to a Transit Gateway and enable ECMP
Create a Client VPN endpoint for the data centre router
Use VPC peering from the data centre to each VPC
Create one Site-to-Site VPN to a virtual private gateway and increase the tunnel size
objective.explanation: Each VPN tunnel gives about 1.25 Gbps and its size cannot be increased. ECMP on a Transit Gateway spreads traffic across multiple VPN tunnels to aggregate bandwidth. A virtual private gateway does not support ECMP across connections, VPC peering cannot connect on-premises networks, and Client VPN is for individual users.

objective.question: A bank uses a dedicated AWS Direct Connect connection. A new compliance rule says all traffic between on premises and AWS must be encrypted in transit. What should the architect do?
options: Enable MACsec on a supported dedicated connection, or run an IPsec Site-to-Site VPN over the Direct Connect
Switch the private VIF to a public VIF
Enable encryption on the Direct Connect gateway
Nothing, because Direct Connect encrypts traffic by default
objective.explanation: Direct Connect is private, but traffic is not encrypted by default. MACsec, on supported dedicated connections, or an IPsec VPN over DX adds encryption. A public VIF and the Direct Connect gateway do not provide encryption.

objective.question: A company has one Direct Connect connection for a production workload. It wants a backup path at the lowest cost and accepts lower bandwidth during a failure. What should it do?
options: Add a Site-to-Site VPN as a backup path
Add a second private VIF on the same connection
Add connections at two different DX locations
Add a second Direct Connect connection at the same DX location
objective.explanation: A Site-to-Site VPN is the low-cost backup for Direct Connect when lower bandwidth is acceptable. Connections at two DX locations give the highest resiliency but cost much more. A second VIF on the same connection, or a second connection at the same location, does not remove the single point of failure.

objective.question: A company wants to move 300 VMware vSphere VMs to AWS quickly. It wants no changes to the VMs and wants to keep its existing VMware tools and skills. Which migration strategy fits best?
options: Relocate using VMware Cloud on AWS
Replatform to Amazon ECS
Repurchase to a SaaS product
Rehost using AWS Application Migration Service
objective.explanation: Relocate moves VMs as they are to VMware Cloud on AWS, so the team keeps vSphere tooling and does not convert the VMs. Rehost with MGN turns the servers into EC2 instances, so VMware tools no longer apply. Replatform and repurchase both change the application.

objective.question: A company must lift and shift 200 on-premises Linux and Windows servers to Amazon EC2 with the least operational overhead and a short cutover window. Which approach should it use?
options: Use AWS Application Migration Service (MGN) with continuous block-level replication
Rebuild each server manually from AMIs and copy data with rsync
Use AWS DMS to replicate the servers
Write custom scripts to export disk images and import them with VM Import
objective.explanation: MGN is the managed rehost service. It replicates continuously and gives short, testable cutovers. Custom scripts and manual rebuilds add operational overhead, and DMS migrates databases, not whole servers.

objective.question: A company runs steady workloads on EC2, and it often changes instance families and Regions. It also runs containers on AWS Fargate and functions on AWS Lambda. It wants a commitment-based discount that covers all of these. What should it buy?
options: Compute Savings Plan
Spot Instances with a Spot Fleet
Standard Reserved Instances
EC2 Instance Savings Plan
objective.explanation: A Compute Savings Plan applies across EC2 families and Regions, and also covers Fargate and Lambda. An EC2 Instance Savings Plan is locked to one family and Region. Standard RIs do not cover Fargate or Lambda, and Spot is not a commitment discount and can be interrupted.

objective.question: A security team must deploy an IAM role and an AWS Config rule to every account in the Workloads OU. New accounts are added to this OU each month, and the resources must appear in them with no manual work. What is the best solution?
options: CloudFormation StackSets with service-managed permissions and automatic deployment enabled, targeting the OU
A Lambda function that runs every month and calls CreateStack in each account
A nested stack in the management account
CloudFormation StackSets with self-managed permissions, updated monthly
objective.explanation: Service-managed StackSets that target an OU, with automatic deployment on, deploy to accounts that join the OU later. Self-managed permissions need manual account lists and roles. Nested stacks work only in one account, and a custom Lambda adds operational overhead.

objective.question: A CloudFormation stack contains an Amazon RDS DB instance. The team wants a final copy of the data to stay available if someone deletes the stack by mistake, and it wants to avoid paying for a running instance after deletion. What should it set on the DB resource?
options: UpdateReplacePolicy: Delete
A stack policy that denies Update:*
DeletionPolicy: Delete
DeletionPolicy: Snapshot
objective.explanation: DeletionPolicy Snapshot takes a final snapshot when the resource is deleted, so the data survives without a running instance. Delete removes the data. A stack policy protects against updates, not stack deletion.

objective.question: A developer runs 'cdk deploy' for the first time in a new account and Region. The deployment fails because the assets bucket and deployment roles do not exist. What should the developer run first?
options: cdk diff
cdk init
cdk bootstrap
cdk synth
objective.explanation: cdk bootstrap creates the CDKToolkit stack, which holds the asset bucket, the ECR repository and the IAM roles CDK uses to deploy. synth and diff only produce or compare templates, and init creates a new project.

objective.question: A team deploys a Lambda function through AWS CodeDeploy. It wants 10% of traffic sent to the new version first, and the remaining 90% shifted after 5 minutes if no problems occur. It also wants automatic rollback if the error rate rises. Which configuration meets this?
options: CodeDeployDefault.LambdaAllAtOnce with a pre-traffic hook
A weighted Route 53 record with 10% weight
CodeDeployDefault.LambdaCanary10Percent5Minutes with CloudWatch alarms attached to the deployment group
CodeDeployDefault.LambdaLinear10PercentEvery1Minute with no alarms
objective.explanation: Canary10Percent5Minutes shifts 10% of traffic and then, after 5 minutes, the rest. CloudWatch alarms on the deployment group trigger automatic rollback. Linear shifts in equal steps, AllAtOnce has no gradual shift, and Route 53 weighting does not manage Lambda alias versions or roll back automatically.

objective.question: An operations team gets paged many times during one incident, because separate CloudWatch alarms for CPU, latency and 5xx errors all fire together. It wants one page only when high latency and high 5xx errors happen at the same time, with the least operational overhead. What should it do?
options: Write a Lambda function that reads all alarms every minute and decides whether to page
Increase the evaluation periods on every alarm
Send all alarms to an SQS queue and deduplicate them
Create a CloudWatch composite alarm using AND on the latency and 5xx alarms, and send notifications only from the composite alarm
objective.explanation: Composite alarms combine alarm states with rule expressions such as AND, which reduces alarm noise with no custom code. A custom Lambda or SQS deduplication adds overhead, and longer evaluation periods only delay alerts without linking the conditions.

subjective.question: Explain how Service Control Policies work and how they combine with IAM policies to give effective permissions.
subjective.answer: An SCP is an organisation policy attached to the root, an OU or an account. It sets the maximum permissions for IAM users and roles in member accounts. It never grants anything. A user can do an action only if every SCP in the path from root to account allows it, the IAM identity or resource policy allows it, and no explicit deny exists anywhere. By default, the FullAWSAccess SCP is attached. You can use deny lists, such as denying the disabling of CloudTrail or the use of unapproved Regions, or allow lists, where you replace FullAWSAccess. SCPs do not affect the management account or service-linked roles. Because of this, I keep workloads out of the management account and use it only for billing and governance.
keyPoints: SCPs set guardrails and never grant permissions
Effective permission is the intersection of SCP and IAM, and an explicit deny always wins
Deny-list and allow-list strategies
No effect on the management account or service-linked roles

subjective.question: Design a multi-account landing zone for a mid-sized company using AWS Control Tower. Describe the OUs and accounts.
subjective.answer: I would start Control Tower in the management account and choose the home Region and governed Regions. It creates the Security OU with the Log Archive account, which holds central CloudTrail and Config logs, and the Audit account, which gives the security team cross-account access. I would add an Infrastructure OU for shared networking, such as Transit Gateway, the Direct Connect gateway and shared services. Then I would add a Workloads OU split into Prod and Non-Prod, a Sandbox OU with tight budget controls, and a Suspended OU for accounts being closed. Identity goes through IAM Identity Center with permission sets. I would enable mandatory and strongly recommended controls, add a Region deny control, and vend accounts through Account Factory. Security tools such as GuardDuty and Security Hub use the Audit account as delegated administrator.
keyPoints: Management, Log Archive and Audit accounts, with the last two in the Security OU
Separate OUs for infrastructure, prod/non-prod workloads, sandbox and suspended accounts
IAM Identity Center for central access
Controls and Region deny applied by OU
Delegated administrator for security services

subjective.question: How would you make every new account vended by Control Tower get a standard baseline, such as VPC, IAM roles and Config rules, with minimum manual work?
subjective.answer: I would use Account Factory to create accounts, so they are enrolled and governed from day one. For the baseline, I have three managed options. Customizations for AWS Control Tower (CfCT) deploys CloudFormation templates and SCPs when lifecycle events such as account creation happen. Account Factory for Terraform (AFT) does the same if the team uses Terraform. A simpler option is service-managed CloudFormation StackSets targeted at an OU with automatic deployment, so any account that joins the OU gets the stacks. Networking can be shared through AWS RAM, for example by sharing Transit Gateway attachments or subnets. I would avoid custom scripts. In exam terms, 'least operational overhead' points to these managed features.
keyPoints: Account Factory for vending
CfCT or AFT driven by lifecycle events
StackSets with automatic deployment by OU
Prefer managed options over custom scripts

subjective.question: Design hybrid connectivity between an on-premises data centre and 50 VPCs across two Regions.
subjective.answer: I would put a Transit Gateway in each Region as the hub and attach the VPCs to it, using route tables to keep prod and non-prod separate. For the main path, I would use Direct Connect with a transit VIF to a Direct Connect gateway that is associated with both Transit Gateways. This gives one private link that reaches both Regions. For backup, I would add Site-to-Site VPN attachments on the Transit Gateways. ECMP lets several tunnels add up to more bandwidth, since each tunnel is about 1.25 Gbps. BGP route preferences keep DX as the primary path. The two Transit Gateways can peer for inter-Region traffic. For DNS, I would use Route 53 Resolver inbound and outbound endpoints in a shared networking account, shared through AWS RAM.
keyPoints: Transit Gateway as the regional hub
DX with transit VIF and DX gateway for multi-Region reach
VPN backup with ECMP and BGP preference
Route 53 Resolver endpoints for hybrid DNS
Central networking account shared through RAM

subjective.question: A customer says Direct Connect is private, so it is encrypted. How do you respond, and how do you make DX resilient?
subjective.answer: Private is not the same as encrypted. Direct Connect traffic travels over a dedicated path, but AWS does not encrypt it by default. If compliance needs encryption in transit, I would enable MACsec on supported dedicated connections, which gives layer-2 encryption at line rate. Another option is an IPsec Site-to-Site VPN over the DX connection, often over a public or transit VIF. Application-level TLS also helps, but auditors often want network encryption. For resiliency, one connection is a single point of failure. The strongest design uses connections at two different DX locations, so a whole location can fail. If budget is tight, I would add a Site-to-Site VPN as a low-cost backup and accept the lower bandwidth during failover.
keyPoints: DX is not encrypted by default
MACsec or IPsec VPN over DX
Multiple DX locations for maximum resiliency
VPN as a cheap backup path

subjective.question: Explain the 7 Rs of migration with a short example of each.
subjective.answer: Retire means switching off apps nobody uses, such as an old reporting server. Retain means keeping an app on premises for now, perhaps because of a recent hardware refresh or a licence constraint. Rehost is lift and shift to EC2 with AWS Application Migration Service. Relocate moves VMware workloads as they are to VMware Cloud on AWS. Replatform makes small optimisations without changing the core code, such as moving a self-managed MySQL database to Amazon RDS. Repurchase means moving to a SaaS product, such as replacing an on-premises CRM. Refactor, or re-architect, redesigns the app for cloud-native services, such as breaking a monolith into Lambda and DynamoDB. In exams, the key words point to the answer: 'quickly, no code change' means rehost, and 'scalability and agility, accept effort' means refactor.
keyPoints: All seven: retire, retain, rehost, relocate, replatform, repurchase, refactor
One concrete example of each
Map scenario keywords to the strategy
Rehost uses MGN; relocate uses VMware Cloud on AWS

subjective.question: Walk through the AWS tools you would use for a large data-centre migration, from discovery to cutover.
subjective.answer: First, I assess. Migration Evaluator builds the business case, and AWS Application Discovery Service collects server inventory, utilisation and dependencies, using agents or the agentless collector. I track everything in AWS Migration Hub and group servers into applications and waves. The landing zone is ready beforehand through Control Tower. For servers, I use AWS Application Migration Service (MGN). It replicates continuously and lets me launch test instances before a short cutover. For databases, I use AWS DMS, with the Schema Conversion Tool if the engine changes, and change data capture to keep the target in sync. For large offline data, I use the Snowball family, and for file data I use DataSync. After cutover, I right-size using Compute Optimizer.
keyPoints: Assess with Migration Evaluator and Application Discovery Service
Track waves in Migration Hub
MGN for servers, DMS and SCT for databases
DataSync or Snowball for bulk data
Test launches before cutover, then right-size

subjective.question: What are the main cost optimisation levers on AWS, and in what order would you apply them?
subjective.answer: First, I get visibility. I use Cost Explorer, tagging with cost allocation tags, AWS Budgets, and Cost Anomaly Detection across the organisation. Then I remove waste, such as idle instances, unattached EBS volumes, old snapshots and unused Elastic IPs. Next, I right-size using Compute Optimizer and move to Graviton where the workload supports it. I add scheduling or Auto Scaling so non-prod resources are not running at night. Only after right-sizing do I commit, with Savings Plans or Reserved Instances for the steady baseline. I use Spot for fault-tolerant work such as batch jobs or CI. For storage, I use S3 lifecycle rules, S3 Intelligent-Tiering and gp3 volumes. For networking, I cut NAT and inter-AZ data transfer by using VPC endpoints. Committing before right-sizing locks in waste.
keyPoints: Visibility first: tags, Cost Explorer, Budgets, anomaly detection
Remove waste, then right-size
Commit with Savings Plans after right-sizing
Spot for fault-tolerant work
Storage tiering and data transfer reduction

subjective.question: Compare Compute Savings Plans, EC2 Instance Savings Plans, Reserved Instances and Spot Instances.
subjective.answer: All except Spot are commitments, usually for one or three years. A Compute Savings Plan commits to an hourly spend and applies across EC2 families, sizes, operating systems and Regions, and also to Fargate and Lambda. It is the most flexible. An EC2 Instance Savings Plan gives a deeper discount but is locked to one instance family in one Region, though size and OS can change. Reserved Instances are older. They still matter for services like RDS, ElastiCache and OpenSearch, which Savings Plans do not cover in the same way, and zonal RIs also reserve capacity. Spot gives the largest discount on spare capacity but can be reclaimed with a two-minute warning. I would use it for stateless, interruption-tolerant work. A common design is Savings Plans for the baseline, On-Demand for peaks and Spot for batch.
keyPoints: Compute SP: flexible across family, Region, Fargate and Lambda
EC2 Instance SP: deepest SP discount, one family and Region
RIs still matter for databases and for capacity reservation
Spot: cheapest, interruptible, for fault-tolerant work

subjective.question: How do you manage CloudFormation safely at scale across many teams and accounts?
subjective.answer: I split templates into layers, such as network, security and application. I use nested stacks for reuse and exports or SSM parameters to share values. Every change goes through a change set, so reviewers see exactly what will be replaced. Critical resources get a DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy of Retain or Snapshot, a stack policy to block risky updates, and termination protection on the stack. I run drift detection on a schedule to catch manual changes. For multi-account rollout, I use StackSets with service-managed permissions, targeting OUs with automatic deployment, and I set failure tolerance and maximum concurrent accounts so a bad change stops early. I run cfn-lint and cfn-guard in the pipeline. Templates live in Git and deploy only through CodePipeline, not from the console.
keyPoints: Change sets, stack policies, deletion policies, termination protection
Drift detection
StackSets with OU targets and failure tolerance
Linting and policy checks in the pipeline
Deploy only through a pipeline

subjective.question: What is the AWS CDK, how does it relate to CloudFormation, and what are construct levels?
subjective.answer: The CDK lets you define infrastructure in languages like TypeScript or Python. 'cdk synth' turns the code into a CloudFormation template, and 'cdk deploy' deploys it as a CloudFormation stack. So you keep CloudFormation's rollback and drift features but gain loops, types and reuse. Constructs come in three levels. L1 constructs, named Cfn-something, map one-to-one to CloudFormation resources. L2 constructs add sensible defaults and helper methods, such as bucket.grantRead(role), which writes the IAM policy for you. L3 constructs, or patterns, combine many resources, such as a load-balanced Fargate service. Each account and Region must be bootstrapped once. I use 'cdk diff' before deploying, write unit tests with the assertions module, and use CDK Pipelines for self-mutating delivery.
keyPoints: CDK synthesises to CloudFormation
L1, L2 and L3 construct levels
cdk bootstrap, synth, diff and deploy
Testing with assertions and CDK Pipelines

subjective.question: Compare all-at-once, rolling, blue/green, canary and linear deployments. When would you choose each?
subjective.answer: All-at-once updates every target together. It is fast and cheap but causes downtime and has a large blast radius, so it suits dev environments. Rolling updates in batches. It needs no extra capacity, but capacity drops during deployment and rollback is slow. Rolling with an additional batch avoids the capacity drop. Blue/green builds a full new environment and switches traffic, using a load balancer target group, DNS or a Lambda alias. Rollback is instant, but you pay for double capacity for a short time. Canary sends a small share first, such as Canary10Percent5Minutes, then the rest. Linear shifts in equal steps, such as Linear10PercentEvery1Minute. Canary and linear deployments with CloudWatch alarms give automatic rollback. For production APIs on Lambda or ECS, I would use CodeDeploy canary with alarms.
keyPoints: Trade-offs: downtime, cost, blast radius and rollback speed
Rolling and rolling with an additional batch
Blue/green gives instant rollback at the cost of double capacity
Canary versus linear traffic shifting
Alarm-based automatic rollback

subjective.question: Describe an end-to-end blue/green pipeline for a containerised application on Amazon ECS.
subjective.answer: The source is a CodeCommit, GitHub or Bitbucket repository, connected through CodeStar Connections. CodePipeline triggers CodeBuild, which runs unit tests and security scans, builds the image and pushes it to Amazon ECR with image scanning. A deploy stage uses CodeDeploy with the ECS blue/green deployment type. The ALB has two target groups and a production listener, plus a test listener. CodeDeploy starts the green task set and runs hooks, such as an AfterAllowTestTraffic Lambda for smoke tests on the test listener. It then shifts production traffic using a config such as ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes. CloudWatch alarms on 5xx errors and latency are attached to the deployment group for automatic rollback. Blue tasks are kept for a set wait time before termination. I define the whole pipeline in CDK or CloudFormation and add a manual approval before production.
keyPoints: CodePipeline, CodeBuild and ECR flow
CodeDeploy ECS blue/green with two target groups and a test listener
Lifecycle hooks for smoke tests
Canary traffic shift with alarm rollback
Pipeline defined as code, with approval before prod

subjective.question: How would you design monitoring and automated incident response for a multi-account environment?
subjective.answer: I would collect signals centrally. CloudTrail runs as an organisation trail to the Log Archive account. CloudWatch cross-account observability sends metrics, logs and traces to a monitoring account. GuardDuty, Security Hub and Config use the Audit account as delegated administrator. Applications use CloudWatch metrics, structured logs, X-Ray tracing and Synthetics canaries. I would use composite alarms to reduce noise. For response, EventBridge rules match events such as a GuardDuty finding, a Config non-compliance or an alarm state change. They trigger Systems Manager Automation runbooks, for example to isolate an instance with a quarantine security group or to revoke a key. AWS Systems Manager Incident Manager handles paging, escalation and response plans. After each incident, I hold a blameless review and turn manual steps into runbooks.
keyPoints: Central logging, metrics and security findings
Composite alarms to cut noise
EventBridge plus SSM Automation for remediation
Incident Manager for engagement and escalation
Post-incident reviews feed automation

subjective.question: SAP-C02 and DOP-C02 have long scenario questions. How do you manage time and read them quickly?
subjective.answer: Both exams have 75 questions, of which 65 are scored and 10 unscored, in 180 minutes. That is about 2.4 minutes per question. I read the last sentence first to find what is asked. Then I scan the scenario for constraints: 'least operational overhead', 'most cost-effective', 'minimum downtime', 'without code changes', the RTO and RPO, and compliance words like 'encrypted'. I eliminate options that break a hard constraint, then compare the two remaining options on the qualifier. 'Least operational overhead' usually points to a managed service such as Control Tower, MGN or managed rotation, not custom scripts. If I am stuck after about 3 minutes, I mark the question for review and move on. My target is to finish the first pass with 20 to 30 minutes left. To prepare, I take timed full practice exams and aim to score above 75% before booking.
keyPoints: 75 questions in 180 minutes, about 2.4 minutes each
Read the question line first, then the constraints
Eliminate options using hard constraints and qualifiers
Flag and move on, keep review time
Timed practice above 75% as the readiness check

steps.overview: This step covers the logistics that turn your preparation into a valid certificate. You will choose between online proctoring and a test centre, request the ESL +30 minute accommodation if eligible, book the exam, then claim your Credly badge and plan recertification. Mistakes here, like a name mismatch, a failed system check or forgetting the ESL request, can cost you the exam fee even if you know the content.
objectives: Choose between Pearson VUE online proctoring and a test centre based on your home setup and risk tolerance
Request the ESL +30 minute accommodation in your AWS Certification Account before scheduling an English-language exam
Book, reschedule or cancel an exam within the allowed windows without losing your fee
Claim your Credly digital badge and present the certification correctly on your résumé and LinkedIn
Plan recertification within the 3-year validity period and use the 50% voucher earned from each pass

concepts.explanation: This is your central portal for AWS exams. You schedule exams, request accommodations, view score reports, download certificates and find benefits such as the 50% voucher here. Your legal name in this account must exactly match your government photo ID.

AWS exams are delivered by Pearson VUE. You can take them in person at a Pearson VUE test centre or online from home or office through OnVUE online proctoring. The exam content, length and scoring are the same in both modes.

You take the exam on your own computer while a remote proctor watches through your webcam and microphone. You must pass a system test, show your room and desk, and stay alone and in camera view for the whole exam. Common failure causes are unstable internet, corporate laptops with blocked software, extra monitors, and background noise or people.

You sit the exam at a Pearson VUE centre on its controlled hardware and network. This removes the risk of home internet or system problems. It suits learners with noisy homes, shared rooms or unreliable power, which is common in many Indian cities.

Candidates whose native language is not English can request 30 extra minutes when they take an exam in English. You request it once in the AWS Certification Account under exam accommodations, and it applies to later exams. It must be approved before you schedule, because exams booked earlier do not get the extra time automatically.

Scores are reported from 100 to 1000. The pass mark is 700 for Foundational, 720 for Associate and 750 for Professional. Some questions are unscored and used for research, and you cannot tell which ones they are. The scoring is compensatory, so you do not need to pass each domain separately.

An AWS certification is valid for 3 years. You recertify by passing the current version of the same exam before your certification expires. Passing a higher-level exam can also recertify related lower-level certifications, as listed on AWS's recertification page.

After you pass, AWS sends an email from Credly so you can claim a verifiable digital badge. You can share the badge on LinkedIn and link it in your résumé so employers can confirm it is real and current.

keyFacts: Request ESL +30 minutes BEFORE booking. The extra time only applies to exams scheduled after approval.
Certifications are valid for 3 years from the date you pass. Recertify by passing the current exam version before expiry.
Each pass gives a 50% discount voucher for your next exam. You find it in the Benefits section of your AWS Certification Account.
Exam lengths: CLF-C02 and AIF-C01 are 90 minutes, Associates are 130 minutes, Professionals are 180 minutes. ESL adds 30 minutes to each.
Pass marks are 700 for Foundational, 720 for Associate and 750 for Professional, on a 100–1000 scale.
Reschedule or cancel more than 24 hours before the appointment to avoid losing your fee.
After a failed attempt you must wait 14 days before retaking, and you pay the full fee again.
Your ID name must exactly match your AWS Certification Account name. A mismatch can mean you are turned away and lose the fee.
Results are usually available in your account within 5 business days. The Credly badge email follows after the result is released.

Taking online proctoring on an office laptop with VPN, firewall or admin restrictions. Run the Pearson VUE system test on the exact machine and network you will use.
Using a nickname or leaving out a middle or initial name in your account when your ID shows the full name. Fix your profile name before exam day.
Reading aloud, looking away from the screen often, or letting someone walk into the room during an online exam. The proctor can end your exam without a refund.
Assuming the 50% voucher lasts forever or works on any vendor's exam. It applies to AWS exams only, so check its expiry in the Benefits section and use it in time.
Letting a certification lapse. Once it expires you must pass the exam again as a new candidate, so plan recertification months ahead.
