objective.question: Priya is a non-native English speaker. She plans to take SAA-C03 and wants the ESL accommodation. What should she do first?
options: Book the exam and email AWS Support within 24 hours to add the extra time
Choose a test centre, because ESL only applies to test centre delivery
Request the ESL accommodation in her AWS Certification Account, wait for approval, then book the exam
Book the exam, then request ESL from the Pearson VUE proctor on exam day
objective.explanation: ESL (+30 minutes) must be requested and approved before you schedule, because the extra time only applies to exams booked after approval. Proctors cannot add time on exam day, and ESL is not limited to test centres.

objective.question: Rahul booked DVA-C02 for next week. Two days later his ESL accommodation was approved. What happens to his existing appointment?
options: It gets 15 extra minutes because approval came after booking
It keeps the standard 130 minutes; to get the extra time he must reschedule or cancel and rebook after approval
The appointment is cancelled by AWS and the fee is refunded
It automatically gets 30 extra minutes
objective.explanation: Extra time applies only to exams scheduled after approval, so the existing booking stays at 130 minutes. He should rebook more than 24 hours before the appointment to avoid losing the fee.

objective.question: A candidate with approved ESL accommodation books SAP-C02. How long will the exam appointment be?
options: 210 minutes
160 minutes
200 minutes
180 minutes
objective.explanation: Professional exams are 180 minutes, and ESL adds 30 minutes, giving 210 minutes. The other options use the wrong base time or the wrong extra time.

objective.question: Which pairing of exam and passing scaled score is correct?
objective.explanation: Associate exams such as DEA-C01 need 720 on a 100–1000 scale. Foundational exams (CLF-C02, AIF-C01) need 700, and Professional exams (DOP-C02, SAP-C02) need 750.

objective.question: Anita passed SAA-C03 on 10 March 2026. Which statement about her certification is correct?
options: It is valid for 3 years from 10 March 2026, and she recertifies by passing the current version before it expires
It is valid for life as long as she claims the Credly badge
It is valid until the end of the 2029 calendar year, whatever her pass date
It is valid for 2 years and renews automatically if she keeps her account active
objective.explanation: AWS certifications are valid for 3 years from the date you pass. You keep them active by passing the current exam version before expiry; nothing renews automatically.

objective.question: After passing CLF-C02, where does a candidate find the 50% discount voucher for the next exam?
options: In the Benefits section of the AWS Certification Account
In the AWS Billing console under Credits
On the printed score report at the test centre
In the Credly badge email
objective.explanation: The 50% voucher earned from passing is shown in the Benefits section of the AWS Certification Account. It is not in Credly, a score report, or the AWS Billing console.

objective.question: Karthik's MLA-C01 exam is booked for Friday at 10:00. Something urgent comes up. Which action protects his exam fee?
options: Rescheduling or cancelling before Thursday 10:00, i.e. more than 24 hours before the appointment
Rescheduling up to 1 hour before the exam starts
Calling the test centre on Friday morning to move the slot
Simply not attending; the fee carries over automatically
objective.explanation: You must reschedule or cancel more than 24 hours before the appointment to avoid losing the fee. A no-show or a late change means the fee is lost.

objective.question: Meera failed DEA-C01 on 1 June. Which statement about her retake is correct?
options: She must wait 14 days and pay the full exam fee again
She can use the 50% pass voucher for the retake
She must wait 30 days, but the retake is free
She can retake the next day at half price
objective.explanation: After a failed attempt you must wait 14 days before retaking, and you pay the full fee again. The 50% voucher is earned only by passing, so she does not have one from this attempt.

objective.question: Arjun's passport says 'Arjun Kumar Reddy', but his AWS Certification Account profile says 'Arjun Reddy'. His exam is in a week. What is the best action?
options: Bring a second ID with a shorter name
Tell the proctor about the difference at check-in
Update the AWS Certification Account name to exactly match his ID before the exam
Do nothing; proctors accept partial name matches
objective.explanation: Your ID name must exactly match your AWS Certification Account name. A mismatch can mean you are turned away and lose the fee, so fix it well before exam day rather than relying on the proctor.

objective.question: On an Associate exam with 65 questions, a candidate notices some questions feel unusually unfamiliar. Which statement about scoring is correct?
options: Some questions are unscored and used to test future content; they are not marked, so candidates should answer every question with full effort
Every question is scored and raw marks are converted to a percentage
Unscored questions are labelled 'beta' so you can skip them
Unfamiliar questions carry double marks
objective.explanation: AWS exams include unscored questions that do not affect your result, and they are not identified. Results are reported as a scaled score from 100 to 1000, not a raw percentage.

objective.question: Which statement best describes how AWS reaches a pass or fail result?
options: Your overall scaled score is compared with the pass mark; it is a compensatory model, so strong domains can offset weak ones
Only the highest-weighted domain decides the result
Wrong answers carry negative marking, so you should leave unsure questions blank
You must pass every domain separately
objective.explanation: AWS uses a compensatory scoring model: you pass on the overall scaled score, not domain by domain. There is no penalty for guessing, so blank answers simply count as incorrect.

objective.question: Sandeep lives in a shared flat with frequent power cuts and unstable Wi-Fi. He wants the lowest risk of his exam being interrupted. Which delivery option suits him best?
options: A Pearson VUE test centre
Online proctoring using his phone's mobile hotspot as the only connection
Online proctoring from a café with public Wi-Fi
Online proctoring (OnVUE) from his bedroom
objective.explanation: A test centre provides a controlled room, hardware and network, which removes home power and connectivity risks. Online proctoring needs a private, quiet room and a stable connection; cafés and public spaces are not allowed.

objective.question: Which practice is correct when preparing for an online proctored (OnVUE) AWS exam?
options: Run the Pearson VUE system test on the same computer and network you will use, and clear your desk and room
Use a work laptop with a corporate VPN and firewall turned on
Have a family member sit in the room to help with technical problems
Keep a second monitor connected so you can view notes
objective.explanation: The system test confirms that your webcam, microphone, bandwidth and computer work with OnVUE. Extra monitors, other people in the room and restrictive corporate VPN or firewall settings can stop or invalidate the session.

objective.question: Neha finished CLF-C02 yesterday. When should she expect her result and Credly badge?
options: Both arrive by post within 3 weeks
She must ask the proctor to email the result
The result is usually in her AWS Certification Account within 5 business days, and the Credly badge email follows after the result is released
The badge arrives first; the result follows a month later
objective.explanation: Results are usually available in your AWS Certification Account within 5 business days. The Credly badge email comes only after the result is released.

objective.question: Vikram passed SAA-C03 and has his 50% voucher. He now books DOP-C02 (USD 300) and uses the voucher. Assuming no taxes, what does he pay, and what does he get if he passes DOP-C02?
options: USD 150; a new 50% voucher for his next exam
USD 150; a free exam voucher
USD 300; the voucher only applies to Associate exams
USD 75; no further voucher
objective.explanation: The voucher takes 50% off the next exam, so USD 300 becomes USD 150. Each pass gives a new 50% voucher, so passing DOP-C02 earns another one, not a free exam.

subjective.question: Compare online proctoring (OnVUE) with a Pearson VUE test centre. How would you choose between them?
subjective.answer: Both are delivered by Pearson VUE, and the exam content and scoring are the same. Online proctoring lets me sit at home, often with more slot choices. It needs a private, quiet room, a clear desk, a working webcam and microphone, and a stable internet connection. I must pass the system test on the same machine and network. A proctor watches me throughout, and things like noise, someone entering the room or looking away can end the session. A test centre removes these risks because the room, computer and network are controlled. The cost is travel and fewer slots. I choose a test centre if my home has power cuts, shared rooms or weak internet. I choose online if I have a reliable private setup and want flexibility.
keyPoints: Same exam and scoring through Pearson VUE
OnVUE needs a private room, clear desk, webcam, stable internet and a passed system test
Test centre gives a controlled environment but needs travel
Choose based on the risk in your home setup

subjective.question: Explain the ESL accommodation process and why the order of steps matters.
subjective.answer: If English is not my first language, I can request the ESL accommodation, which adds 30 minutes to the exam. I request it in my AWS Certification Account and wait for approval. Only then do I book the exam. The order matters because the extra time applies only to exams scheduled after approval. If I book first, that appointment keeps the standard time. So CLF-C02 stays at 90 minutes instead of 120, and SAA-C03 stays at 130 instead of 160. If I booked too early, I would reschedule or cancel more than 24 hours before the appointment and rebook after approval, so I do not lose the fee. For a 180-minute Professional exam, the extra 30 minutes is very valuable because the questions are long scenarios.
keyPoints: ESL adds 30 minutes for non-native English speakers
Request in the AWS Certification Account and get approval before booking
Extra time applies only to exams scheduled after approval
Fix an early booking by rescheduling more than 24 hours ahead

subjective.question: How does AWS scaled scoring work, and what are unscored questions? What does this mean for exam strategy?
subjective.answer: AWS reports results on a scaled score from 100 to 1000. The pass mark is 700 for Foundational, 720 for Associate and 750 for Professional. Scaling keeps results fair across different versions of the same exam, which may differ slightly in difficulty. So a scaled score is not a simple percentage. Each exam also includes some unscored questions that AWS uses to test future content. They do not affect my result, and they are not marked, so I cannot tell which ones they are. The model is compensatory, so I pass on my overall score, not domain by domain. There is no negative marking. My strategy is to answer every question, never leave one blank, treat every question as if it counts, and not panic if some questions look unusual.
keyPoints: Scaled score 100–1000; pass at 700/720/750 by level
Scaling keeps different exam forms fair
Unscored questions exist and are not identified
Compensatory model with no negative marking, so answer everything

subjective.question: Interview question: Your AWS Solutions Architect – Associate certification expires next month. What do you do?
subjective.answer: First I check the exact expiry date in my AWS Certification Account. The certification is valid for 3 years from my pass date. To keep it active, I must pass the current version of the exam before that date. I would check the current exam guide, because services and domains change between versions, and plan focused revision on anything new. Then I would book early enough to allow for a retake. If I fail, I must wait 14 days and pay the full fee again, so booking in the final week is risky. I would also check my Benefits section for a 50% voucher from an earlier pass. I would confirm that my ID still matches my account name. After passing, my validity resets and Credly updates the badge.
keyPoints: Validity is 3 years from the pass date; check it in the account
Recertify by passing the current version before expiry
Leave room for the 14-day retake wait
Use an available 50% voucher and confirm the ID matches

subjective.question: How would you use the 50% voucher to reduce the cost of a certification path from Cloud Practitioner to Solutions Architect – Professional?
subjective.answer: Each pass gives a 50% voucher for the next exam, and it appears in the Benefits section of my AWS Certification Account. On a path of CLF-C02, then SAA-C03, then SAP-C02, I pay USD 100 for CLF-C02. Passing it gives me a voucher, so SAA-C03 costs USD 75 instead of USD 150. Passing SAA-C03 gives another voucher, so SAP-C02 costs USD 150 instead of USD 300. That is USD 325 instead of USD 550, before local taxes. The voucher saves the most on expensive exams. Some people therefore save one voucher for a Professional exam. I would check the voucher's expiry date and terms in the Benefits section. The voucher comes only from a pass, so it does not help with a retake after a failure.
keyPoints: Each pass earns a 50% voucher in the Benefits section
Example costs: 100 + 75 + 150 = USD 325 instead of 550
Use it on higher-priced exams for the biggest saving
Check the voucher terms and expiry; it is not earned from a fail

subjective.question: List your exam-day checklist for an online proctored AWS exam.
subjective.answer: The day before, I run the Pearson VUE system test on the same laptop and network I will use. I close VPNs and background apps, and I keep the laptop plugged in. I prepare a private, quiet room with a clear desk: no notes, phones within reach, or second monitors. I keep my government ID ready and confirm that the name exactly matches my AWS Certification Account. On the day, I start check-in early. Check-in needs photos of my face, my ID and my workspace. I tell family not to enter the room. During the exam I stay in camera view, do not read questions aloud, and keep my hands away from my face. I plan as though there are no breaks, so I eat and use the washroom before I start.
keyPoints: Run the system test on the exact machine and network
Private, clear room with no extra devices or people
ID name exactly matches the account name
Check in early and follow the proctor rules throughout

subjective.question: You failed an AWS Associate exam. Describe your recovery plan.
subjective.answer: First I read the score report in my AWS Certification Account. It shows my scaled score and which domains need improvement. Because scoring is compensatory, I focus on the weakest domains, which will lift my overall score fastest. I must wait 14 days before retaking, and I pay the full fee again because vouchers come only from passing. So I treat the retake as a fresh investment. I plan two to four weeks of targeted revision. That includes hands-on labs for weak services, rereading the exam guide and doing timed practice sets to fix pacing. I review why each wrong practice answer was wrong, not just what the right answer was. I book the retake only when my practice scores are steady, and I recheck ESL and ID details before booking.
keyPoints: Use the score report to find weak domains
Wait 14 days and pay the full fee for the retake
Do targeted hands-on revision and timed practice
Book only when practice results are stable

subjective.question: Why does the name on your ID matter so much, and how do you prevent problems?
subjective.answer: At check-in, the proctor or test centre staff compare my government ID with the name in my AWS Certification Account. They must match exactly. If they do not, I can be turned away, and I lose the exam fee. In India this often happens with initials, surnames written in different orders, or missing middle names. For example, the passport says 'S. Lakshmi Narayanan' but the account says 'Lakshmi Narayanan'. To prevent it, I choose the ID I will carry, usually a passport for consistency. I set my account name to match it exactly, letter for letter. I do this well before exam day, not the night before. I also check that the ID is valid and not expired, and that the photo is clear.
keyPoints: The ID name must exactly match the account name
A mismatch can mean being turned away and losing the fee
Watch for initials, name order and middle names
Fix it well before exam day using the ID you will carry

subjective.question: Explain the reschedule and cancellation rules and how they affect your booking strategy.
subjective.answer: I can reschedule or cancel without losing the fee only if I do it more than 24 hours before the appointment. If I miss that window or do not turn up, the fee is lost. That can be USD 150 for an Associate exam or USD 300 for a Professional exam. So I set a calendar reminder about two days before the exam. At that point I make a go or no-go decision based on my latest timed practice scores. I avoid booking during busy work weeks, festivals or travel. For online exams, I also rerun the system test before the 24-hour cutoff. That way, if my setup fails, I can still move to another slot or a test centre without losing the fee.
keyPoints: Change the booking more than 24 hours before to keep the fee
A no-show or late change loses the fee
Make a go or no-go check before the cutoff
Test the online setup early enough to switch if needed

subjective.question: How do you claim and use your Credly badge professionally?
subjective.answer: After my result is released in my AWS Certification Account, usually within 5 business days, I get an email from Credly to claim my badge. I accept it using the email linked to my certification. The badge shows the certification name, the issue date and the expiry date. Anyone can verify it through its public link. I add it to LinkedIn under Licenses & certifications and share the verification link. On my résumé, I list the full official name, for example 'AWS Certified Solutions Architect – Associate (SAA-C03)', with the date and the Credly link. Recruiters prefer a verifiable link to a screenshot. When I recertify, the badge updates, so the public record stays current.
keyPoints: The Credly email follows the result release
The badge is publicly verifiable and shows the issue and expiry dates
Add it to LinkedIn and the résumé with the official name and link
It updates after recertification

subjective.question: How would you manage time on SAA-C03, with and without ESL?
subjective.answer: SAA-C03 has 65 questions in 130 minutes, which is 2 minutes per question. With ESL it is 160 minutes, close to 2.5 minutes per question. I aim to finish a first pass with around 20 minutes left. I answer quickly when I am confident. For long scenarios, I read the last line first to see what is being asked, such as the most cost-effective or the least operational overhead option. Then I remove the clearly wrong options. If I am stuck, I pick my best guess, flag the question and move on, because there is no negative marking. In the review pass, I revisit only the flagged questions. I do not change answers without a clear reason. Practising timed sets beforehand makes this pacing feel natural.
keyPoints: 130 min = about 2 min per question; 160 min with ESL
Read the requirement first and remove wrong options
Guess, flag and move on; no negative marking
Leave time for a review of flagged questions

subjective.question: Interview question: How do you keep your AWS skills current between recertifications?
subjective.answer: The certificate lasts 3 years, but AWS changes every month, so I don't wait for the recertification deadline. I follow AWS What's New and the release announcements for the services I use. I read the Well-Architected Framework updates, because exam scenarios and design reviews are based on them. I do small hands-on labs in a sandbox account with budget alerts set, so I can try new features safely. At work, I apply new features when they cut cost or effort, for example moving workloads to newer instance families or managed services. When an exam version changes, I compare the old and new exam guides to find the gaps. This way recertification is a quick check, not a fresh start, and my day-to-day work improves too.
keyPoints: Follow AWS announcements and Well-Architected updates
Use a sandbox account with budget alerts for hands-on practice
Apply new features at work where they add value
Compare exam guide versions before recertifying

subjective.question: Describe your plan for the final exam week before an AWS certification exam.
subjective.answer: Early in the week I confirm the logistics. My ESL approval, if it applies, is done before booking. The booking is confirmed. My ID name matches my account. For online delivery, the system test has passed. I then do one full-length timed practice exam: 90, 130 or 180 minutes depending on the level, plus 30 minutes if I have ESL. I spend the next days reviewing the wrong answers and my weak domains from the exam guide, not learning new topics from scratch. Two days out, before the 24-hour reschedule cutoff, I decide whether to go ahead. The day before, I only revise lightly, prepare my room or travel plan, and sleep well. On exam day I check in early and stay calm.
keyPoints: Confirm ESL, booking, ID match and system test early
One full timed mock using the correct duration
Review weak domains; avoid new topics
Go or no-go decision before the 24-hour cutoff

subjective.question: A manager asks you to plan certification for a 10-person team over a year. What policies and risks would you explain?
subjective.answer: I would explain the rules that affect cost and schedule. Each person needs an AWS Certification Account with a name that exactly matches their ID, or they risk losing the fee at check-in. Non-native English speakers should request ESL before booking, because it applies only to exams scheduled after approval. Each pass gives a 50% voucher, so a path like Cloud Practitioner, then an Associate, then a Professional gets cheaper at each step. Failures cost the full fee again, with a 14-day wait, so I would budget for some retakes. Bookings must change more than 24 hours ahead, or the fee is lost. Certifications are valid for 3 years, so I would track expiry dates for each person and plan recertification on the current exam version well before they expire.
keyPoints: ID name match and ESL before booking for each person
Use 50% vouchers along the path
Budget for retakes at full fee and the 14-day wait
Track 3-year expiry dates and plan recertification

subjective.question: Written question: Explain the full lifecycle of an AWS certification, from account creation to recertification.
subjective.answer: I create an AWS Certification Account and make sure my name exactly matches my government ID. If English is not my first language, I request the ESL accommodation and wait for approval. Then I book through Pearson VUE, choosing online proctoring (OnVUE) or a test centre. I can reschedule or cancel more than 24 hours before without losing the fee. I sit the exam: 90 minutes for Foundational, 130 for Associate and 180 for Professional, plus 30 with ESL. Scoring is scaled from 100 to 1000, with pass marks of 700, 720 or 750. Results usually appear within 5 business days. After a pass, I claim my Credly badge and find a 50% voucher in Benefits. After a fail, I wait 14 days and pay again. The certification lasts 3 years, and I recertify by passing the current version before it expires.
keyPoints: Account set-up with an exact ID name match, and ESL before booking
Pearson VUE delivery choice and the 24-hour change rule
Exam lengths, scaled scoring and pass marks by level
Results, Credly badge, 50% voucher, 14-day retake and 3-year validity
